articles.title: An App Built for One: Why a Devpost Skill Pack Made Me Spec It Anyway

articles.body_html:
My wife lost her yellow book. So I built her an app.

TL;DR: Cuenta is a small app for my wife's wholesale bakery: count what's left on each cafe's shelf, build the delivery, print and email her branded invoice, and see who owes what. I built it for Devpost's Build With AI: Basics hackathon with their skill pack, which interviews you and writes the plan from your answers. The plan caught real problems before any code existed. It also carried one wrong guess all the way to the end, and only using the app caught it.

Last week E. lost her yellow book.

The yellow book is sacred. It holds all the secrets of her one-person wholesale bakery: her shelf counts for every cafe she delivers to, and her delivery numbers. The counts tell her what to bake. The delivery numbers become her invoices. When the book went missing, all of that went with it, and there was no backup anywhere.

We found it, eventually. (Note to self: Always double check under the front seat of the car.) But I kept thinking about how much of a small business can live in one notebook.

E. runs La Condesa Baking Company, a wholesale bakery in with four cafe accounts. Until now she counted products on paper, filled in invoice forms by hand, did the math by hand, and kept track of who owed her in her head. Net 30, paid by ACH.

So when Devpost opened Build With AI: Basics, a hackathon where you build a new project from an empty folder using their skill pack, I knew what I wanted to make. Something for someone I care about. And a chance to see if a guided process would help me avoid some of my usual costly mistakes.

Cuenta is Spanish for "count" and for "the bill." E. picked the name.

A few days earlier I'd built a tip calculator with Cursor in eight minutes, and ended that post with a question I couldn't answer yet: does that kind of up-front spec discipline hold on something with a real second layer, like state or a backend? Cuenta has a database, email, PDFs, and money that has to add up. This is that test.

earlgreyhot1701D / cuenta

Count, deliver, invoice and ledger app for a small wholesale bakery

Cuenta

Count, deliver, invoice, ledger for a wholesale bakery. Built for La Condesa Baking Company in Santa Barbara.

Live at cuentasb.vercel.app. The app sits behind a PIN, so the demo video below walks through the whole thing.

Demo video

One minute and thirty-nine seconds on the production app, with mock data: Count, Deliver, the invoice, Download PDF, Send email, the Ledger and the menu.

Built from an empty folder to a working app in about 20 hours, sleep included, using the Devpost Learn skill pack.

The problem

Eileen runs a wholesale bakery that serves four cafes. She counted what was left on each cafe's shelf on paper. She filled in her invoice forms by hand and did the math by hand. And she kept track of who owed her, and since when, in her head.

Why Cuenta solves it

Cuenta puts the whole route in one phone-first flow: count…


View on GitHub


What it does

Cuenta takes the yellow book to the cloud. Everything is built for her phone first.

Screen What it does
Count Pick a cafe, count what's on the shelf. Builds a history she can look back on. Planning only, it never touches an invoice.
Deliver Pick a cafe, enter what she dropped off. One menu, same prices for every cafe. Totals add themselves.
Invoice Her own branded invoice. Print it in the kitchen, download the PDF, or email it to the cafe.
Ledger Who owes what, what's overdue, mark it paid when the money lands.
Customers The four cafes and the menu.

The invoice had to look exactly like hers. It's her brand, the cafes know it and importantly keeping that design was absolutely essential to her.

The skill pack interviewed me

The Devpost Learn skill pack is six instruction files an AI coding agent reads, from 1-start to 6-ship. I ran it in Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, inside VS Code.

An app with one user is exactly the kind of build where I'm tempted to skip the planning and just start. The hackathon rules didn't let me. Every entry had to come out of the skill pack, planning docs included. I'm glad they didn't.

What surprised me is who asks the questions. I usually build with Kiro, where I write the spec and the agent works from it. The skill pack flips that. It interviews you, one question at a time, and writes the plan from your answers. Scope first, then the PRD (what the app does, screen by screen), then the spec (how it's built). I approved each document before the next one started.

The interview pushed back, and it caught things I would have paid for later:

  • The server clock. Vercel, where the app runs, keeps time in UTC. An invoice made at 5:30pm in Santa Barbara would have gotten tomorrow's date and the wrong invoice number. Caught in the spec.
  • Linked prices. If an invoice points at the current price of a flan, raising the flan from $4.00 to $4.25 rewrites every old invoice. Invoices now keep their own copy of every price, and every amount is stored in whole cents, so a total can't drift by a rounding penny. (A commenter on the Propina post, flatin.pt, pointed out the penny I'd left floating there. Cuenta counts in cents from the start.)
  • Two finish lines. My definition of done said "E. uses it for her business." My demo plan said "mock data on camera." The agent pointed out the demo could pass while the real goal failed. We split it into hackathon done and project done.
  • Count and invoice are different jobs. My scope draft implied the shelf count fed the invoice. It doesn't. Counting is for planning what to bake. Caught on paper. The 36 questions I wrote for E. before any of this were too many. A person running a bakery can sit through about 8 before her eyes glaze over, so I cut it to 8. Overkill is a real cost, and I'd rather plan for it than pretend it isn't there.

Claude Code flagged its own calls

Once the plan was approved, the skill pack split the build into 8 small slices, each checked before the next one started.

Every slice report from the agent ended with a section called "Calls I made that you should check." Decisions it made that the plan didn't cover, listed for me to approve or overrule. A discard prompt it added when you switch cafes mid-delivery. A darker pink for overdue text, because the brand pink failed the contrast check. Locking the cafe account on an existing invoice, because switching wasn't free.

I’ve never had an agent hand me its own decisions like that before. Normally an agent's judgment calls stay invisible until I trip over them. Here they came to me as a list, while they were still cheap to change.

The same thing showed up when it said no. On slice 7 a permission check blocked a production deploy, so the agent couldn't run the void test the normal way. It could have edited the database directly to make the test pass. It refused, because the point of the test was to go through the real Void button, and handed it back to me.

The build had three seats. Claude Code wrote the code. A second Claude chat wrote my prompts and checked the repo between slices. I directed, tested and decided.

Starting fresh on purpose

This was the first time I ended a long agent conversation on purpose.

I used to keep conversations going because I was afraid of losing context. Long chats get slower, cost more, and eventually compress themselves. Here, the context didn't live in the conversation. It lived in the files: scope.md, prd.md, spec.md, and a checklist with every decision written down. A fresh chat read them and picked up exactly where the last one stopped.

The skill pack says this outright: starting a fresh conversation between skills is fine, because the files carry context forward. I didn't believe it until I tried it. The docs aren't paperwork for the judges. They're the memory.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code

On day two I did a timed run by hand, the way E. would. I found two problems. Neither one was a bug.

The first was small. Sending an email takes 5 to 8 seconds while it builds the PDF, and the button didn't change. The code already blocked a double send, but it looked frozen. Now it says "Sending…" while it works.

The second was bigger. Every cafe had its own product list. E. has one menu, and any cafe can order anything on it.

The agent traced it. The scope, the PRD and the spec all said "each cafe's standing list." The code did exactly what the plan said. Eight slices and a passing end-to-end test, all checking the plan faithfully, and the plan was wrong.

Then we traced where the plan got it. Before I ever ran the skill pack, I wrote a planning brief with Claude. That brief looked at E.'s sample invoices, saw cookies on one cafe's invoice and not the others, and guessed that each cafe had its own list. An invoice shows what a cafe ordered that day, not what it's allowed to order. I brought that guess into the scope interview as if it were already decided, so the interview never asked E.

I think that's the lesson I'm keeping. The interview checks your answers. It can't check what you bring in. Checking against the plan can't catch a mistake in the plan. Only using the thing the way the real person does could.

The comments on the Propina post saw this coming. @mattbusel put it as "the thing that checks can't be the thing that built it," and suggested treating the spec as a hypothesis, not a contract. @vladzoff added that the builder should never get to edit the answer key. Cuenta's end-to-end test was written from the same plan as the code, so the two agreed with each other perfectly, and both were wrong in the same way. The fix went into the spec first and the code second, with a dated line in the checklist saying why.

I had a choice. A data patch (put every product on every cafe's list) would have taken minutes. The full fix (one shared menu, drop the per-cafe table, correct the docs) took longer. I took the full fix, a week before the deadline, because E. is the user after the video, and a sixth product shouldn't have to be added four times forever.

The 20% leaks earlier now

I told the skill pack at 1-start what I wanted to learn: my builds land at about 80% of what I imagined, and I wanted to find where the other 20% leaks.

I kept thinking of things after the fact. Again.

Late item Where it came from When
Counts separated by cafe Me, after seeing the design mockup before build
Paid by ACH, not check E. before build
Invoice numbering by cafe code and date E. PRD
Special order lines Me spec
Past counts (her paper book) Me build
4-digit PIN not safe Me build
Getting back from an invoice on a phone Me build
One menu, not one per cafe Me, testing by hand after build

Most of these lived in E.'s head, not mine. The rest showed up when I saw something concrete, like a mockup or the phone in my hand. Recognition beats recall. And on my full list of late items, seven were in the 28 interview questions I cut.

The difference this time is where they landed. Most landed on paper, or landed cheap. The interview didn't stop the 20%. It moved it earlier.

So, back to the Propina question. Does spec discipline hold once there's a database and money involved? Mostly. It held for everything that was written down as a decision. The one real miss was a guess written down as if it were a decision.

Things that went wrong anyway

  • Real data in the mockups. I used Google Stitch to sketch the screens from E.'s invoice. Stitch copied her kitchen address, phone and email straight into the mockups, and the first commit included them. The agent caught it, rewrote that commit and cleared it from git history before anything was pushed. AI design tools copy your reference data into their output.
  • The PIN. The app sits behind a PIN so E. doesn't need an account. The first version was 4 digits with no limit on guesses. I googled "is a 4-digit PIN safe?" and the answer was no. I added more digits for the PIN, with a lockout after too many wrong tries.
  • Fonts in the PDF. The PDF is made by a headless browser on the server, and that browser has no fonts. The spec missed it. The one spike we ran before building, a timeboxed test with a pass or fail answer, found it. It passed in 10 of its 60 minutes.
  • The video was too short. The first take of the demo was 59.9 seconds. The rules say 1 to 3 minutes. Re-took it at 1:39. We re-routed work twice. Nothing was fatal, because every slice was small and checked before the next one started.

The numbers

Moment When
Empty folder Sat Oct 17, about 4:30pm
Planning docs approved Sat, about 6:20pm
First commit Sat, 6:48pm
Slices 1 to 7 deployed Sat, by 9:51pm
Slice 8, full test passing on the live site Sun Oct 18, 10:45am
README live Sun, 12:37pm

About 20 hours on the clock, sleep included, and 30 commits. The full run on the live site, from counting a shelf to marking the invoice paid, takes 15.9 seconds when a test script drives it.

It runs on Next.js hosted on Vercel, a Neon Postgres database, and Resend for email.

Software for one person, with money in it

Two weeks ago I wrote about Le Voyage, a trip app I built for six people. Software so specific nobody would build a company around it, and that didn't need to become a business to justify existing. I also wrote that if an app like that ever moved money, I'd be having a very different conversation with myself.

Cuenta is that conversation. It's software for one person, and it doesn't move money, but it's how she gets paid. So it got the things a trip planner never needed: a multi-digit PIN with a lockout, invoices that keep their own copy of every price, a void that never deletes, and a paid hosting plan once it runs her business.

Is it micro SaaS, the small, one-founder kind of software business? Not today. There's one user, no subscription, and nobody paying. But E. knows a lot of chefs who are one-person shows, running their businesses out of their own yellow books. Looking at what's custom in Cuenta, it's mostly data: her brand, her numbering, her menu, her cafes, her terms. The core is the same for any small wholesale food business.

So I keep wondering whether that's 20 custom builds, or one small, predictable tool that feels custom to each of them. I'd like to hear what you think.

What it can't do

  • One PIN, no user accounts. It's built for one person.
  • For the first few weeks, every invoice email goes to her own inbox instead of the cafe, so she can check them before cafes get anything.
  • Products and cafes can't be edited in the app yet. That comes with the handoff.
  • No Excel export, no overdue aging report, no payment reminders. Stubbed for later.

Try it

Watch the 1:39 demo. Cuenta is my entry for Build With AI: Basics. The live app is behind E.'s PIN, so the video is the way in. The planning pages, the scope, PRD, spec and app map, are published from the repo, and every decision and wrong turn is in the checklist.

Next is my favorite part. Her menu, her cafes, her email domain and a new PIN are already in. Now E. starts testing Cuenta on real deliveries, and I listen to her first week and decide what to add, or not.

She lost the yellow book once. Now her counts and invoices live in the cloud, not in a notebook that can go missing.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect.

Built with AI assistance in October 2026. These tools move fast, so always check the source.

articles.title: Stop Shipping Marketing Pages Like Product Features
articles.description: A marketing page workflow should help your team launch campaigns, update messaging, and improve...
articles.body_html:
A marketing page workflow should help your team launch campaigns, update messaging, and improve conversions without turning every small website change into a development project.

Yet, in many B2B SaaS companies, updating a headline, adding a customer story, or launching a new landing page can require the same process as shipping a product feature. Marketing submits a request, engineering reviews it, priorities compete for attention, and a simple update waits in the backlog.

This usually happens because teams use one process for two different kinds of work. Product developers have roadmaps, technical tasks, and deadlines of their own. They need time to build and maintain the product, while marketing needs to keep the website and campaigns up to date.

Over time, this setup can slow down campaigns, delay conversion improvements, and leave marketing teams waiting for developers to make routine changes. It can also push teams toward quick fixes that lead to inconsistent designs, tracking issues, and extra technical work later.

A better marketing page workflow gives marketing more freedom while keeping engineering involved where technical skills matter. The goal is to make website updates easier to publish, safer to maintain, and easier to measure.

TL;DR

Stop shipping marketing pages like product features by creating a dedicated marketing page workflow with clear ownership, reusable components, the right publishing permissions, and simple quality checks.

Marketing should handle routine content and campaign updates through an approved process. Engineering should set the technical standards, maintain shared components, and review changes that affect security, architecture, integrations, or complex features.

Before a page goes live, the team should check its mobile layout, links, forms, analytics, SEO basics, and performance. This approach helps B2B SaaS teams launch campaigns faster without sacrificing website quality or reliability.

Why Marketing Page Updates Get Stuck in the Product Backlog

When marketing page updates follow the same process as product features, they compete for time with work that may have a higher priority on the engineering roadmap.

A marketing team might need to change a headline before a campaign launches, add a new customer story, or test a landing page. However, the request may wait days or weeks while developers work on product releases, bug fixes, and technical projects.

These delays affect more than publishing dates. A campaign may launch with outdated messaging, a useful conversion improvement may sit on hold, or a small change may miss its window entirely.

The issue often comes from the workflow, not the people involved. Marketing requests often compete with product work because engineering backlogs are built around product priorities. Developers need to protect their time for complex technical work, while marketers need a reliable way to make approved website changes.

A dedicated marketing page workflow helps separate routine website updates from product development.

It gives each type of work a clear path, with the right people involved at the right time.

For example, changing a headline should usually be a simple content update. Adding a new feature that connects to an application API may need engineering input. Treating both requests the same way creates extra work for everyone.

Marketing Pages Have Different Requirements From Product Features

Product features and marketing pages support different goals. Product teams focus on functionality, reliability, and user needs. Marketing teams focus on messaging, campaigns, lead generation, and conversion rates.

Those goals affect how each type of work should move through a team.

Area Product features Marketing pages
Main goal Improve the product experience Attract, inform, and convert visitors
Common changes Application logic, APIs, and user features Headlines, landing pages, testimonials, and campaign content
Priorities Product roadmap, customer needs, and reliability Campaign dates, messaging, and conversion opportunities
Publishing process Development, testing, and release Content review, quality checks, and publishing
Success measures Product usage, reliability, and retention Leads, conversions, engagement, and campaign results

These are common patterns, not fixed rules. A complex landing page with custom integrations may need substantial engineering work, while a small product copy change may be easy to publish.

The important thing is to match the process to the work. A marketing page workflow should let teams handle routine updates quickly while keeping the right technical checks in place for more complex changes.

Build a Marketing Page Workflow That Fits the Work

A useful workflow gives every website request a clear path from the first idea to the final results. It should also make ownership, review needs, and expected turnaround times easy to understand.

A simple process can include five stages:

  1. Request: Marketing explains the goal, audience, content, and deadline.
  2. Create: The team builds the page using approved templates and components.
  3. Review: The right people check the content, design, functionality, and tracking.
  4. Publish: An authorized team member launches the page and checks the live version.
  5. Measure: The team reviews performance and uses the results to guide future changes.

Not every request needs the same level of review. A headline change may only need a quick content check, while a new lead form could require testing, analytics checks, and an engineering review.

Clear ownership also prevents requests from getting lost. Marketing should know who prepares the page, who approves the content, and who can publish it. Engineering should know when a request needs technical review.

With these steps in place, a marketing page workflow becomes easier to follow and less dependent on ad hoc requests.

Give Marketing Reusable Components, Not Unlimited Freedom

Marketing teams need room to create pages that fit different campaigns. However, building every page from scratch can lead to inconsistent layouts, repeated work, and more maintenance for developers.

Reusable components offer a practical way to balance speed and consistency. These can include:

  • Testimonials and customer story blocks
  • Product comparison tables
  • Customer logo sections
  • FAQs and call-to-action blocks
  • Lead forms and contact sections

When the team uses approved components, marketers can assemble pages without rebuilding common elements each time. Developers can maintain those components in one place, making it easier to fix issues and improve the overall design.

Still, reusable components need clear rules. Teams should document which parts marketers can edit, what they can customize, and when a new component requires engineering support.

The right setup depends on the website platform and the team's needs. A content management system (CMS) with flexible page templates may offer enough control for routine updates. More complex pages may still need custom development.

The goal is to give marketing useful tools and clear boundaries, so the team can work independently without creating avoidable technical problems.

Set Clear Publishing Permissions and Quality Checks

A good marketing page workflow should explain who can edit, review, and publish each type of change. These permissions help teams move quickly while protecting the website from mistakes.

For example, marketers may be able to edit page copy and use approved components. Engineering may handle shared templates, JavaScript, complex integrations, and changes that affect security or site-wide behavior.

This setup keeps routine work moving while giving technical changes the attention they need.

Use a Simple Pre-Publish Checklist

Before publishing a landing page, check the areas that can affect visitors, conversions, and search visibility.

  • Content: Is the copy accurate, clear, and free of errors?
  • Mobile layout: Does the page work well on different screen sizes?
  • Links and forms: Do links, form submissions, and confirmation messages work?
  • Analytics: Do conversion events and tracking tools record the right data?
  • SEO: Are the page title, metadata, canonical URL, and indexing settings correct?
  • Performance and accessibility: Does the page load well, and can people use it easily?
  • Publishing safety: Can the team restore the previous version if something goes wrong?

For Google's guidance on making pages eligible to appear in search results, review the Google Search Essentials guidelines.

Not every update needs a full technical review. A small text change may need only a quick check, while a new form or custom integration deserves more testing.

After publishing, someone should check the live page to confirm that it looks right and works as expected. This final step can catch problems that were missed during review.

Measure Whether Your Marketing Page Workflow Is Working

A marketing page workflow should make publishing easier, but teams need a way to tell whether it is helping. A few useful measures can show where delays remain and whether the process is improving.

Start with the time it takes to move from a request to a live page. If routine updates still wait in the backlog, the team may need clearer ownership or a simpler approval process.

It also helps to track how often campaign deadlines are missed, how many issues appear after publishing, and whether forms and conversion events work as expected.

Conversion rates matter, too, but they need context. A page may attract more visitors while generating fewer qualified leads. Teams should look at campaign goals, lead quality, and tracking reliability alongside conversion numbers.

Use these results to improve the workflow over time. If content reviews cause delays, clarify who approves copy. If pages often break on mobile, improve the shared templates or pre-publish checks.

The aim is not to add more reporting. It is to understand where the process slows down and make the next update easier to ship.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a marketing page workflow?

→ marketing page workflow is the process a team follows to plan, create, review, publish, and measure website updates. It defines who handles each step, which changes need approval, and what checks must happen before a page goes live. A clear workflow helps marketing teams publish updates with fewer delays and fewer avoidable errors.

Why shouldn't marketing pages follow the same process as product features?

→ Marketing pages and product features have different goals, deadlines, and technical needs. Routine page updates often need a quick review, while product features may require development, testing, and release planning. A dedicated marketing page workflow helps teams publish campaign updates faster while keeping engineering involved in changes that need technical expertise.

How can marketing teams update website pages without depending on developers?

→ Teams can use a CMS, approved page templates, and reusable components to handle routine website changes. Clear publishing permissions and simple guidelines also help marketers understand what they can update on their own. Developers can then focus on shared components, complex features, integrations, and technical issues that need their attention.

What should teams check before publishing a landing page?

→ Teams should review the content, mobile layout, links, forms, analytics, SEO settings, performance, and accessibility. They should also confirm that the correct page version is live and that a rollback is possible if an issue appears. The depth of the checks should match the type and risk of the change.

Who should own a B2B SaaS marketing website?

→ A B2B SaaS company should assign clear responsibility for its marketing website. Marketing usually owns messaging, campaign priorities, and conversion goals, while engineering maintains technical standards and handles complex changes. A WebOps lead can connect these responsibilities, improve the publishing process, and help the website support the company's growth goals.

Final Thoughts

Marketing teams should not have to choose between publishing quickly and keeping their website reliable. A clear marketing page workflow helps them handle routine updates, launch campaigns on time, and test new ideas without sending every small request to engineering.

The key is to give each team clear responsibilities, provide reusable components, set sensible publishing permissions, and apply quality checks that match the work. Engineering can protect the technical foundations while marketing gets more control over everyday website updates.

For B2B SaaS companies, this is an important part of WebOps: keeping the marketing website useful, reliable, and ready to support business goals.

What website change is your team waiting too long to ship, and what would make that process easier?

articles.title: How I landed a dev job with no degree
articles.description: I don't have a computer science degree. I have a job writing software, and I've had one for a while...
articles.body_html:
I don't have a computer science degree. I have a job writing software, and I've had one for a while now. For about a year before that, I did almost everything you're "supposed" to do to make up for the missing degree — and I want to tell you that it worked, because then this would be a nicer story. It didn't. The things I did to compensate for not having a degree were a dead end, and the thing that actually got me hired had nothing to do with the degree at all.

Here's the part that took me far too long to understand: a degree is not the thing employers want. It's a stand-in for the thing they want. And I spent months building a worse stand-in instead of just handing them the real thing.

What I thought "no degree" meant (and what it actually meant)

When you don't have the degree, the whole world tells you the same thing: you have a gap, so go fill it. So I did. I collected certificates — the free ones, then the ones with a logo people recognize. I started a LeetCode streak because a forum told me that's how you prove you're "rigorous" like the CS grads. I enrolled in enough of a bootcamp to get a bootcamp line on my résumé.

Every one of those was me trying to build a replacement credential. A thing I could point at and say: see, I'm as legitimate as the degree. I was playing the degree's game, just with cheaper pieces.

And it got me nothing. Not one interview traced back to a certificate. Not one interviewer asked about my LeetCode. The bootcamp line never came up in a room where someone decided whether to hire me. I had spent months manufacturing proof of the wrong thing.

The rule: when you don't have the credential, the instinct is to build a substitute credential. That's the trap. A certificate is a weaker copy of a degree, and nobody was ever going to want your weaker copy of the thing they already don't fully trust.

The question the degree is actually answering

Here's the reframe that changed everything, and it's the whole article, so I'll say it plainly.

When an employer sees a CS degree on a résumé, they are not thinking "ah, four years of theory." They're a human being trying to de-risk a hire, and the degree answers exactly one question for them:

"Will this person take something hard and ambiguous, with no syllabus and no answer key, and actually finish it?"

That's it. That's what the degree buys. Four years of someone being handed vague, difficult problems and grinding them to completion whether they felt like it or not. The employer doesn't care about the compiler-theory exam. They care that you've got a track record of finishing ambiguous hard things, because that's the entire job, and hiring someone who can't do that is expensive.

The degree is a proxy for finish-ability. A decent one — which is why it works as a filter. But it's a proxy. And once I saw that, the move was obvious and it was not "get a better proxy."

The rule: you cannot out-credential a degree. You will always lose that fight. So don't have it. Skip the proxy entirely and hand them the thing the proxy only gestures at — direct, checkable evidence that you finish hard things nobody scoped for you.

A certificate is also a proxy for finish-ability — a much weaker one, because everyone knows a course is scoped so you can't fail. That's precisely why it carries no weight. I'd been trying to beat a strong proxy with a weak proxy. The answer was to stop competing on proxies and show up with the real signal.

What the real signal looks like

The real signal is embarrassingly simple to describe and genuinely hard to fake: something you built that a stranger uses and that broke on you and that you kept running anyway.

That sentence has three load-bearing parts, and a tutorial project has none of them:

  • A stranger uses it. Not you, not the instructor's spec — a person who does things you didn't plan for. A course project can't have this; the scope is fixed so you always win.
  • It broke. Real usage produces real failure. The todo app from a tutorial never breaks, because nobody's hammering it at 9pm on a Saturday with input you didn't imagine.
  • You kept it running. This is the finish. Not "I built it," which is the fun part, but "it fell over and I was the one who had to get up and fix it with no next-lesson button." That is the exact thing the degree was vouching for.

When you have that, the degree question doesn't just get answered — it stops being asked. Which brings me to the room.

The moment it actually stopped mattering

I'll give you the specific interview, because it's where the abstract thing became real.

Interviewer looks at my résumé, no degree line, and asks the question you're dreading — some polite version of "so, no formal background?" The old me would have gone into defense: listed the certs, mentioned the bootcamp, talked about how much I'd studied. Defending the weak proxy. It reads as exactly what it is — an apology.

Instead I said: "Right — let me tell you about the booking tool I built for a small business. It double-booked two real customers on a Saturday because of a race condition in my code, the owner called me, and I found it and fixed it that morning before they reopened." And I watched the question evaporate. We spent the next twenty minutes on the race condition. Nobody came back to the degree, because I'd just answered the only thing the degree was ever a proxy for, with a story that was checkable and specifically mine.

The rule: you don't win the "no degree" conversation by defending the gap. You make the gap irrelevant by answering — before they can even finish asking — the one question the degree was standing in for. A real war story closes that door in a sentence. A certificate reopens it.

The difference between "I studied this" and "this happened to me and I handled it" is the difference between a proxy and the real thing. One of them is a vibe. The other is checkable, and in the room, checkable wins.

The uncomfortable part: how I shipped enough real things in time

Here's the bit that stings, and I'd rather say it straight. You cannot produce that signal from reading. The signal only exists on the other side of shipped and used, and you need more than one, and you don't have four years. There's a brutal chicken-and-egg here: the evidence that gets you the job can only be made by doing the job, and nobody's employing you to do it yet.

The only way I got through it was to stop treating "build the app" and "understand the app" as the same task. I'd get something live as fast as I possibly could — real database, real URL, a real person able to hit it — and then go back and read it, break it on purpose, and rebuild the parts I didn't understand. Backwards from how courses teach it. It's also the only order that produces a real user, because a thing that's live is a thing that can break on you, and a thing that breaks on you is the only thing that generates a war story.

The rule: a deployed app with one real user teaches you more in a week than a tutorial does in a month — because the user does the thing you swore nobody would do, and now it's your problem with no answer key. That problem is the curriculum, and it hands you the exact fundamentals you need in the exact order you need them.

I learned more real fundamentals debugging that live booking race than in every course combined. The point was never "don't learn." The point is that the live app was the learning, and it also happened to be the evidence. One activity, both outputs.

If you're where I was

You don't need my exact path and you definitely don't need my mistakes. Stop manufacturing proof of the wrong thing and start manufacturing the right one:

  • Quit collecting proxies. One more certificate will not move the needle. You are not trying to look as legitimate as a grad; you're trying to make legitimacy irrelevant.
  • Pick something one real person actually needs. Not a clone. Your cousin's bookings, your own invoices, the spreadsheet your team is drowning in. Small and real beats big and fake, every time.
  • Ship it before it's good. A live URL with one user beats a flawless repo with none. Deploy embarrassingly early — the point is to get it into the hands that will break it.
  • Then go understand what you shipped. Break it on purpose. Read your own code like a stranger wrote it. That's where fundamentals finally stick and where the war stories come from.
  • Keep the war stories. Every "it broke and I fixed it" is a sentence that answers the degree question and out-performs your entire skills list in the room.

The degree gets people past some automated filters, and I won't pretend it doesn't — I got rejected by plenty of them. But filters aren't where you get hired. You get hired in the room, by a human de-risking a decision, and in that room the only thing that moves is evidence you can take something ambiguous, make it real, and keep it running when it breaks.

The rule: the fastest way to look like a senior while you're still a junior — and the fastest way to make "no degree" a non-event — is to have already shipped something that survived contact with a real user. You can't fake that. And you don't need a degree to have it.

articles.title: They Charge Me to Export My Own WhatsApp Contacts. I Shipped a Free Alternative in One Day 🔓
articles.description: Most WhatsApp export extensions stop at 10 to 30 contacts on the free plan. WAVault is free, open source and unlimited: contacts, group members, chats with media and statuses to Excel, CSV, vCard, Google and Outlook.
articles.body_html:
By Md. Habibullah Sharif — Full-Stack Engineer | CSE, Northern University Bangladesh

633 contacts in my WhatsApp Business account.
The "free" exporters let me take 10.
The other 623 had a price tag.

My own contacts. From my own account. Already loaded in my own browser tab.

And someone wanted a monthly subscription to hand them back to me.

The Paywall

My account had grown the way every long-lived WhatsApp account grows: years of phones, several synced devices, customers, suppliers, groups. 957 raw contact records for 633 actual people. I needed them in a spreadsheet.

WhatsApp has no export button. That part is well known.

So I checked the Chrome Web Store. Pages of exporters, polished icons, confident promises. I tried them one after another, and every one I tried followed the same script:

Free plan: 10 contacts. Some stretch it to 30.
Everything else: upgrade to Premium.

I build backends and data pipelines for a living. I know exactly what sits behind that "Premium" button: the data is already in the page's memory, and serialising it to CSV is a few dozen lines. There is no server cost to cover and no expensive API behind it. The paywall isn't covering a cost. It's a toll on your own data.

That was the part I refused to accept.

I closed the tab and started building. WAVault shipped the same day.

What You Get, For Nothing

WAVault is a free, open-source browser extension for WhatsApp Web and WhatsApp Business.

No premium tier. No contact limit. No account. No server.

It adds a dashboard to WhatsApp Web with four sections.

1. Contacts, every one of them

One row per real person, merged from the address book, chats and groups. 15 one-click lists:

Saved · Unsaved · Invite list · Chatted · Unread · Read · With username · Without username · Business · Personal · Group members · Hidden number · Blocked

Combine them with Any/Yes/No filters, WhatsApp Business labels and group membership. Search works across scripts (Bangla, Arabic, Hindi, emoji) and across number formats: +44 7700 900123, 07700900123 and 447700900123 resolve to the same person.

2. Group members

The member list of every group you belong to, with roles (Owner, Admin, Member). Excel output gives one sheet per group. This is the feature paid tools tend to lock hardest.

3. Full chat backup, with media

Whole conversations, loaded page by page, with photos, videos, voice notes and documents decrypted locally. The output is a ZIP with a folder per chat, an index page, and an HTML viewer that reads like WhatsApp itself: bubbles, replies, inline media, search. It opens offline, in any browser, on any machine.

4. Status downloader

Every current status, grouped by contact. Save one, or select many and get a ZIP with a gallery page.

Formats

Format Built for
Excel (.xlsx) Spreadsheets; numbers stored as text so + survives
CSV CRMs and tools; UTF-8 with BOM so non-Latin names render in Excel
Google Contacts CSV Direct import at contacts.google.com
Outlook CSV Outlook and Microsoft 365
vCard 3.0 / 4.0 iPhone, Android, iCloud
JSON Automation
Numbers list / HTML / PDF Quick lists, sharing, printing

The Architecture

WhatsApp Web exposes no public API for any of this. It doesn't need to: the data is already in the tab. The engineering problem is reading it safely, read-only, and without a single byte leaving the machine.

[Launcher tab / toolbar]
        │
        ▼
[Content script — React 19 dashboard inside a Shadow DOM]
        │   window.postMessage RPC (progress events, transferable ArrayBuffers)
        ▼
[Bridge script — injected into the page's main world]
        │   read-only calls
        ▼
[WhatsApp Web's internal modules: contacts, chats, groups, messages, media]
Decision Reason
WXT One codebase, native builds for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Firefox and Safari
Shadow DOM Full style isolation in both directions
Main-world bridge Content scripts run in an isolated world and can't reach page objects
postMessage RPC Typed requests, streamed progress, cancellation, binary-safe media
Custom .xlsx writer (~130 lines) A spreadsheet library would outweigh the entire extension
fflate Streaming ZIP, so large chat backups don't need the whole archive in memory

Permissions: web.whatsapp.com and storage. Nothing else. No analytics, no telemetry, no remote code.

Five Problems the Paid Tools Don't Talk About

Exporting ten rows is easy. Exporting everything, correctly is where it gets interesting.

1. One person, two identities

WhatsApp now assigns every user a private LID alongside their phone number. The same person can appear as …@c.us and as …@lid, and in many groups members appear only as a LID with the number hidden.

A naive exporter gives you duplicates and calls it a feature. WAVault first builds the full LID ↔ phone map, then folds the address book, chats, group participants and block list into a single record per person.

957 raw records → 633 real people. That number is the difference between a list and a clean list.

2. WhatsApp changes its internals without notice

Mid-build, the function that pages through chat history changed its signature from (chat) to ({ chat, msgCollection, ... }). Users update WhatsApp Web at different times, so both shapes have to work. The resolver tries each and caches the winner:

let loadEarlierStyle = null; // 'object' | 'positional'

async function loadEarlier(loader, chat) {
  const styles = loadEarlierStyle ? [loadEarlierStyle] : ['object', 'positional'];
  let lastError;
  for (const style of styles) {
    try {
      const r = style === 'object'
        ? await loader.loadEarlierMsgs({ chat, msgCollection: chat.msgs })
        : await loader.loadEarlierMsgs(chat);
      loadEarlierStyle = style;
      return r;
    } catch (e) {
      lastError = e;
      if (!(e instanceof TypeError) || loadEarlierStyle) break;
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}

Every internal access goes through one module with fallbacks. When WhatsApp moves something, WAVault reports which part is unavailable instead of failing silently. That design choice matters more than any single feature.

3. Media decryption expects instrumentation

WhatsApp's media pipeline now requires a performance-logging object on every download. WAVault logs nothing, so it passes a self-returning no-op that satisfies any call chain:

const noopLogger = new Proxy({}, {
  get: (_, key) => (key === 'then' ? undefined : () => noopLogger),
});

The then guard keeps it from being treated as a thenable. Verified against a live account: decrypted size matches the declared size byte for byte, JPEG header ff d8 ff e0.

4. Spreadsheets are hostile to phone numbers

Open a naive CSV in Excel and +447700900123 becomes 4.477E+11. Names in Bangla turn into à¦°à¦¹à¦¿à¦®. And a contact named =HYPERLINK("http://…") becomes a live formula on someone else's machine.

WAVault writes real .xlsx with numbers as text, adds a UTF-8 BOM to CSV, and neutralises formula injection while leaving genuine phone numbers untouched. Contact data is user-controlled input; it gets treated that way.

5. Your build artifacts can leak what git never saw

Firefox Add-ons requires a sources zip, and build tools zip the project folder by default, including local test output that .gitignore keeps out of the repo. A release built on a developer machine can quietly ship screenshots and logs from real accounts.

WAVault's build excludes every local artifact explicitly. Before release, every published file (git history and all four release zips) was scanned against the 1,111 real phone numbers in my own backup. Zero matches. Every screenshot here uses fictional data from number ranges reserved for film and TV.

💡 For anyone shipping a data tool: .gitignore protects the repo, not the artifact. Run unzip -l on every zip before it goes public.

Is It Safe?

  • Read-only. It never sends messages and never modifies chats, contacts or groups.
  • Local. No server, no account, no network requests of its own.
  • No automation. It reads what your tab has already loaded; it doesn't drive WhatsApp.
  • Auditable. MIT licensed, every line on GitHub.

It is an independent project, not affiliated with WhatsApp or Meta. Use it on your own account.

Install in Two Minutes

  1. Download the zip for your browser from the latest release and unzip it.
  2. Open chrome://extensions (or edge://, brave://), enable Developer mode, click Load unpacked, and select the folder. Firefox: about:debugging → Load Temporary Add-on.
  3. Open web.whatsapp.com and click the WAVault tab on the right edge.

Guides for every feature, including importing into Google Contacts, iPhone, Android and Outlook, are in the docs.

To run it without logging in, there's a demo mode with generated data:

git clone https://github.com/md8-habibullah/wavault-whatsapp-web-backup.git
cd wavault-whatsapp-web-backup
npm ci && npm run preview   # http://127.0.0.1:4789

Why It Stays Free

Your contacts were never a premium feature. They're yours.

Charging people to read data that already sits in their own browser is a business model built on the assumption that users can't see how simple the work behind the paywall is. Now there's a free, open alternative that does more than the paid ones, and anyone can verify every line of it.

WAVault will not get a premium tier. That is the one roadmap item that never changes.

Coming next: Chrome Web Store, Edge and Firefox Add-ons listings, incremental backups, and a Bangla interface. Issues and pull requests are open on GitHub.

If WAVault saved you a subscription, a ⭐ on the repo is how other people find it. And if you've hit the same 10-contact wall, tell me which tool in the comments.

This post was written with AI assistance and edited by me.

articles.title: Self-Hosted Vercel Alternative: Git Push to HTTPS on a VPS | Levelrail
articles.description: Self-Hosted Vercel Alternative: Git Push to HTTPS on a VPS   Levelrail is an open-source,...
articles.body_html:
Self-Hosted Vercel Alternative: Git Push to HTTPS on a VPS

Levelrail is an open-source, self-hosted alternative to Vercel and Coolify. You install one binary on a Linux server, connect a git provider, and every push builds and deploys your app behind automatic HTTPS, with preview environments for pull requests, logs, metrics and one-command rollback. It uses Apache 2.0, with one edition and no license key.

This post is the hands-on version. I will take you from an empty VPS to a deployed app on its own domain, then tell you plainly what Vercel still does better. I build Levelrail, so read the comparison sections with that in mind.

TL;DR

You want Levelrail gives you Where it stops
Deploy on git push Webhooks from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Gitea A native git push remote exists but is beta
HTTPS Built-in Caddy, Let's Encrypt behind one toggle The default certificate is self-signed until you turn that on
Preview deployments One per pull request, removed when it closes Per pull request, not per branch
Rollback One command, previous images stay pinned Only while the image still exists
Logs and metrics Stored on your node, searchable in the dashboard No visitor analytics
Edge network None Put a CDN in front if you need one

What you need

A Linux server with systemd and root access, amd64 or arm64. One vCPU and 1 GB of RAM boots the platform. Plan on 2 vCPU and 2 GB if you build images on the same box, which is where a $5 to $10 VPS starts to matter. Ports 80 and 443 must be reachable from the internet. A domain is optional at first, because Levelrail can hand out a free sslip.io address.

Self-hosted Vercel alternative: install it

Run the installer as root on the server.

curl -fsSL https://levelrail.com/install.sh | sudo sh

It checks the host, installs Docker if it is missing, downloads the newest release and verifies its checksum, starts a levelrail systemd service, and waits until the service is healthy. At the end it prints a dashboard link with a one-time setup token, plus a reminder to back up /var/lib/levelrail-data/master.key. Do that now. That key encrypts every stored secret, and nothing can recover it once you lose it.

Open the link, choose a password, and you are the admin. The install page lists the other options: a container, a pinned version, a source build.

Automatic HTTPS, with one honest caveat

The ingress is Caddy, embedded in the control plane. There is no separate proxy to run. Out of the box every domain gets a certificate from Caddy's internal issuer, so browsers show a warning. That is fine for a first look and wrong for anything public.

The first-run screen has an Enable HTTPS button that needs no DNS. It gives the dashboard a <dashed-ip>.sslip.io name and asks Let's Encrypt for a real certificate. From a terminal, the same thing is:

levelrail-cli settings ingress https enable --wait 2m
levelrail-cli settings ingress https status

Once HTTPS is on, sign in over the https address, because plain HTTP sign-in stops working. For your own domains, switch on real issuance with the Domains page toggle, or:

levelrail-cli settings ingress set --acme-enabled --acme-email you@yourdomain.com

The docs record one live Let's Encrypt run on a public VPS, including what failed before it worked. Renewal and wildcard certificates through DNS-01 are not yet verified in a live run, so check your certificates after the first renewal window. The details are in Domains and ingress.

Deploy from GitHub to your own server

Point the CLI at your first repository. Without --deploy, it only prints a plan: the build method, port, environment variables, volumes and any warnings. Nothing is created.

levelrail-cli import https://github.com/glincker/levelrail
levelrail-cli import https://github.com/glincker/levelrail --deploy --name web

If you are on your laptop rather than the server, run levelrail-cli login --device first. It prints a code that you approve in the dashboard, much like gh auth login. Use levelrail-cli import --help for the full flag list, including --port and --env KEY=VALUE.

Then watch it come up.

levelrail-cli apps status web
levelrail-cli apps logs web --follow
levelrail-cli open web

apps status lists the reconciler's conditions, and each condition carries a reason, so a failed deploy says why instead of retrying silently. A deploy only goes live after the new container passes its readiness probe. If readiness fails, the old container keeps serving.

Environment variables are one command, and --apply redeploys with them.

levelrail-cli env set web DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host/db --apply

Frameworks that inline variables at build time, such as NEXT_PUBLIC_* in Next.js, need them at build, not just at runtime. The Vercel migration guide walks through that trap.

Make every git push deploy

An import reads a public repository once. To deploy on every push, connect a git provider. This step happens in the dashboard on purpose, because each provider ends in a browser redirect to GitHub, your GitLab instance, Bitbucket or Gitea. For GitHub, open Settings, GitHub App, let Levelrail create the App, and install it on the repositories you choose. GitHub's flow needs a public primary domain, which the HTTPS step above already set.

Then link the repository to your app. This also registers the webhook.

levelrail-cli github-app use-as-source your-org your-app --app-name web --branch main

From now on a push to main builds and deploys. GitLab, Bitbucket and Gitea have matching gitlab-app, bitbucket-app and gitea-app commands. If you would rather deploy only on tags or releases, there is a trigger mode for that, and path filters keep a docs-only commit from rebuilding a service. A git push remote hosted on the server itself exists, but it is beta, so this tutorial sticks to webhooks. See Git integrations.

Add your domain

Create an A record for your domain pointing at the server's public IP, then attach it to the app.

levelrail-cli domains check web app.example.com
levelrail-cli apps domains add web app.example.com

If something does not load, ask the control plane instead of guessing.

levelrail-cli domains diagnose app.example.com

Diagnose runs a fixed list of checks with no AI involved: what three resolvers answer, whether the name points at this server, Cloudflare proxy detection, CAA records that block Let's Encrypt, ports 80 and 443, and the stored certificate. Each failure comes with a fix. Some the platform applies for you, some show the exact DNS record to create. Add --fix to apply the automatic ones. More in the domain doctor docs.

Preview deployments for pull requests

Previews are opt-in per app.

levelrail-cli apps previews enable web
levelrail-cli apps previews list web

With them on, opening a pull request deploys an independent copy named web-pr-<number>, with its own address of the form pr-<number>.<app>.<primary-domain>. New commits redeploy it in place, and closing or merging the pull request removes it. Levelrail posts a status and keeps one comment on the pull request, edited in place, with the preview URL. Previews copy the parent app's environment, and you can override single keys for previews only.

Two limits. Previews are stable on GitHub and beta on GitLab and Bitbucket. Pull requests from forks get no preview until you opt in per app, because a fork's code would run on your server. By default an app can have 10 live previews and the platform 50, with a seven day expiry.

Roll back, and see what happened 

levelrail-cli rollback web

That redeploys the previous successful release. Older images stay pinned so cleanup cannot delete a rollback target. Nothing rebuilds from an old commit, so a rollback takes seconds, not a build. Logs and metrics are stored on the node that runs the app, with request rate, errors and latency percentiles per app. The dashboard overlays deploy markers on the charts, so "did that deploy cause this" is a visual question.

Vercel vs Levelrail

Vercel Levelrail
Where it runs A managed cloud Linux servers you own
Git deploys and previews Yes Yes, previews per pull request
Rollback Instant One command to a pinned image
Edge network and edge runtime Yes No
ISR revalidation Yes No
Image optimization Built in No
Visitor analytics Yes No, request metrics only
Blob and KV storage Yes No, managed Postgres and Redis instead
Cost model Usage and seats The servers you rent

The full table is on the Vercel comparison page.

What Vercel still does better

If your app leans on the edge, stay. Vercel serves from a global network, runs middleware at the edge, revalidates static pages incrementally and resizes images for you. Levelrail has none of that. It runs your app in containers on the servers you pick, so a visitor far from your VPS pays the latency. A CDN in front of Levelrail closes part of that gap, but it is a part you assemble yourself.

Vercel also has years of production mileage and a team on call. Levelrail's single-server mode is labeled production ready, but multi-node, native git push and the previews for GitLab and Bitbucket are beta. The feature status page shows the evidence behind each label. If you move a real workload, run both for a week and keep DNS ready to switch back.

Where Levelrail wins is the bill. A flat server price does not grow with traffic or seats, and your secrets, logs and metrics stay on machines you control.

Coolify alternative: how Levelrail differs

If you already self-host, the question is usually Coolify. Coolify manages servers over SSH and has the broadest one-click catalog. Levelrail installs an agent on each node that dials out to the control plane over mutual TLS, so managed nodes need no inbound ports, and a reconciler keeps each node converging on its desired state. It ships about 360 templates, though only a sample is deployed end to end in testing.

The move is a read-only import.

levelrail-cli import platform coolify --url "$COOLIFY_URL" --dry-run

The importer reads apps, databases and settings from the old instance and never writes to it. It creates databases and volumes empty, so their contents do not move, and certificates, DNS and deploy history stay behind. Set the source token in APP_IMPORT_SOURCE_TOKEN. Dokploy and CapRover work the same way. See the Coolify migration guide and the side by side comparison.

Try it on your laptop first

You do not need a server to look around. With Docker running and the control plane binary next to the CLI, one command starts a private instance bound to 127.0.0.1, and apps appear at <app>.localhost.

levelrail-cli dev

It serves plain HTTP and is for trying things, not for hosting. When you move to a real server, levelrail-cli doctor runs one health check for Docker, disk, ports, firewall, DNS, certificates, backups and nodes, and levelrail-cli doctor --fix applies the safe fixes after asking you.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a self-hosted Vercel alternative?

Yes. Levelrail covers git deploys, preview environments, HTTPS, logs, metrics and rollback on your own Linux servers. It does not provide an edge network, an edge runtime, ISR or image optimization.

Is Levelrail a Coolify alternative?

It is one. The main differences are an agent that dials out instead of SSH, built-in metrics and log search, and identity features such as OAuth sign-in, IAM policies and an audit log in the free edition.

How much does it cost?

The software is free under Apache 2.0, with no license key. You pay for the server.

Does it work with Next.js?

Yes, as a container built from your Dockerfile. There is no Vercel importer, so you move the settings by hand.

Can I deploy from GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea?

Yes. All four providers support webhook deploys. Previews are stable on GitHub and beta on GitLab and Bitbucket.

Go deeper

  • Levelrail docs
  • Getting started: first app in about ten minutes
  • Self-hosted Vercel alternative, full feature table
  • Coolify alternative
  • Install Levelrail on a VPS in five minutes

Try it, and star the repo

The install is one command, and the repo is open. A star helps other people find it, and an issue tells me what to fix next.

glincker / levelrail

Free, self-hosted alternative to Vercel, Heroku, Railway, Coolify and Dokku. Push to git, get HTTPS, logs, metrics and one-click rollback on your own servers. One Go binary, no Kubernetes.

Levelrail

The lightweight, self-hosted alternative to Vercel, Heroku, Railway, Coolify and Dokku.
Push to git. Get HTTPS, logs, metrics and one-click rollback on your own servers.
One Go binary · Docker runtime · agents instead of SSH · observability built in · no Kubernetes


Website · Docs · Install · Production ready · Compare · Guides · Roadmap · Changelog · Discussions · Discord


Levelrail is an open source (Apache 2.0) self-hosted PaaS: a Vercel and Heroku alternative that runs on any Linux server you own, from a $5 VPS to a rack. It turns plain servers into a private cloud with Git deploys, automatic HTTPS, databases with verified backups, metrics, logs and alerts, without Kubernetes and without the monitoring stack you would otherwise bolt on.

Install in one command

Needs a Linux server (amd64 or arm64) with systemd and root. Docker is installed for you if…
