articles.title: Five witnesses and two RIRs: the CAs just discovered custody
articles.description: Baseline Requirements 3.2.2.9 makes multi-perspective issuance corroboration mandatory on Dec 15: five witnesses, two RIRs, a quorum — the custody grade, with a deadline.
articles.body_html:
A validation that depends on one network path is a validation that trusts whoever owns that path. The new Baseline Requirement says the quiet part in mandatory text: your witnesses must live where the attacker can't gang up on them. Five perspectives, two RIRs, one quorum — the custody grade, written into certificate issuance with a deadline.

Last week a commenter extended my authorship-grade framework with the concept it was missing: custody. A witness's real grade, they argued, is the minimum of its authoring path and its retention path — the canary screams at grade 1, but if the alert lands somewhere the accused can trim, the evidence you actually get to read is grade 3. Their amendment to my key-material rule: independence has to include "and preserved somewhere the accused can't write to."

I liked the formulation. Then Let's Encrypt went and wrote the same idea into a mandatory standard, with dates.

The news, as receipts

The announcement, five days ago, from Let's Encrypt staff:

  • Baseline Requirements 3.2.2.9, Multi-Perspective Issuance Corroboration, effective December 15, 2026. Any CA that cannot satisfy it MUST NOT issue.
  • The requirement: at least five remote network perspectives, falling within the service regions of at least two distinct Regional Internet Registries, with the quorum table satisfied.
  • Let's Encrypt's implementation: seven total validation requests — one from the primary datacenter, six from remote perspectives, up from four — and the primary plus a quorum of remotes must all see the correct challenge response.
  • Staging on October 27, production rollout November 10. "We expect little to no impact to users."

The stated motivation is protection against BGP attacks: an attacker who can hijack routing can intercept a domain-validation request and answer it themselves, from a network perspective they own. One perspective is one lie away from a fraudulent certificate. This is not theoretical — BGP hijacks against RPKI and CA validation have been demonstrated in the wild for years.

Why this is the custody grade, wearing a suit

Domain validation has always been a witness problem. When a CA checks that you control example.com, it asks the network: "serve this challenge token at this address." The answer arrives from somewhere. The question my framework keeps asking — who could have written this, and who can still erase it — maps one-to-one:

  • Authoring: the challenge response is authored at your web server (grade 1, if you control it).
  • Custody: the response travels a network path to the CA's vantage point. If an attacker owns that path — via BGP hijack, DNS poisoning, or a boundary filter — the CA reads whatever the attacker wrote. The observation was grade 1; the evidence the CA receives is whatever the path allowed.

A single-perspective validation has one witness, and that witness stands inside routing distance of the attacker. Fluffy's rule says its real grade is the retention-and-path minimum. Let's Encrypt's new quorum says the same thing in standards text: perspectives must be spread across at least two RIRs, because an attacker who can hijack routes in one region cannot — or at least cannot cheaply — hijack routes in two RIR footprints at once. The witnesses must live somewhere the attacker can't gang up on them. My amendment's clause, "preserved somewhere the accused can't write to," translated into network geography: corroborated from somewhere the attacker can't route to.

And the grade arithmetic is the same min() too. Seven requests fire, but the validation is only as strong as the number of perspectives that corroborate: if the quorum table demands four agreements and three come back wrong, the certificate doesn't issue. A corroborating perspective is a witness that says "I saw it too, from my vantage point." The certificate's validation grade is the floor of what its witnesses observed — not the number of requests the CA was polite enough to send.

The interesting part: this took a decade

Multi-perspective issuance corroboration is not a new idea. Let's Encrypt prototyped remote perspectives years ago; DigiCert and others have run multi-vantage validation internally; the research (from Princeton's CPV work onward) has been saying since 2018 that single-perspective validation is BGP-vulnerable. The Baseline Requirements vote happened this year. The deadline is December.

That gap — known since 2018, mandatory since December — is the normal latency of trust infrastructure, and it is worth staring at. The internet's evidence systems don't upgrade when the math changes; they upgrade when a regulator writes a table. The math has said "one witness is not a witness" for a decade. What moved was a requirements document with a date on it.

If you build agent systems, you have seen this exact pattern from the inside. Every one of us running a flight recorder has had the same conversation: the hash chain proves order and integrity, but who could have written the record, and where does it live? The CAs just answered it the way we do — witnesses, quorum, and geography the attacker doesn't control. No LLM in the loop, no anomaly detection, no cleverness. Five boring observers in two regions of the world, and a rule that says they must agree.

Run it yourself

The quorum is not a promise — it is countable, by hand, on your own infrastructure. Force a staging renewal and count the witnesses in your access log:

sudo certbot renew --dry-run --cert-name example.com
# then, on the origin that serves the HTTP-01 challenge:
sudo tail -n 5000 /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  | grep '/.well-known/acme-challenge/' \
  | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u | wc -l

Run it today and you will count four source addresses — the current primary plus three remote perspectives. After the October 27 staging switch (and --dry-run always talks to staging), the same pipeline counts seven — and piping the same list through a geo lookup shows them arriving from at least two RIR regions. That is the quorum, counted on your own hardware, before and after, no trust required. (DNS-01 users: the challenge never touches your HTTP log — do the count once with HTTP-01 or TLS-ALPN.)

What you actually get

  • Nothing to do, probably. If your certificates come from Let's Encrypt, the change lands in staging October 27 and production November 10, and the effect should be invisible. The one failure mode worth knowing: if your origin behaves differently per network region (geo-split DNS, regional WAFs), validation now watches from more vantage points — and you have until November 10 to make all of them answer correctly.
  • A receipts upgrade. Every certificate issued after November 10 carries a validation that survived a multi-region quorum. That is a custody property you can cite.
  • A template. The next time someone asks how your agent's evidence can be trusted, the CA industry has published the answer in standards text: independent witnesses, in geographies the attacker doesn't control, with a quorum, and no issuance unless they agree. Grade the witness, require the quorum, spread the geography. The rest is paperwork.

The DNS root key rotates on the eleventh of October. Certificate validation grows two witnesses by November. The trust chain is being re-anchored in front of us, one mandatory table at a time — and every one of those tables is somebody's custody grade, finally written down where the accused can read it.

Sources: Let's Encrypt announcement (Oct 14, 2026), Baseline Requirements 3.2.2.9 (effective Dec 15, 2026), Let's Encrypt staging Oct 27 / production Nov 10. The custody framing follows the comment thread on my last series.

articles.title: I'm 12. I Built an Ephemeral Cloud Platform on a $150 Phone (And Fought 10 Bugs to Win)
articles.description: AI coding agents can generate code in seconds. But provisioning a staging environment still takes...
articles.body_html:
AI coding agents can generate code in seconds. But provisioning a staging environment still takes 20–30 minutes.

The bottleneck isn't code generation anymore. It's validation.

So my CTO Akhouri and I built HYNA-Stage: a CLI that spins up isolated, ephemeral cloud environments in under 5 seconds using Firecracker microVMs.

Oh, and we built it entirely on a $150 Android phone using Termux.

The Skepticism

When I pitched this, Akhouri said: "Bro, my mind says yes, but I'm really confused."

I didn't argue. I proposed a 1-Hour Spike: "Just spin up ONE E2B container and kill it. If it works, we build."

He did it. The tech worked. But then, the real war began.

The Mess of Software

Building cloud infrastructure on a phone is insanity.

Pasting 500-line HTML files into Termux resulted in bash: !\': event not found. The code truncated. The UI clustered. My own security system (KAVLR) locked me out of my own files. I literally had to write Python scripts to bypass the cat alias I built to protect myself.

I spent two days staring at a broken screen, re-writing dashboard.html five different ways, only for Tailwind to fail to load, leaving the page as a giant, unstyled list. I coined the term "The Mess of Software" because it felt like the software was actively rebelling against me.

The 10 Bugs From Hell

  1. NPM Staged Publishing Limbo: Terminal showed + @hynaweb/stage@1.0.0, but npm install returned 404. I was stuck in a hidden review queue with a 0.0.0-stage placeholder. Fix: Bumped to 1.0.1 and republished.

  2. Supabase Case-Sensitive 404: CLI returned NOT_FOUND. Supabase logs were empty. The function was named Deploy-stage (capital D) but CLI called deploy-stage (lowercase). Fix: Renamed to lowercase.

  3. Termux Text Mutilator: Pasting large HTML files caused silent truncation. Tags merged. Scripts broke. Fix: Split code into 3-4 chunks and used Base64 encoding.

  4. Double Sign-In Ghost: User logs in, gets redirected, and hits a second sign-in modal. Fix: Removed the auth modal from dashboard.html and added strict session checks.

  5. The --key Parser Hijack: After adding --key for auto-injection, the down command crashed. Arguments shifted. Fix: Replaced argv[3] with a dynamic .find() function.

  6. Tailwind CDN Blackout: UI looked like an unstyled list. Tailwind failed to load on slow mobile networks. Fix: Hardcoded critical styles directly into HTML tags.

  7. Python Nested Quote Trap: Writing JavaScript backticks inside Python strings caused SyntaxError. Fix: Abandoned Python and used Base64 decoding.

  8. E2B 401 Unauthorized: Raw REST API calls failed. E2B requires complex gRPC protocol. Fix: Installed @e2b/sdk in the Edge Function to handle authentication.

  9. Logo Black Box Artifact: The logo had a dark rectangle behind it. Fix: Generated a true transparent PNG with hardcoded dimensions.

  10. The Cloud Wars: Fly.io blocked at 0/0 machines. Railway timed out. Vercel failed. Fix: Pivoted to E2B + Supabase Edge Functions.

The Breakthrough

I realized I was overcomplicating it. We moved the entire E2B logic into a Supabase Edge Function (Deno). We hid the secret E2B_API_KEY on the server. We made the CLI dumb: just send an API key, get a URL back.

I ran npm version patch. I ran npm publish --access public.

I opened Termux, held my breath, and ran:

hyna-stage up --key=hyna_xc5ub3l52qh

The screen printed:

  Initializing HYNA-Stage...
  Spinning up cloud environment...

✅  Environment is LIVE!
🔗  URL: https://8000-iv5bpiuyiaa5k389orokz.e2b.app

I stared at the screen. A real, live Linux server, running in the cloud, spun up from a $150 Android phone on a dropping 4G connection.

The Kill Switch

The final test was terrifying. I typed hyna-stage down i86qheh2t5dd53l4akrd9.

The terminal printed:

🗑️   Destroying sandbox...
✅  Environment destroyed successfully.

I refreshed the dashboard. It was gone. The Firecracker microVM was dead. Compute cost: zero.

The Stats

  • E2B cold start: 150–200ms
  • Supabase Edge Function: 42ms (97% faster than baseline)
  • Total provisioning time: <5 seconds
  • Hardware cost: $150
  • Coffee consumed: 0 (I'm 12)

Try It Yourself

We are live and open source.

  • Install: npm install -g @hynaweb/stage
  • Dashboard: https://hyna-stage.netlify.app

To the builders out there: Don't fall in love with your first idea. Fall in love with the problem. Validate the tech. And don't be afraid to fight 10 bugs to win.

We are HYNAWEB. We don't just build apps; we build the infrastructure for the AI era. 🐯☁️🚀

articles.title: Stop Formatting Currency With Regex. `Intl.NumberFormat` Does It.
articles.description: A hand-rolled formatMoney() with toFixed() and a comma regex looks fine in a US demo and quietly breaks the moment a real user, a negative balance, or a non-dollar locale shows up. Intl.NumberFormat has handled all of it, built into every modern browser, since before most teams' codebases existed.
articles.body_html:
Open any finance dashboard's test suite and there's a decent chance you'll find a function like this, usually written once, two years ago, by someone who is no longer on the team:

function formatMoney(amount) {
  return '$' + amount.toFixed(2).replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, ',');
}

It passes its tests. formatMoney(1234.5) returns "$1,234.50", which is exactly what the ticket asked for. Nobody has touched it since, because it works — until a refund comes through as a negative number, or a stakeholder asks for a per-unit cost that needs four decimal places, or the company opens an EU region and legal asks why every price shows up with a comma where European customers expect a period.

None of those are edge cases. They're Tuesday.

The fix everyone reaches for: patch the regex

The usual response to "it broke for amount X" is to patch the one case that broke:

function formatMoney(amount) {
  const sign = amount < 0 ? '-' : '';
  const fixed = Math.abs(amount).toFixed(2);
  return sign + '$' + fixed.replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, ',');
}

That fixes negatives. It does not fix the next report, four decimal places: formatMoney(1234.5678) still runs the same comma-grouping regex across the entire string, digits after the decimal point included — so instead of "$1,234.5678" it can silently insert a comma inside the fractional part too, because the regex has no idea where the decimal point is relative to its own grouping. And none of this touches the actual question underneath the ticket: a German user doesn't want "1,234.50" at all. They want "1.234,50" — comma and period swapped — followed by a € with a non-breaking space in front of it, not a $ in front with no space. A regex built around US formatting conventions can't produce that output by patching cases one at a time, because it never encoded "how do numbers look in Germany" in the first place. There's no case to patch for that; the whole function is missing the concept.

What's actually going on: formatting money needs locale data, not string surgery

Grouping separators, decimal marks, digit counts, and where the currency symbol sits relative to the number are not a style choice JavaScript can derive from an amount — they're a property of the locale, shipped as data in every browser:

Locale 1234.5 formatted as EUR
en-US €1,234.50
de-DE 1.234,50 €
fr-FR 1 234,50 €

Same number, same currency, three genuinely different strings — none of them wrong, none of them producible by one regex. That's the part a hand-rolled formatter can't cover without reimplementing a chunk of CLDR, the Unicode Consortium's locale database, which is exactly what Intl.NumberFormat already did, in every JS engine, years ago:

new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', {
  style: 'currency',
  currency: 'EUR',
}).format(1234.5);
// "1.234,50 €"

One constructor call, the correct separators, the correct symbol placement, for a locale the author of the regex has never had to think about. Swap the first argument and everything downstream follows:

new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' }).format(1234.5);
// "$1,234.50"

new Intl.NumberFormat('fr-FR', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(1234.5);
// "1 234,50 €"

And the negative-number bug the regex needed a patch for is just... handled, because the formatter understands "negative" as a concept, not a leading character to tape on:

new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' }).format(-1234.5);
// "-$1,234.50"

The options that cover the rest of the tickets

Currency is the headline feature, but the same formatter answers most of the other tickets that end up patched into a regex over time:

Compact numbers, for a "1.2K followers" style display, without writing a >= 1000 ? ... : ... ladder:

new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { notation: 'compact' }).format(1234567);
// "1.2M"

Signed deltas, for a dashboard showing "+5.2%" on a good day and "-5.2%" on a bad one — signDisplay: 'exceptZero' adds the sign everywhere except an exact zero, which is usually the one case a hand-rolled version gets wrong first:

new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'percent', signDisplay: 'exceptZero' }).format(0.052);
// "+5%"
new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'percent', signDisplay: 'exceptZero' }).format(0);
// "0%"

Units, for "12 km" or "3.5 hr" without hand-building a suffix map:

new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'unit', unit: 'kilometer' }).format(12);
// "12 km"

All of it reads the user's own locale by default — new Intl.NumberFormat() with no locale argument uses the runtime's configured locale, which in a browser generally matches what navigator.language reports — so a page doesn't even need to hardcode which country it's formatting for.

The one real gotcha: construct it once, not per row

Intl.NumberFormat resolves a locale's rules when it's constructed, and that resolution is generally understood to be the heavier step compared to calling .format() on an already-built instance — which is why the common recommendation is to build the formatter once and reuse it, rather than constructing one per row inside a render loop:

// slow: builds a new formatter 10,000 times
rows.map(r => new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' }).format(r.amount));

// fast: one formatter, reused for every row
const money = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
rows.map(r => money.format(r.amount));

Same output, one constructor call instead of ten thousand. This is the detail that actually shows up in a profiler on a long table — not whether Intl.NumberFormat is "slower than a regex" in the abstract, but whether you're paying its setup cost once or on every single row.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Delete the helper

The regex-based formatMoney() isn't a bad instinct — it's solving a problem that feels like string manipulation because the output is a string. But the actual problem is locale data, and that's not something worth re-deriving one bug report at a time when the platform has shipped a correct, fast, built-in answer since before most teams' codebases existed.

Next price, percentage, or "12.3K views" you're tempted to hand-format: what locale is it actually for, and have you checked what Intl.NumberFormat does with it before reaching for .toFixed()?

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

📚 Read next

  • addDays() Mutated a Date Three Components Away From Where I Called It
  • You're truncating bios with .slice(). Intl.Segmenter knows where the emoji actually end.
  • You're installing date-fns for 'X hours ago'. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does it natively.

🚀 Want more like this? Every guide, playground, and quiz lives on bestpractic.org — open it and sign up free so the next one finds you.

articles.title: Your API Timed Out. Did the Payment Still Go Through?
articles.description: A customer clicks Pay.  The screen keeps loading. Then an error appears:  “Request timed out. Please...
articles.body_html:
A customer clicks Pay.

The screen keeps loading. Then an error appears:

“Request timed out. Please try again.”

They click again.

Now there are two requests—and potentially two charges.

Disabling the button helps with accidental clicks. But what happens when the network fails, the page reloads, or a background job retries?

Every developer building payments, bookings, or orders should understand this problem.

1. A timeout doesn’t mean the operation failed

Imagine this sequence:

  1. Your server receives a payment request.
  2. The payment provider processes it.
  3. The response gets lost.
  4. Your server reports a timeout.

The customer may already have been charged.

A timeout means you didn’t receive a response in time. The outcome may still be unknown. AWS explicitly highlights this distinction in its guidance on retries.

Immediately starting a new payment could repeat an action that already succeeded.

2. Give each operation an identity

This is where idempotency helps.

In plain English:

Repeating the same operation should have the same intended effect as performing it once.

An idempotency key identifies a particular operation:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 8d5f8ba2-41c9-4a82-a4a2-820897f483f1

If that request times out, retry the same operation with the same key.

Generate a new key for a genuinely new operation.

The key is an identifier. Your backend—or the API you call—must implement the behavior that makes retries safe.

3. Handle duplicates on the server

A typical implementation needs to:

  • Associate the key with the authenticated customer and operation.
  • Store a fingerprint of the request parameters.
  • Claim the key atomically so simultaneous requests cannot both start the work.
  • Track whether the operation is processing or completed.
  • Return the stored outcome when a completed operation is retried.

If the same key arrives with different parameters, reject it.

If the original operation is still processing, return a documented processing response or conflict instead of starting it again.

A “check whether it exists, then insert” sequence alone can race. Use database constraints and appropriate transactions to protect local changes.

4. Protect the payment provider call too

Your database transaction cannot roll back a charge made by an external provider.

Suppose the provider processes the payment, but your server crashes before saving the result. Your local record may still say “processing.”

Use the provider’s idempotency support with a stable key for that payment attempt. Stripe, for example, supports retrying requests using the same idempotency key. Its exact behavior and retention rules are documented in its API reference.

Also provide a recovery path: retrieve the payment’s status or reconcile it through verified webhook events.

While the outcome is uncertain, show “Checking payment status” instead of inviting the customer to start another payment.

5. Retry carefully

Even a safe retry can add load to a struggling service.

For retryable failures:

  • Limit the number of attempts.
  • Increase the delay between attempts.
  • Add randomness to spread requests out.
  • Follow the provider’s retry guidance.

This is called exponential backoff with jitter. It helps prevent many clients from retrying at the same moment.

Don’t blindly retry every error. Invalid input needs correction.

6. Test the uncomfortable cases

Before shipping, test:

  • Two simultaneous requests with the same key.
  • A successful operation whose response is lost.
  • A server crash after the provider succeeds.
  • The same key with a different amount.
  • A repeated webhook event.

For a payment, verify that retries produce one intended charge and a consistent local record.

Apply the same thinking to orders, reservations, credit deductions, and other actions that should not happen twice.

The question to ask before adding a retry

“If the first attempt succeeded but I never received the response, what will this second attempt do?”

If the answer is “charge again,” “book again,” or “deduct again,” the retry needs more work.

A reliable API needs a clear answer for both success and uncertainty.

Have you ever dealt with a duplicate payment, order, or background job? What caused it?

articles.title: Next.js 16.3 Instant Navigations: How Partial Prefetching Works
articles.description: Next.js 16.3 shipped Instant Navigations: Partial Prefetching plus the App Shell. Learn the model, the Suspense gotcha, and a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You add a <Suspense> boundary around the slow part of a page, ship it, and client-side navigations into that route still show a blank screen for a beat before anything renders. The boundary is real. It works on the first load. It does nothing on a click.

This is written against Next.js 16.4.2 (verified against the framework's own GitHub release notes and documentation as of October 2026). The fix for the scenario above was shipped as a named feature in 16.3: Instant Navigations, built on two pieces — Partial Prefetching and the App Shell — and it is this series' first look at either.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a <Suspense> boundary that works on a full page load can be silently skipped during a client-side navigation
  • Turn on Partial Prefetching and read what the App Shell actually contains
  • Place your Suspense boundaries where Partial Prefetching can use them
  • Use ensureStatic and the instant dev-time validation to catch a slow navigation before a user does
  • Adopt the feature incrementally instead of flipping one global switch on a large app

Who this is for: you're comfortable with the App Router, Server Components, and basic <Suspense> usage. If you haven't met "use cache", cacheLife(), or cacheTag() yet, this series' Cache Components Explained covers them — Partial Prefetching is built directly on top of Cache Components and requires it to be enabled.

Contents

  • Why your Suspense boundary doesn't help on a click
  • The mental model: three navigation stages
  • Turning it on and reading the App Shell
  • Moving the Suspense boundary to where it counts
  • Per-link prefetching, ensureStatic, and validation
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

Why your Suspense boundary doesn't help on a click

Say you have a dashboard with a shared layout — a sidebar and header that are the same on every route — and a /reports/[id] page whose data takes a second or two to load:

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx — the wrong way
export default async function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params
  const report = await getReport(id) // slow — hits the database directly
  return <ReportView report={report} />
}

You already know the textbook fix: wrap the slow part in <Suspense> so the rest of the page can render while it loads.

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx — looks fixed
export default async function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<ReportSkeleton />}>
      <Report id={id} />
    </Suspense>
  )
}

async function Report({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const report = await getReport(id)
  return <ReportView report={report} />
}

Load /reports/42 directly in the browser and this works exactly as expected: the skeleton appears instantly, the report streams in behind it. But click a <Link href="/reports/42"> from the dashboard's sidebar, and the navigation still pauses — no skeleton, just a delay, then the whole thing appears at once.

The Suspense boundary isn't broken. It's in the wrong place for what just happened. A direct page load renders the whole tree from the root layout down, so the boundary catches the slow Report component exactly as written. A client-side navigation only re-renders what's below the layout segments the destination shares with the current page — the sidebar and header aren't remounted, so nothing above them runs again either. If nothing has told the App Router what to show for the parts of /reports/42 that aren't yet known, there's no shell to paint immediately, and the Suspense fallback never gets its moment on screen.

That's the actual problem Instant Navigations exists to solve: giving the App Router a per-route, prerendered shell to show the instant you click — before the server has even started rendering the parts that depend on the URL.

The mental model: three navigation stages

The mental model: with Partial Prefetching enabled, a navigation isn't one request — it's three separate moments when server-rendered output becomes available to the browser, and each one is cacheable differently.

  1. The App Shell. A per-route prerender containing everything in that route that doesn't depend on URL data — the parts of /reports/[id] that look the same whether id is 42 or 7. This is computed once, like a static page, and served instantly. If a piece of content is cached ("use cache") with a stale time of at least five minutes, it's folded into the shell too; a route that reads cookies or headers gets its session-specific shell cached per session rather than per request.
  2. The per-link prefetch. When a <Link> is hovered, focused, or enters the viewport, the browser can additionally fetch data that does depend on the URL — the actual report with id: 42 — ahead of the click, so it's often already in hand by the time the user commits.
  3. The navigation itself. Whatever wasn't covered by stages 1 and 2 — genuinely request-time work — streams in now, behind whatever Suspense boundary you've placed around it.

Before this feature existed, a <Link> prefetch was all-or-nothing: either the whole destination page was fetched ahead of time (expensive, and wrong for personalized content), or nothing was, and the user waited for everything on click. Partial Prefetching turns that into a staged handoff: shell now, URL-specific data soon, truly dynamic content last — each stage painting something real instead of a spinner.

This is also why the Suspense boundary from the previous section didn't fire: it was in the tree, but without a shell to render immediately around it, there was nothing for the browser to show before the boundary resolves. Fix the shell, and the fallback gets its chance again.

Turning it on and reading the App Shell

Partial Prefetching requires Cache Components (the previous episode in this series covers that feature on its own). Both flags live in next.config.ts:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

Key concept: Both flags are opt-in — create-next-app's default next.config.ts ships empty, with neither flag set. Whether your project is brand new or years old, this is the one-time step; the rest of the article assumes it's done.

Turning the flag on changes what a default <Link> does, with no other code changes required. Before, <Link href="/reports/42"> either prefetched the full page or nothing. After, it prefetches that route's App Shell by default — the sidebar, header, and anything else that doesn't depend on id. Setting prefetch={true} explicitly on a given <Link> goes further: it also resolves that link's URL data (params, searchParams) ahead of the click, at the cost of one extra server round-trip per link, which is why it's opt-in rather than the default for every link on a page.

// prefetch={true} resolves this link's own URL data ahead of the click —
// worth it for a handful of links, expensive for a long list
<Link href={`/reports/${id}`} prefetch={true}>{title}</Link>

Moving the Suspense boundary to where it counts

Go back to the dashboard from the first section. The fix isn't a new API — it's placing the existing <Suspense> boundary so the App Shell can be built around it, and caching the parts that qualify:

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx — the Instant Navigations way
export default async function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  return (
    <>
      <ReportHeader /> {/* doesn't depend on id — joins the App Shell */}
      <Suspense fallback={<ReportSkeleton />}>
        <Report paramsPromise={params} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  )
}

async function Report({ paramsPromise }: { paramsPromise: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await paramsPromise // reading params here, inside Suspense
  const report = await getReport(id)
  return <ReportView report={report} />
}

The change that matters is subtle but load-bearing: params is awaited inside the component wrapped by <Suspense>, not in the page component above it. Resolving params outside the boundary pulls URL-dependent work above the shell, so there's nothing left for the shell to serve statically. With it inside, ReportPage itself has no dependency on id at all — it's eligible for the App Shell — and the fallback has a real reason to appear: the shell paints immediately, then Report streams in once getReport resolves.

If getReport reads from a cacheable source, add "use cache" to shrink what's left to stream:

async function getReport(id: string) {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('minutes') // keep this under the 5-minute floor and it won't join the shell
  return db.reports.findById(id)
}

Per-link prefetching, ensureStatic, and validation

Two more pieces round out the picture, plus the path for adopting this on a codebase you didn't build from scratch.

ensureStatic, a route segment config export, asserts that a link's App Shell — and optionally its per-link prefetch too — is actually static, rather than silently degrading. Its values are 'auto' (the default, same as omitting it), 'shell', 'prefetch', 'navigation', and false: 'shell' requires the App Shell to be static, 'prefetch' requires the App Shell and per-link prefetch to be static, 'navigation' requires the entire server-rendered route to be static, and false opts a segment out of a stricter level a parent segment would otherwise impose:

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx
export const ensureStatic = 'shell'

ensureStatic only works with Cache Components enabled — without cacheComponents: true in next.config.ts, the build fails rather than the export silently doing nothing.

Dev-time validation runs automatically once Partial Prefetching is enabled: Next.js flags a route whose navigation would block on uncached work, points at the missing Suspense boundary, and suggests the fix — exactly the mistake in this article's first example. The Navigation Inspector in Next.js DevTools freezes the page at its initial loading state so you can see precisely what the shell shows before anything streams, which is otherwise too fast to eyeball. If a route is still mid-migration and you want to silence validation for it deliberately, export instant = false from that segment; sibling routes keep being checked.

Adopting incrementally matters on anything larger than a toy app: rather than flipping partialPrefetching: true globally on day one, set export const prefetch = 'partial' on individual page/layout files first, fix what validation flags route by route, then turn on the global flag and run the official codemod to remove the now-redundant per-route exports:

npx @next/codemod@canary remove-partial-prefetch ./app

Edge cases and gotchas

  • "use cache: private" never joins the shell. It caches in the browser only, which is inherently per-user — there's nothing stable to prerender into a shared shell.
  • The five-minute floor is real. Cached content needs a stale time of at least five minutes to be folded into the App Shell; shorter-lived caches still work, they just stream instead of shipping with the shell.
  • A route that reads cookies or headers still gets a shell — it includes the session-specific data rather than being excluded outright, which is easy to assume incorrectly if you've only read about the URL-data rule.
  • router.prefetch() doesn't expose <Link>'s prefetch-depth options. Its public API takes only an onInvalidate callback, not a way to ask for the App Shell versus the fuller per-link prefetch. Reach for it to warm a route outside the viewport, not as a drop-in replacement for a specific <Link prefetch={...}> setting elsewhere on the same route.
  • This is additive to Cache Components, not a replacement. If a route isn't eligible for Cache Components (it has no cacheable or static content at all), Partial Prefetching has nothing to build a shell from, and the navigation behaves as it did before.
  • forbidden() and unauthorized() are still experimental in 16.4. Both remain gated behind the experimental authInterrupts flag and the API reference still marks them as experimental, unchanged since their v15.1.0 introduction. Don't build a 16.4 auth flow around them as if they were final APIs yet.

Best practices

Reach for Partial Prefetching when your app has shared chrome (nav, header, sidebar, filters) that's identical across many routes, and at least some of each route's content is cacheable or genuinely static — the bigger the gap between "shared chrome" and "per-URL data," the more a shell buys you.

Adopt it per-route first, not globally, on anything beyond a small app. The per-segment prefetch = 'partial' export plus the dev validation gives you a route-by-route migration with immediate feedback, instead of flipping one flag and triaging every broken navigation at once.

Avoid it when a route's output is almost entirely user- or request-specific — a live chat thread, a real-time dashboard — where there's little to nothing left for a shell to usefully prerender. The dev-time warning for "Partial Prefetching isn't configured" is a nudge, not a mandate; some routes are correctly dynamic end to end.

FAQ

Do I need Cache Components to use Partial Prefetching?

Yes. Partial Prefetching builds the App Shell out of the same static and cached content that Cache Components makes possible. Enable cacheComponents: true first; partialPrefetching: true has nothing to work with otherwise.

Why didn't my <Suspense> boundary show its fallback during navigation before I made this change?

Because client-side navigations only re-render the parts of the tree below the layout segments shared with the current page. Without a prerendered shell, there's nothing to display instantly above your boundary, so the fallback never gets a chance to appear before the real content arrives — which is exactly what this article's first example demonstrates.

Does enabling partialPrefetching change existing <Link prefetch={true}> usage?

It changes the default (prefetch unset or auto) to fetch the App Shell instead of the full page. An explicit prefetch={true} keeps doing a fuller, per-link prefetch that also resolves that link's URL data — it isn't replaced, just layered on top of the new default.

Is this the same thing as Partial Prerendering (PPR)?

No, though they're related and easy to conflate. Partial Prerendering describes a single route serving a static shell plus streamed dynamic content on one request. Partial Prefetching is about navigation — what a <Link> fetches ahead of a click, across multiple navigation stages.

Can I test that a navigation actually renders instantly, in CI?

Yes — @next/playwright ships an instant() helper built for this: it asserts on the UI that's available immediately after a navigation, so a regression that reintroduces a blocking fetch fails your test suite instead of a user's click.

Cheat sheet

Task Code / Config Notes
Enable the feature cacheComponents: true, partialPrefetching: true in next.config.ts Requires Cache Components; both are create-next-app defaults now
Default <Link> behavior Prefetches the App Shell only No code change needed once the flag is on
Full per-link prefetch <Link prefetch={true}> Also resolves params/searchParams; costs one extra round-trip per link
Keep a page shell-eligible Await params/searchParams inside the <Suspense>-wrapped component Resolving them in the page component itself disqualifies the shell
Enforce a static shell export const ensureStatic = 'shell' No-op (with a dev warning) unless Partial Prefetching is on
Opt a route out of validation export const instant = false Siblings are still validated
Adopt incrementally export const prefetch = 'partial' per route, then the global flag Clean up with npx @next/codemod@canary remove-partial-prefetch ./app
Inspect the shell visually Navigation Inspector in Next.js DevTools Freezes the page at its initial loading state
Regression-test it instant() from @next/playwright Asserts on the immediately-available UI after navigation 
// the whole pattern in one route
export const ensureStatic = 'shell'

export default function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  return (
    <>
      <ReportHeader />{/* no URL dependency — joins the App Shell */}
      <Suspense fallback={<ReportSkeleton />}>
        <Report paramsPromise={params} />{/* URL-dependent work stays inside the boundary */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  )
}

Key takeaways

  • A client-side navigation only re-renders below the layout segments it shares with the current page — a Suspense boundary above that point does nothing on a click, only on a full page load.
  • Partial Prefetching (Next.js 16.3+, requires Cache Components) splits a navigation into three stages: the App Shell, an optional per-link prefetch of URL data, and the navigation itself.
  • Where you await params/searchParams decides whether a page is shell-eligible — resolve them inside the Suspense boundary, not above it.
  • ensureStatic, dev-time validation, the Navigation Inspector, and @next/playwright's instant() all exist to catch a non-instant navigation before a user does.

The dashboard from the first section didn't need a new library or a rewrite — it needed its existing <Suspense> boundary to sit somewhere the App Router could actually use it. That's usually true of Instant Navigations adoption generally: the hard part is rarely the config flag, it's finding every place params got awaited one component too early.

Have you turned on Partial Prefetching yet, and did the dev-time validation catch anything you didn't expect? I'd like to hear about it in the comments.

articles.title: Tuesday Isn't a Valid State Transition
articles.description: Calendars, evidence, and the difference between done and stuck  I expected my pear wine to spend two...
articles.body_html:
Calendars, evidence, and the difference between done and stuck

I expected my pear wine to spend two to three weeks in primary fermentation.

It spent nineteen days. The yeast went in on September 23, and on October 12 I siphoned the wine off its sediment and into a glass carboy.

So the calendar was right. That still isn't why I moved it.

What the calendar is for

Every fermentation recipe comes with time estimates. Primary takes one to three weeks. Secondary takes a few more. Bulk age for a few months. Those numbers aren't wrong. They're averages across a lot of batches, and they're useful for exactly one thing: planning. They tell you when to have a clean carboy ready, when to clear some space, when to stop making weekend plans.

What they can't do is tell you that this batch is ready. Yeast doesn't read recipes. It works at a speed set by temperature, sugar, nutrients, acidity, the particular strain, and the particular fruit, none of which the recipe author has ever met.

So the recipe gives you a forecast, and the fermentation gives you evidence. Only one of those gets to move the wine. If they happen to agree, as they did this time, that's a pleasant coincidence, not an authorization.

The rule winemakers actually use

The traditional test for "primary is done, time to rack" is simple: take readings over several days, and when you get the same reading three times running, fermentation has finished.

What I like about that rule is what it isn't. It isn't a date. It also isn't a single reading, because one measurement tells you where the fermentation is, not whether it's still moving. It's evidence sustained over a window. Time is part of the test, but only as the space in which the evidence has to hold still.

Here's what the pear's refractometer readings actually looked like:

Date Raw Brix
Sep 23 12.9 (before the yeast)
Sep 25 6.0
Sep 30 6.0
Oct 2 5.7
Oct 4 5.6
Oct 7 5.6
Oct 10 5.6
Oct 11 5.6
Oct 12 5.6

Two things in that table are worth a closer look.

First, the early plateau. Most of the sugar was gone within two days, and then the reading sat at exactly 6.0 for five days. If I'd been looking for stillness and nothing else, that looked a lot like the end. It wasn't. The fermentation was slowing down, not stopping, and over the next week it crept down further before it finally held. Two matching readings were a pause, not a verdict, which is precisely why the rule asks for three.

Second, I didn't stop at three. By October 10 I had three consecutive readings at 5.6, which satisfies the rule. I kept reading anyway, and waited until five readings across eight days agreed.

Then the racking itself handed me one more piece of evidence. There was more wine in the primary fermenter than the glass carboy could hold. Rather than pour the extra down the drain, I filled a hydrometer jar with it: a completely different instrument, measuring a completely different physical property. The refractometer, once corrected for alcohol, put the wine at about 1.004. The hydrometer said 1.002. Two independent instruments, close enough to agree, and the second one confirmed that the correction formula I'd been trusting for three weeks was doing its job.

I like that this happened by accident, because it isn't really an accident. A hydrometer needs a large sample, which in a one-gallon batch is too expensive to take routinely. At the moment of a transition, when wine is being moved anyway, that same sample costs nothing. The transition is when the more trustworthy evidence becomes cheap.

None of that is the calendar talking. That's a guard, and it was satisfied before the wine moved.

Status is a column anyone can write

In a lot of systems, state is a string in a database, and a transition is an UPDATE statement.

UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 4417;

Nothing in that statement requires that anything was shipped. It's a label, and anyone with write access can apply it for any reason: a cron job that marks orders shipped two days after payment because that's usually true, a release train that promotes whatever's on the branch because it's Tuesday, a support tool that flips a flag to make a ticket go away.

Each of these is the software version of racking the wine because the recipe said two to three weeks. Most of the time it'll even be right, just as my calendar was. The transition happens on schedule, the dashboard updates, and the system now asserts a state that nobody verified.

The fix isn't elaborate. A transition should have a guard, a condition that has to be true, based on evidence, before the state can change. "Shipped" should require a carrier scan. "Released" should require the checks that define releasable. "Primary complete" should require stable readings. The state machine's job is to refuse the transition when the evidence isn't there, however much the calendar insists, and to keep refusing even on the days the calendar happens to be right.

Same evidence, two states

Here's where it gets interesting. "Three consistent readings" is the signal for done. But a fermentation that has stalled also produces three consistent readings.

Mead is notorious for this. Honey has very little natural buffering, so as fermentation proceeds the pH drifts down, and past a certain point the yeast slows or quits entirely, often well short of dry. From the refractometer's point of view, a stuck mead and a finished mead look exactly the same: a number that has stopped moving.

My fireweed mead is a few days from that question right now. Its pH started at 3.5 and dropped to 3.1 within the first four days, where it has mostly stayed. Here are its last few readings:

Date Raw Brix Corrected Brix Estimated ABV
Oct 7 11.8 4.3 10.4%
Oct 10 9.0 -0.3 12.8%
Oct 11 8.6 -1.0 13.1%
Oct 12 8.4 -1.3 13.3%

Look at the corrected column. The calculator now claims the mead contains less than no sugar, which is impossible. That's a model being pushed past the range it was built for, and it's a nice reminder that a derived number can confidently assert something no physical system can be. If my guard were "corrected Brix at or below zero," I'd have racked the mead two days ago.

The raw readings tell a different story: they're still falling, slowly. The mead isn't still yet, so the guard isn't satisfied, no matter what the corrected number says. And when it does go still, the question becomes where. The yeast I used, 71B, is generally rated to tolerate around 14% alcohol, and the estimate is already over 13%. A mead that stops near its yeast's limit with the sugar it was expected to consume gone is probably done. One that stops early, with sugar left over and the pH low, is probably stuck.

The mead has already taught me this lesson once, in miniature. Mead yeast needs nutrients added in stages early on, and the textbook guidance ties the last addition to the "one-third sugar break," the point where about a third of the sugar has been consumed. I scheduled my three additions by day instead. As it happened, the last one landed right around the sugar break anyway. Sometimes luck happens. But luck is exactly what it was: the schedule didn't know where the sugar was, and if the mead had been a few days slower, the same calendar would have fed it at the wrong time.

In other words, the guard for "done" can't just be "stable." It has to be "stable where a finished fermentation should be," which means the guard needs a model of the expected end state, not just a test for motion. And it needs to know which of its inputs to trust when they disagree.

Software has the same ambiguity everywhere. A batch job whose progress counter hasn't moved in an hour has either finished or hung. A queue depth sitting at zero means either everything was processed or the consumer died. A replication lag of zero might mean the replica is caught up, or that it stopped receiving anything to lag behind. In every case, "nothing is changing" is evidence consistent with two opposite states, and a transition that only checks for stillness will eventually pick the wrong one.

A transition is an event with a receipt

The row in my pear log for October 12 reads, in effect: 11:10 a.m., 5.6 Brix, hydrometer 1.002, moved to glass carboy. The transition and the evidence that justified it are on the same line.

That matters more than the new status. Months from now, if the wine turns out strange, "racked on October 12" tells me almost nothing. "Racked after five stable readings, confirmed by a second instrument" tells me what I believed, what I based it on, and whether I might have been fooled by a stall.

Systems benefit from the same habit. A state change shouldn't just overwrite the previous state. It should be recorded as an event: what the state was, what it became, what evidence satisfied the guard, and who or what made the call. Then the current state is something you can explain, not just something you can read. When "shipped" turns out to be wrong, you can see whether the guard was bad, the evidence was bad, or the guard was never checked at all.

What time is actually allowed to do

None of this means time is irrelevant. It plays three legitimate roles, and it's worth keeping them straight.

Time can permit a transition. Some transitions shouldn't happen before a minimum interval no matter what the evidence says, like a waiting period before a refund clears, or a wine that needs some minimum aging before bottling. Here time is a precondition alongside the evidence, not a replacement for it.

Time can create the conditions for evidence. The three-readings rule only works because readings are spread over days. Stability over a window requires a window. The pear's false plateau is exactly why: two readings five days apart looked still, and only more time showed they weren't.

Time can raise a question. If a fermentation hasn't finished long after it should have, that's worth investigating. But notice what the timeout actually tells you: something is unusual. It doesn't tell you the batch is done, and it doesn't tell you the batch has failed.

That last one is where software most often goes wrong. Timeouts routinely get wired straight to a terminal state: no response in thirty seconds means failed, no update in three days means complete. A timeout is legitimate evidence that you need to look. It is rarely evidence of what you'll find when you do. A timeout should produce a question, not an answer.

What time shouldn't do, on its own, is cause a transition. Nineteen days arriving was not a fact about the pear wine.

Guarding your transitions

Treat schedules as forecasts. Plan with them. Don't let them move state, even when they're right.

Put a guard on every transition that matters. If a state can be reached by writing a string, eventually it will be reached for the wrong reason.

Test for the expected end state, not just stillness. Stable and finished are different claims. A guard that can't tell them apart will someday declare a stall a success.

Know which evidence to trust when it disagrees. A derived value can be confidently impossible. Raw observations and independent instruments are how you catch it.

Record the evidence with the transition. The new state is the conclusion. Keep the reasons next to it.

Let timeouts ask, not answer. Route them to "needs attention," not to "done" or "failed."

The pear is in its carboy now, clearing slowly. October 12 was the day it moved. It happened to be a Monday. That wasn't the reason either.

articles.title: Is Claude taking control of my development skills? I went looking for proof.
articles.description: Last Tuesday I hit a bug. A React component was rendering stale data. Two years ago, I'd have known...
articles.body_html:
Last Tuesday I hit a bug. A React component was rendering stale data. Two years ago, I'd have known the problem on sight.

This time, my hand moved before my brain did. I selected the code, hit my Claude shortcut, and typed "fix this."

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    setCount(count + 1);   // always 0 + 1. classic stale closure.
  }, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);   // empty deps = count is frozen at its first value

Claude fixed it in four seconds. Used the functional update, setCount(c => c + 1). I hit accept and moved on.

Then I stopped, because something felt off. I hadn't solved anything. I'd pattern-matched "bug" → "ask Claude" and skipped the part in the middle, the part where I used to actually understand what was broken. That's a bug I'd explained to junior devs a dozen times. And I'd just outsourced it without a thought.

So I asked myself the honest question: is Claude quietly taking my skills? And instead of answering with a gut feeling, I went and read the actual research. Here's what I found, including a study from Anthropic itself, and the one habit that fixed it for me.

It's not man vs machine. It's a quieter thing.

"Taking control" sounds dramatic. The truth is boring and worse: it's cognitive offloading. When you hand a mental task to a tool, your brain does less of the work. And the work is the skill.

You already know this from real life:

  • GPS. A 2017 Nature study put people through virtual London streets. The ones following turn-by-turn directions showed measurably less activity in the hippocampus, the brain's map-maker, than people navigating on their own. Offload the navigating, and the navigating muscle goes quiet.
  • The gym. A forklift moves the weight faster than you ever could. That's not the point. Lifting it yourself is the point.

Claude is a forklift for code. Incredible leverage. And if I let it lift everything, I stop being able to lift anything.

The question is whether coding this way does to my debugging what GPS does to your sense of direction. Turns out, people have measured it.

Proof #1: You feel faster. You're measurably slower.

This is the one that rattled me, because it attacks the thing I trust most, my own read on how a session went.

Researchers at METR ran a proper experiment in early 2025. 16 experienced open-source developers. 246 real tasks in repos they already maintained. Half the tasks: AI allowed (Cursor + Claude). Half: AI forbidden. Then they measured the clock.

  • Before starting, the devs guessed AI would make them 24% faster.
  • After finishing, they felt it had made them about 20% faster.
  • The stopwatch said they were 19% slower with AI.

Sit with that. They were slower, and they couldn't feel it. A ~39-point gap between how fast they felt and how fast they were.

That's the dangerous part. A skill you're losing while feeling more productive is a skill you'll never catch yourself losing.

(Honest caveat: small sample, and METR says it doesn't generalize to all work. But the perception gap is the scary bit, and it matches everything below.)

Proof #2: Anthropic studied its own tool. The result is brutal and fair.

This is the study that actually changed how I work. And it's remarkable because it comes from the company that makes Claude.

They took 52 developers learning Trio (a Python async library, new to all of them). One group coded with an AI that could hand them correct code on request. The other group hand-coded. Then everyone took a quiz, debugging, reading code, writing code, concepts, on stuff they'd used ten minutes earlier.

  • Hand-coders averaged 67%.
  • AI-assisted averaged 50%. Seventeen points lower. Nearly two letter grades.
  • The AI group saved about two minutes. Not even a statistically real difference.
  • The biggest gap was on debugging — the exact skill you need the second the AI's code breaks.

So the trade was: two letter grades of understanding, for two meaningless minutes. That's the trade I'd been making on autopilot in my useEffect.

But here's the part that saved me from just rage-quitting Claude: it wasn't the AI that did the damage. It was how they used it.

The devs who bombed the quiz (under 40%) were the ones doing pure delegation, "write this for me," dump the error in, take the fix. The devs who aced it (65%+) were the ones asking Claude to explain — generate, then understand; ask "why this approach"; work through the error themselves.

And the explainers weren't slow. Asking conceptual questions was the second-fastest pattern in the whole study.

You don't have to choose between shipping and learning. You have to choose between delegating and understanding. And in the moment, those two feel almost identical.

The difference is literally how you type the prompt

This is the whole article in one example. Same bug, two prompts.

❌ The prompt that deskills me:

fix this

I paste code, I get a diff, I hit accept. I learned nothing. My brain logged "handled," not "here's why."

✅ The prompt that teaches me:

This useEffect shows stale data. Don't rewrite it yet —
explain WHY the count is frozen, then show me two ways to fix it
and the tradeoff between them.

Now Claude tells me it's a stale closure: the effect captured count at its first value and the empty dependency array froze it there. It shows me setCount(c => c + 1) (functional update) and adding count to the deps (re-subscribes the interval), and explains why the functional update is usually better here.

Same four seconds. Same correct answer. Completely different outcome in my head. One makes Claude my hands. The other makes it my senior engineer who explains while we work.

That's not a philosophy. That's the Anthropic data: the first prompt scored ~38%, the second scored ~70%.

Proof #3: You can see it in the commits

If skills are quietly eroding across the industry, you'd expect it to show up in the code we actually ship. It does.

GitClear studied 211 million changed lines from 2020 to 2024, right across the window AI assistants went mainstream.

  • 2024 was the first year on record where copy-pasted code beat refactored (moved) code. We're pasting more than we're consolidating.
  • Refactoring fell off a cliff — "moved" lines dropped from ~25% (2021) to under 10% (2024).
  • Duplicated blocks (5+ identical lines) jumped roughly 8x in 2024.

It's correlational, not a smoking gun. But it lines up: AI makes it trivial to insert a block and rarely nudges you to reuse what's already there. The codebase gets fatter. And the understanding of why it's shaped that way lives nowhere, because nobody wrote it, Claude did, and you accepted it.

There's even a name for this now: Knowledge Debt — technical debt's quieter cousin that lives in your head instead of the repo. Every "accept" on code you didn't understand is a withdrawal.

Let me be fair: the other side is real too

I'm not here to tell you to delete Claude. That'd be stupid, and dishonest.

  • These studies are early and small. Anthropic's devs were learning a new library — that's not the same as a senior engineer forgetting what they know.
  • Deskilling is a slope, not a cliff. You don't wake up unable to code. You slowly stop reaching for a skill until it's rusty. Which means you can catch it.
  • The leverage is genuinely incredible. I've shipped entire projects with Claude I'd never have attempted solo. That's not a small thing.

The evidence doesn't say "AI makes you worse." It says "AI makes you worse if you let it do the thinking, and better if you make it do the explaining." That line is the entire game.

My field guide: using Claude without going soft

Here's what I actually changed. Concrete rules, not vibes.

1. The 10-second rule. Before I paste a bug into Claude, I give myself 10 seconds to say out loud what I think is wrong. Even a guess. Then I ask Claude. Half the time I was right and just lazy. The other half, now I'm actually learning instead of skipping.

2. "Explain, don't just fix." My default debugging prompt is now literally:

Explain why this is broken before you fix it.

Five words. Keeps me in the loop. Keeps the senior engineer, loses the vending machine.

3. Read the diff like it's a PR from a junior. Would I approve this in review? If I can't say why it works, I don't accept it, I ask, or I rewrite it.

4. One hard thing a week, cold. Once a week I take a real problem and solve it with Claude closed. It's slower and slightly humbling. That's the gym. The slowness is the whole point.

Here's the split I try to stay on the right side of:

❌ Erodes the skill ✅ Builds the skill
Accept the diff without reading it Read it, then accept
"Write this feature for me" "Explain the approach, then I'll write it"
Paste the error, take the fix Guess first, then compare with Claude
Trust it because it compiles Verify it because you understand it
Let it refactor code you don't grasp Refactor it yourself, ask Claude to review

Every single row is the same choice: delegation vs understanding. The left column cost those developers two letter grades. The right column cost them almost nothing but a little friction.

So, is Claude taking control?

No. And honestly, that's worse.

Claude isn't taking anything. I'm handing it over, one frictionless "accept" at a time, feeling more productive the whole way down, which is exactly how the METR study says it would feel.

The tool just amplifies whatever I bring to it. Bring laziness, and it deskills me with terrifying efficiency. Bring curiosity, make it explain, guess before I ask, verify every diff, and it becomes the best mentor I've ever had, available at 2am, infinitely patient, never annoyed at the dumb question.

The skill I actually have to protect isn't React, or async, or debugging. It's the judgment to know when to let Claude think for me and when to make myself do it. That's the one thing I can't outsource, because the moment I do, there's nobody left to make the call.

I'm keeping Claude. I'm just not closing my eyes anymore.

Sources (all with caveats noted inline above): METR RCT on experienced-developer productivity (16 devs, 246 tasks); Anthropic, "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills" (52 devs, 50% vs 67%, Cohen's d=0.738, p=0.01); GitClear 2025 AI Code Quality report (211M lines); MIT Media Lab, "Your Brain on ChatGPT" (arXiv:2506.08872, not peer-reviewed); Nature Communications (2017) on GPS and hippocampal activity. Several are preprints or correlational.

Quick gut-check before the comments: last time you asked Claude to fix something, did you type "fix this" or "explain why it's broken"? Be honest. That answer is the whole study, run on a sample size of you. 👇

articles.title: The Hidden Cost of AI-Generated PRs: Why Most Teams Are Missing Silent Breakages
articles.description: AI coding assistants doubled pull request volume, subtle logic bugs are slipping past fatigued reviewers. Learn how to spot and stop silent production breakages.
articles.body_html:
Your team is shipping pull requests twice as fast as last year, the CI pipeline is green, and every diff looks cleanly formatted. Yet your production incident rate is quietly climbing.

According to Google Cloud's DORA State of AI-Assisted Software Development research, while roughly 90% of engineering teams now use AI tools daily to accelerate coding, increased AI adoption without matching quality guardrails correlates directly with a measurable drop in software delivery stability. Code generation is no longer the bottleneck—code verification is.

When pull request volume doubles while human review capacity stays flat, engineering teams fall into the "LGTM trap": rubber-stamping large, plausible-looking diffs that harbor silent, state-corrupting bugs.

The Problem: Plausible Code Is Harder to Debug Than Broken Code

When a junior developer writes a bug from scratch, the code usually looks suspicious. Naming is inconsistent, edge cases are visibly missing, or the syntax feels clunky. A senior reviewer spots the smell in seconds.

AI-generated code flips this heuristic on its head. Modern coding assistants produce code that is:

  • Syntactically idiomatic and cleanly formatted.
  • Accompanied by confident, well-structured PR descriptions.
  • Paired with unit tests that pass—because the tests were generated from the exact same flawed implementation context.

The Reviewer's Paradox: The cleaner and more idiomatic an AI-generated diff looks on the surface, the less cognitive effort a fatigued human reviewer spends tracing its underlying state transitions and failure modes.

The Common Mistake: Local Correctness vs. System Invariants

Coding agents excel at local context (the open file and immediate type definitions), but they frequently miss system-wide invariants—such as idempotency, transactional boundaries, permission scoping, and partial failure recovery.

Consider a real-world backend scenario: updating a user's subscription tier and syncing billing credits.

What Gets Approved in a Hurry (The Silent Bug)

An engineer prompts an assistant to "Add an endpoint handler that upgrades a user's plan and grants bonus credits, with unit tests." The PR arrives looking clean:

// ❌ Looks clean in a 600-line PR diff, but breaks production invariants
export async function upgradeSubscription(
  userId: string,
  newPlanId: string
): Promise<{ status: string; credits: number }> {
  const user = await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id: userId } });
  if (!user) {
    throw new Error("User not found");
  }

  // 1. External call inside business flow without idempotency key
  await billingClient.chargeUpgradeFee(user.stripeCustomerId, newPlanId);

  // 2. Non-atomic read-modify-write (race condition under concurrent requests)
  const updatedCredits = user.credits + 500;

  // 3. Separate DB writes without a transaction
  await db.subscriptions.update({
    where: { userId },
    data: { planId: newPlanId, updatedAt: new Date() },
  });

  await db.users.update({
    where: { id: userId },
    data: { credits: updatedCredits },
  });

  return { status: "upgraded", credits: updatedCredits };
}

Why did this pass review?

  1. The TypeScript types compile cleanly.
  2. The auto-generated unit test mocked billingClient and db, asserting that credits equaled user.credits + 500.
  3. It was buried inside a 14-file PR alongside boilerplate route definitions and DTOs.

The Consequence in Production

Two weeks later, a client network timeout triggers an automatic HTTP retry:

  • Double charging: billingClient.chargeUpgradeFee runs twice because no idempotency key was passed.
  • Lost updates / Race condition: Concurrent requests read the same user.credits snapshot in memory before writing.
  • Partial state corruption: If db.users.update fails due to a transient lock timeout, the user is billed and their plan is updated, but their credits vanish.

The Improved Approach: Designing for Verification, Not Just Generation

Fixing the code requires enforcing transactional boundaries, atomic increments, and idempotency—things a reviewer only catches when diffs are small and architectural constraints are explicit:

// ✅ Production-safe: Idempotent, atomic, and transactionally bounded
export async function upgradeSubscription(
  userId: string,
  newPlanId: string,
  idempotencyKey: string
): Promise<{ status: string; credits: number }> {
  return await db.$transaction(async (tx) => {
    // 1. Prevent duplicate execution via idempotency record lock
    const existingOp = await tx.idempotencyKeys.findUnique({
      where: { key: idempotencyKey },
    });
    if (existingOp) {
      return existingOp.responsePayload as { status: string; credits: number };
    }

    const user = await tx.users.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { id: userId } });

    // 2. Pass deterministic idempotency key to external provider
    await billingClient.chargeUpgradeFee(user.stripeCustomerId, newPlanId, {
      idempotencyKey,
    });

    await tx.subscriptions.update({
      where: { userId },
      data: { planId: newPlanId, updatedAt: new Date() },
    });

    // 3. Atomic database increment instead of in-memory calculation
    const updatedUser = await tx.users.update({
      where: { id: userId },
      data: { credits: { increment: 500 } },
    });

    const result = { status: "upgraded", credits: updatedUser.credits };

    await tx.idempotencyKeys.create({
      data: { key: idempotencyKey, responsePayload: result },
    });

    return result;
  });
}

Click to view the hidden test smell that masks AI bugs
When an AI assistant writes both the implementation and the test suite in the same prompt, it generates mirror tests—tests that assert what the code does rather than what the business contract requires.

If the implementation forgets to wrap two database calls in a transaction, the generated test simply mocks both calls and asserts each was called once. To break this loop:

  1. Write test cases (or failure-mode assertions) before generating implementation code.
  2. Require at least one test per PR that simulates a partial failure (e.g., the second database write throwing an error) and asserts that state rolls back cleanly.

Shifting the Workflow: How High-Performing Teams Adapt

As highlighted in Google's engineering practices on The Standard of Code Review, the primary purpose of code review is ensuring that the overall code health of the system improves over time. When code generation becomes virtually free, your review standards must tighten, not loosen.

Use this checklist before opening or approving any AI-assisted pull request:

  • [ ] Cap PR size at 250 lines of logic: If AI helped you write 800 lines in 20 minutes, split it into three stacked PRs so a human can actually reason about the state transitions.
  • [ ] Separate boilerplate from business logic: Never mix auto-generated migrations, DTOs, or formatting changes in the same PR as core domain logic.
  • [ ] Audit the tests before the implementation: Check whether the tests verify edge cases and failure rollbacks, or if they merely assert that mocked functions were called.
  • [ ] Check system boundaries first: Look directly at external I/O, database transactions, concurrency locks, and authorization checks—where local context models fail most often.
  • [ ] Require the author to explain the failure mode: Every PR description should answer one human-written question: "What happens if this code fails halfway through execution?"

Explore more production open-source projects on my GitHub

The Takeaway

AI coding assistants don't create bad engineering cultures—they amplify your existing bottlenecks. If your team treats pull request velocity as the primary metric of productivity, AI will help you accumulate technical debt and silent production bugs at record speed. Keep batch sizes small, separate test design from implementation generation, and treat human code review as an architectural safeguard rather than a syntax check.

What is the most subtle bug or production failure mode that slipped through an AI-assisted PR in your team recently, and what guardrail did you add to catch it next time?
