articles.title: Top 13 Web Scraping Tools Every Developer Should Know
articles.description: Web scraping sounds simple until your script hits a website that loads content with JavaScript,...
articles.body_html:
Web scraping sounds simple until your script hits a website that loads content with JavaScript, changes its HTML structure, limits requests, or returns data in an unexpected format. A quick Python script might work perfectly on ten pages and become difficult to maintain when you need to collect thousands of records regularly.

That is why choosing the right web scraping tool matters. Some projects need only an HTTP client and an HTML parser. Others need a real browser, a visual scraping interface, an AI-ready extraction API, or managed infrastructure that handles retries and proxy configuration.

I put together this list of 13 web scraping tools developers should know, covering open-source libraries, no-code tools, AI-powered scrapers, and enterprise data platforms. The goal is not to find one tool that does everything. It is to understand which tool fits your data source, technical skills, scale, and maintenance requirements.

Quick Comparison: 13 Web Scraping Tools

Tool Category Best for Coding required?
Scrapy Open-source framework Large, structured crawling projects Yes
Beautiful Soup Python library Parsing HTML and extracting data Yes
Requests Python library Fetching pages and HTTP resources Yes
Playwright Browser automation JavaScript-heavy websites and interactive flows Yes
Puppeteer Browser automation Chrome and browser automation with JavaScript Yes
Web Scraper Browser extension Visual, sitemap-based extraction Minimal
Instant Data Scraper Browser extension Quickly extracting visible tables and lists Minimal
Octoparse No-code platform Visual scraping and managed workflows Usually no
Firecrawl AI-ready scraping API Turning web pages into clean content for LLMs Some
Browse AI AI-powered platform No-code extraction and website monitoring Usually no
Apify Scraping and automation platform Reusable cloud scrapers and scheduled jobs Optional
Bright Data Enterprise data platform Large-scale extraction and data access infrastructure Depends on product
Decodo Scraping API and proxy platform Managed extraction with browser rendering and proxy options Some

Open-Source Code Libraries and Frameworks

If you want control over how data is collected and processed, start here. These tools are especially useful when you need custom extraction logic, repeatable pipelines, and integration with your existing codebase.

1. Scrapy

Scrapy is an open-source Python framework built for web crawling and structured data extraction. It provides more than basic HTML parsing, including request scheduling, concurrent crawling, selectors, item pipelines, and feed exports. Its architecture is designed to handle many requests efficiently while allowing developers to control crawl behavior.

Where it fits

Imagine you are building a product catalog containing thousands of public product pages. You need to follow category links, collect product names and prices, handle pagination, validate records, and export the results to a database.

Scrapy gives you a framework to organize that work instead of building a crawler from scratch.

What I like

  • Asynchronous crawling and configurable concurrency.
  • CSS and XPath selectors for extraction.
  • Pipelines to clean and validate scraped items.
  • Export options for formats such as JSON, CSV, and XML.
  • An extensible architecture for larger scraping projects.

Limitations

Scrapy has a learning curve, especially if you are new to crawlers, middleware, and pipelines. It also does not automatically make every JavaScript-heavy website easy to scrape. You may need browser rendering or another integration for pages that depend on client-side execution.

My take: Choose Scrapy when scraping is a recurring part of your application or data pipeline, rather than a one-time task.

2. Beautiful Soup

Beautiful Soup is a Python library that turns HTML or XML into a navigable structure. You can search for elements, inspect attributes, find text, and extract information using familiar Python code. It is a parser, not a complete crawling platform.

That distinction matters. Beautiful Soup is excellent at processing HTML you already have, but it does not independently manage a large crawl, schedule requests, or render a browser page.

A typical workflow combines it with Requests:

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

url = "https://example.com"

response = requests.get(
    url,
    timeout=15,
    headers={"User-Agent": "ExampleResearchBot/1.0"}
)
response.raise_for_status()

soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")

title = soup.title.get_text(strip=True) if soup.title else ""
headings = [
    heading.get_text(" ", strip=True)
    for heading in soup.select("h1, h2")
]

print({"title": title, "headings": headings})

Replace the example URL with a site you are authorized to access.

What I like

  • Simple, readable Python syntax.
  • Useful CSS-selector and tree-navigation methods.
  • Helpful when HTML is imperfect or inconsistent.
  • Easy integration with HTTP clients and data-processing libraries.

Limitations

It cannot execute JavaScript. If the information appears only after a browser runs scripts, Beautiful Soup may never receive that content unless you fetch it through another method.

My take: Beautiful Soup is a great starting point for developers who want to extract structured information from ordinary HTML without adopting a full scraping framework.

3. Requests

Requests is a popular Python HTTP library. It handles common HTTP operations, query parameters, headers, cookies, authentication, connection pooling, and timeouts through a straightforward interface.

For scraping, Requests typically retrieves the page. Another tool, such as BeautifulSoup, extracts data from the response.

Where it fits

Use Requests when the information is already present in the server’s HTML or when the website provides a documented API that you are permitted to use.

It is also useful for retrieving public files, downloading pages, or communicating with HTTP endpoints as part of a larger pipeline.

What I like

  • A straightforward API for HTTP requests.
  • Session support for maintaining cookies.
  • Connection pooling and configurable timeouts.
  • Easy integration with parsers and data-processing tools.

Limitations

Requests does not behave like a full browser. It will not execute page JavaScript, click interactive elements, or automatically solve a site’s access challenges.

My take: Requests is often the first component I would reach for in a Python scraping project. If the server already sends the data you need, a browser may be unnecessary overhead.

4. Playwright

Playwright is a browser automation framework that supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Developers can interact with pages, wait for elements, navigate through workflows, and inspect rendered content.

This becomes useful when the data you need appears only after JavaScript executes or after a user interaction.

For example, a directory might load additional records when someone clicks a “Load more” button. A traditional HTTP request may return only the initial page, while Playwright can interact with the rendered interface.

What I like

  • Support for multiple browser engines.
  • Browser interaction and page evaluation.
  • Useful waiting mechanisms for dynamic content.
  • Support for screenshots and debugging.
  • Integration with automated testing and application workflows.

Limitations

Running browsers usually consumes more resources than fetching raw HTML. Browser installation, page timeouts, selectors, and changing interfaces also add maintenance work.

My take: Use Playwright when the browser is genuinely part of the problem. For a simple static page, start with an HTTP client instead.

5. Puppeteer

Puppeteer is a JavaScript library that provides a high-level API for controlling browsers, especially Chrome and Chromium, through browser automation interfaces. It supports navigation, interaction, screenshots, page evaluation, and other browser tasks.

Puppeteer is a natural fit for Node.js projects that need to automate browser workflows or collect information from rendered pages.

What I like

  • A familiar JavaScript and Node.js workflow.
  • Control over browser navigation and page interactions.
  • Useful debugging and screenshot capabilities.
  • A good fit for browser-based automation pipelines.

Limitations

Browser automation can be resource-intensive, and the scraper still needs to account for changing page structures, timeouts, and access restrictions. Puppeteer does not eliminate the need for data validation or responsible request handling.

My take: If your team already uses Node.js and needs browser control, Puppeteer is worth considering. If cross-browser testing is a major requirement, compare its needs with Playwright before choosing.

No-Code and Browser Extension Tools

Not every scraping task deserves a custom script. Browser extensions and visual tools are useful when you need a small dataset quickly, want to validate an extraction idea, or prefer to define data fields visually.

6. Web Scraper

Web Scraper is a browser extension that lets users define a sitemap, select elements on a page, and specify how to navigate between pages. It is useful for creating structured extraction workflows without writing a complete crawler.

For example, suppose you need a list of book titles, prices, and product links from a publicly accessible catalog. You can define selectors for those fields and configure navigation to follow category pages or pagination.

What I like

  • Visual selection of page elements.
  • A sitemap-based approach to organizing extraction.
  • Useful for repeated patterns across multiple pages.
  • A lower barrier to entry than writing a custom crawler.

Limitations

You still need to understand how page elements and pagination work. A website redesign can break selectors, and complex JavaScript interactions may require a different tool or additional configuration.

My take: Web Scraper is a practical option for developers and analysts who want a visual way to build repeatable extraction workflows.

7. Instant Data Scraper

Instant Data Scraper is designed to detect tabular or repeated data on a web page and help users export it without building a scraper manually.

It is especially convenient when the information is already visible in a regular table, directory, or list.

What I like

  • Very little setup for straightforward extraction.
  • Useful for quickly collecting rows and repeated fields.
  • A convenient way to test whether a dataset is accessible.
  • A simple starting point for small research tasks.

Limitations

Automatic detection can select the wrong elements or miss fields when a page has a complicated layout. Highly dynamic websites and multi-step navigation can also exceed what a quick browser extension is designed to handle.

My take: Use Instant Data Scraper when you need a small dataset quickly. If the task needs reliable scheduled collection, custom validation, or complex pagination, consider a more structured solution.

8. Octoparse

Octoparse provides a visual web scraping workflow and managed options for collecting structured data. Users can configure extraction tasks, use templates, and export results without necessarily writing code. Its current platform also promotes cloud-based scraping and data workflows.

It can help teams that need recurring data collection but don't want to maintain every part of a custom scraper.

What I like

  • Visual workflow configuration.
  • Templates for common extraction scenarios.
  • Options for running tasks in the cloud.
  • Data export for further analysis.

Limitations

Visual workflows still require testing and maintenance when websites change. Before using Octoparse for recurring jobs, evaluate plan limits, task frequency, export options, and whether the required interaction patterns are supported.

My take: Octoparse is worth considering when you want a more managed, low-code workflow than a browser extension provides.

AI and LLM-Ready Web Scrapers

AI applications often need website content in a cleaner format than raw HTML. They may need Markdown for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured JSON for downstream processing, or extracted fields that match a predefined schema.

These tools help reduce the work between collecting web content and using it in an AI application.

9. Firecrawl

Firecrawl provides APIs to scrape individual pages, crawl websites, and return content in formats such as Markdown and structured JSON. It is designed for applications that need web content as context for AI systems.

Imagine building a documentation assistant that answers questions about a software product. Instead of writing a custom crawler and cleaning every HTML page yourself, you can use a scraping or crawling workflow to collect relevant content and feed it into your indexing pipeline.

What I like

  • Clean content extraction for AI workflows.
  • Crawling multiple pages across a site.
  • API-based integration with applications.
  • Support for structured extraction and downstream processing.

Limitations

Extracted content still needs validation. Navigation elements, repeated text, outdated pages, and missing details can reduce retrieval quality. You should also check crawling limits, API pricing, and how it handles target websites before using it at scale.

My take: Firecrawl is a strong candidate when the final destination is an LLM, a RAG pipeline, or an AI agent that needs useful web context.

10. Browse AI

Browse AI lets users configure robots to extract website data and monitor changes without writing a scraper from scratch. It supports visual setup, structured data extraction, and recurring monitoring workflows.

This is useful for tasks such as tracking publicly listed prices, monitoring changes to product pages, or collecting updates from a directory.

What I like

  • A visual setup process.
  • Reusable extraction robots.
  • Website monitoring and change alerts.
  • Structured output for downstream workflows.

Limitations

Automated extraction doesn't guarantee every site will remain accessible or that every field will always be captured correctly. Website changes, access restrictions, and dynamic layouts can still affect reliability.

My take: Browse AI is worth considering when you need recurring extraction and monitoring but do not want to maintain the underlying browser automation yourself.

11. Apify

Apify is a web scraping and automation platform built around reusable programs called Actors. An Actor can accept structured input, run a scraping or automation task, and produce results you can store, export, or pass to another workflow. Actors can be run manually, through APIs, or on schedules.

The platform is useful when scraping needs to become a repeatable part of an application or business process. You can use existing Actors from its marketplace or build your own with the libraries and logic your project requires.

What I like

  • Reusable scraping and automation tasks.
  • API-based execution and scheduling.
  • Structured datasets and export options.
  • A marketplace of ready-made Actors.
  • Integration opportunities for larger data workflows.

Limitations

The platform introduces its own usage and operational considerations. Review Actor quality, maintenance, pricing, data retention, and resource requirements before depending on a third-party Actor in a critical pipeline.

My take: Apify is a good option when you want to move beyond a local script and run reusable scraping jobs as part of a cloud workflow.

Enterprise Data Platforms and Unblockers

Some scraping projects become difficult because of infrastructure, not extraction logic. Teams may need to handle high request volumes, geographic differences, JavaScript rendering, retries, proxy configuration, and changing access conditions.

Enterprise data platforms can provide some of that infrastructure through managed services or APIs. They do not remove the need to respect access permissions, applicable laws, or website policies.

12. Bright Data

Bright Data offers web data collection products and infrastructure, including scraping APIs, datasets, and proxy services. It is relevant to teams that need to collect public web data across many targets and integrate the results into larger data pipelines.

For example, an e-commerce analytics team might need to collect public product information across multiple markets. Building and maintaining all the infrastructure independently could take substantial engineering effort, so a managed service may be worth evaluating.

What I like

  • A range of web data collection products.
  • Managed infrastructure for large-scale workflows.
  • Options for API-based data retrieval.
  • Support for data pipelines and enterprise use cases.

Limitations

The product range can make selection more involved. Pricing, target compatibility, data delivery formats, service requirements, and the level of control you retain should all be evaluated against your workload.

My take: Bright Data is worth investigating when collection scale and infrastructure requirements make a basic scraper difficult to maintain.

13. Decodo

Decodo offers scraping APIs and proxy infrastructure intended to simplify web data collection. Its Scraping API supports structured extraction workflows, with options such as browser rendering, proxy selection, and prebuilt templates. Developers can integrate it into applications via API requests rather than maintaining the entire collection infrastructure themselves.

What I like

  • API-based access to scraping functionality.
  • Managed proxy options.
  • Browser-rendering capabilities for supported workflows.
  • Templates that can reduce setup for common targets.
  • Integration with Python, Node.js, and other application stacks.

Limitations

A managed API doesn't guarantee every request will succeed. Validate output quality, supported target behavior, request limits, pricing, and failed-request handling before using it in a production pipeline.

My take: Decodo is worth comparing with Bright Data when you want managed scraping infrastructure and prefer an API-first integration.

Which Web Scraping Tool Should You Choose?

The easiest way to narrow this list is to start with the problem, not the tool.

Your requirement Tools to evaluate first
Fetch static HTML and parse it in Python Requests + Beautiful Soup
Crawl many pages with custom logic Scrapy
Interact with JavaScript-rendered pages Playwright or Puppeteer
Extract a small table without coding Instant Data Scraper
Build visual, repeatable extraction tasks Web Scraper or Octoparse
Monitor website changes without maintaining code Browse AI
Collect clean website content for an LLM Firecrawl
Run reusable scraping jobs in the cloud Apify
Collect data at larger scale with managed infrastructure Bright Data or Decodo

You don't need an enterprise platform for a simple page, and you don't need a browser extension to handle a complex production data pipeline.

Start with the simplest tool that can reliably collect the required data. Add browser automation or managed infrastructure only when the target website or workload justifies it.

What Developers Should Check Before Scraping a Website

Choosing the tool is only part of the work. A scraper can return data successfully while still creating a fragile or irresponsible workflow.

Check whether an API already exists.

A documented API is often more stable than parsing page HTML. If a site offers an API that provides the data you need and you are authorized to use it, evaluate that option before building a scraper.

Inspect the page before selecting a library.

Check whether the required data appears in the initial HTML or only after JavaScript executes. This simple test often tells you whether Requests and Beautiful Soup are enough or whether a browser is necessary.

Handle errors and timeouts.

Production scrapers should account for failed requests, malformed responses, timeouts, and temporary server errors. Use sensible retry limits and exponential backoff where appropriate. Unbounded retries can increase load and worsen failures.

Validate the extracted data.

A successful HTTP response does not mean your scraper captured the correct fields. Validate required values, normalize formats, detect duplicates, and monitor unexpected changes in record counts.

Respect access restrictions

Review the website’s terms, applicable law, published crawling policies, and any access restrictions. Use reasonable request rates and avoid collecting personal or sensitive information without a valid basis. Do not treat proxy rotation or browser automation as permission to bypass access controls.

Track maintenance costs

A scraper is software that needs upkeep. Measure failure rates, data freshness, and the engineering time required to maintain selectors and workflows. For a recurring job, the cheapest initial setup may not be the least expensive option over time.

Final Thoughts

The best web scraping tool depends on how much control you need and how complicated the target website is.

For a straightforward Python workflow, Requests and Beautiful Soup are often enough. For recurring crawls, Scrapy provides a more complete framework. Playwright and Puppeteer are useful when you need browser interaction, while Web Scraper, Instant Data Scraper, and Octoparse lower the barrier for visual extraction.

If the goal is to feed web content into an AI application, Firecrawl is a natural candidate. Browse AI helps with no-code extraction and monitoring, while Apify lets you run reusable scraping jobs in the cloud. For larger collection workloads, Bright Data and Decodo are worth evaluating for their managed data collection infrastructure.

My recommendation is simple: start with the smallest reliable solution, test it against the pages you actually need, and measure maintenance effort before scaling up. A good scraper is not just one that collects data today. It keeps producing accurate, useful data as your project grows.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is the best web scraping tool for developers?

Scrapy is a strong choice for structured crawling projects, while Requests and Beautiful Soup work well for simpler Python tasks. Playwright is useful for JavaScript-heavy pages. For managed extraction, developers can evaluate Firecrawl, Apify, Bright Data, or Decodo based on their requirements.

2. Which web scraping tools do not require coding?

Instant Data Scraper, Web Scraper, Octoparse, and Browse AI offer visual or no-code workflows. They help you extract data without building a full scraper, though complex sites may still require configuration and maintenance.

3. What is the difference between Scrapy and Beautiful Soup?

Scrapy is a complete crawling and scraping framework with scheduling, concurrency, and data pipelines. Beautiful Soup parses HTML and helps extract information. They solve different problems and can be used together with an HTTP client when appropriate.

4. Which web scraping tools are suitable for AI applications?

Firecrawl is designed to return clean web content for LLM and RAG workflows. Apify can run reusable scraping tasks and expose their results through APIs. Other tools can also support AI applications if you clean, validate, and transform their output into the format the model or pipeline needs.

5. Is web scraping legal?

Web scraping is not automatically legal or illegal in every situation. The answer depends on factors such as the data being collected, authorization, website terms, access restrictions, privacy obligations, and applicable law. Developers should review those requirements and use appropriate, responsible collection practices before scraping a site.

articles.title: Every DIY Project Starts as Automation and Ends as Art
articles.description: We tell ourselves we're optimizing. What we're really doing is leaving fingerprints on...
articles.body_html:
We tell ourselves we're optimizing. What we're really doing is leaving fingerprints on silicon.

You know the lie.

It starts in the most reasonable way possible. You have a problem that is objectively stupid and therefore must be solved.

"The fern is dying."
"The light switch is too far."
"The mailbox doesn't tell me when there's mail."

And you, being a person who knows what an ESP32 is, think: I can automate that.

This is how it begins. Every time. A clean, utilitarian, defensible justification for ordering another dev board you absolutely do not need.

I have a drawer full of these justifications. None of them ended as automation.

Phase 1: The Automation Delusion

The automation phase is pure engineer brain. It's elegant. It's logical. It's a lie.

You open Arduino IDE — or PlatformIO if you've seen the light — and you write the most honest code you'll ever write in the project:
Beautiful. Simple. Utilitarian. You could put this on a resume.

You wire up an ESP32, a capacitive soil sensor, a tiny pump. You flash it. It works. For exactly 47 minutes. Then the sensor corrodes, the pump clogs, the ESP32 decides it no longer likes your Wi-Fi password, and your fern is somehow more dead than before.

This is the first lesson hardware teaches you that software never will: Hardware doesn't care about your intentions. It cares about physics.

Your code can be perfect. Your solder joint can still be cold. Your 3.3V rail can still sag when the pump kicks on and brown-out the whole board. Your "low power deep sleep" is pulling 80mA because you left the power LED on like an amateur.

Software forgives. Hardware remembers.

And yet, we stay. Why?

Because somewhere between the third time you re-solder that header and the first time your janky prototype actually waters the plant by itself, something shifts.

You stop caring about whether the fern lives.

Phase 2: The Creep

This is the phase no one talks about on YouTube tutorials. The scope creep that isn't about features. It's about feel.

You got it to water the plant. Automation: complete. You should be done.

But the bare PCB on the soil looks sad. So you design a little enclosure. Just a simple box in Fusion 360. 30 minutes, tops.

Four hours later you are debating 0.2mm vs 0.16mm layer height, whether matte black PETG says "I am a serious adult who waters plants" and if you should add a tiny embossed fern leaf on the lid because... why not?

Then you think: the LED is too harsh. It should fade in slowly, like a sunrise, when it waters. Not just blink. Breathe.

So you rewrite digitalWrite() into a PWM fade loop with an ease-in-out curve you copied from a frontend animation library. For a plant. A plant does not care about easing functions.

Then you add an OLED. Just to show moisture percentage. Then you add a little animation of a happy fern when moisture is good and a droopy fern when it's not. You spend a whole evening drawing 8x8 pixel art ferns.

You came to automate. You stayed to anthropomorphize.

This is the moment every DIY project crosses the line from engineering into art. You are no longer solving the problem. You are expressing how you feel about the problem.

Automation asks: "Does it work?"
Art asks: "Does it feel like me?"

Phase 3: Why The ESP32 Made Us All Artists

The old Arduino Uno was honest. It had 32KB of flash. It could barely hold your code and a grudge. It kept you humble. You built what you needed because you had to.

The ESP32-S3 is a dangerous thing. It's a $7 supercomputer that pretends to be a microcontroller. Dual core 240MHz, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 8MB PSRAM, camera interface, Touch, Hall sensor, stuff you'll never use but love knowing is there.

It has so much headroom that you stop asking "Can I do this?" and start asking "What if I did this beautifully?"

That's why an ESP32 project never ends. There's always one more peripheral. One more sensor. One more ridiculous idea that the chip can absolutely handle, even if you can't.

You start with a mailbox sensor. You end with a mailbox that sends you a Telegram message with a haiku about the mailman, logs the temperature and humidity inside the box, and plays the Metal Gear Solid alert sound when junk mail arrives.

Is that automation? No. Is that necessary? Absolutely not. Is it yours? Completely.

We used to buy objects that were made for us. Now, for the first time in industrial history, normal people can make objects that are like us. Flawed, over-engineered, weirdly sentimental, with inside jokes baked into the firmware.

My house is full of objects that don't make sense to anyone else. A light that turns warm when it rains because I like rainy days. A switch that needs to be double-tapped because single taps are too impatient. A little desktop friend that just sits there and blinks at me when my build fails.

None of these automate anything. All of them make the place feel inhabited.

The Real Circuit

Here's what I actually think after a decade of burning my fingers with a soldering iron that was definitely off:

We tell ourselves we are building smart homes, but we are building haunted homes. Not haunted by ghosts, but haunted by our own attention.

Every time you choose a warm white LED over a cool white one, every time you tune a sensor threshold by hand, every time you add a silly little animation that only you will ever see — you are leaving a fingerprint in the machine.

The big tech companies are trying to make devices that work for everyone. We are making devices that work for one person. That's not a bug. That's the entire point.

Automation is the excuse we give our partners and our wallets. Art is the reason we actually do it at 1 AM on a Tuesday.

So the next time your "simple automatic plant waterer" has a custom PCB, a web dashboard you designed from scratch, and a name — you didn't fail at keeping scope small.

You succeeded at making something human.

You started as an engineer trying to save a fern. You ended as an artist who gave a fern a little robot guardian that breathes.

And honestly? The fern is still going to die. But what a way to go.

If this hit, you'll want what's on my workbench:

I turn these late-night spirals into buildable field kits. No cloud, no subscriptions, just hardware that feels like yours.

1. Hardware Signals Field Pack — ESP32 & Sub-GHz RF Research Lab
The lab I wish I had when I started. ESP32-S3 + CC1101 BOM, portable listening platform, real-world RF capture workflows, and the glue scripts so you stop re-writing the same Python parser for the 100th time. Build a defensive tool you can actually carry.
→ numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/hardwaresignals

2. ESP32 Phantom Networks — Portable Mesh & Offline Infrastructure
For when your art wants to leave the house. How to get ESP32s talking to each other with no router, no cloud, no ISP — wardriving instincts, pocket mesh, offline messaging. The foundation for every "what if it worked off-grid?" project.
→ numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/esp32phantom

Both live on numbpilled.gumroad.com — grab the one that matches the haunting you're building.

Clap 50x if your "quick weekend project" is now 6 months old and has a name. I see you.

articles.body_html:
I Tried Hono v5 RC: What Changed from v4, and What Breaks?

Will your app break when you upgrade to v5? Mine did.

TL;DR

With the Hono v5 release candidate out, I set up separate v4 and v5 environments and ran identical code in both. I measured five areas: type checking, runtime behavior, routing, performance, and size.

  • Every type-related breaking change was caught by the type checker. Start your migration with tsc --strict.
  • The real risks are three changes the type checker won't catch: c.json(undefined), the composition of onError() handlers, and changes to wildcard matching.
  • “Smaller” refers to the installed package. The final bundle actually grew by 302 bytes.

Here is the environment I used:

Item Value
Test date 2026-10-18
v4 hono@4.13.13
v5 hono@5.0.0-rc.1
Node.js v24.22.0
TypeScript 7.0.2
Machine Apple M4 (arm64)

Experimental code and raw data

Let me state my main takeaway up front:

The things that break in v5 are the places where v4 was permissive. c.req.json() returned any; c.req.query() concealed the possibility of undefined; and onError() silently overwrote previous handlers. Those were all places where v4's API gave a misleading picture. v5 is simply more honest. Migration may be inconvenient, but that is a different question from whether the design is sound.

This is a hands-on account of testing Hono v5 RC, written for Hono users who want to know what will break when they upgrade.

v5 is a release candidate. Behavior may change before the stable release. Everything here reflects testing on October 18, 2026.

1. Hono v5 Is “Hono for AI”

Before listing breaking changes, it's worth understanding what v5 is trying to accomplish. Once you see that, the individual changes start pointing in the same direction.

At Hono Conference 2026, creator Yusuke Wada described v5 as “Hono for AI.”

He described the goal of AI-friendly APIs as:

Abstracted, with fewer choices.

That was the key to understanding v5.

Changing c.req.json() so it no longer returns any, and turning onError() from a special function that can only be registered once into ordinary middleware, are part of the same idea: remove special cases and reduce the number of ways to do things.

A human might see any and reason, “Well, this will actually be a string, so it'll be fine.” When an LLM writes the code, that implicit assumption may not survive. If the types lie, the generated code can carry the same lie forward.

With that in mind, the changes below make a lot more sense.

2. Setting Up the Test Environments

I completely separated the directories to prevent v4 and v5 dependencies from mixing.

cd sandbox/v4
npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install hono@4
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node

cd ../v5
npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install hono@next      # installed 5.0.0-rc.1
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node

The RC is distributed under the next dist-tag. npm install hono@next is the method recommended by the official migration guide.

Here are the actual installed versions:

$ (cd sandbox/v4 && npm ls hono typescript)
v4@1.0.0
├── hono@4.13.13
└── typescript@7.0.2

$ (cd sandbox/v5 && npm ls hono typescript)
v5@1.0.0
├── hono@5.0.0-rc.1
└── typescript@7.0.2

$ node --version
v24.22.0

All tests used app.request() or app.fetch(). Since I didn't start an HTTP server, no runtime adapter was needed.

3. Stricter Types

c.req.json() Changes from any to unknown

In v4, this code passes type checking:

import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()

app.post('/users', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json() // any

  return c.json({
    name: body.name.toUpperCase(), // TypeScript accepts this
  })
})

If a number is sent as name, the code crashes at runtime. The type system provides no protection.

Running the same code through tsc --strict with v5 gives:

src/typecheck-json.ts(9,11): error TS18046: 'body' is of type 'unknown'.

You now have to narrow the type before accessing its properties.

There are three approaches. The first one listed in the official guide is supplying a type argument:

const body = await c.req.json<{ name: string }>()

But this is not runtime validation. The type argument merely declares what you expect. You can still make a false declaration and the compiler will accept it. Personally, I think silencing the error this way misses the point of returning unknown: inspect the value before using it.

The straightforward alternative is a type guard. This passed v5's type checker:

app.post('/users', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json()

  if (
    typeof body !== 'object' ||
    body === null ||
    !('name' in body) ||
    typeof body.name !== 'string'
  ) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Invalid body' }, 400)
  }

  return c.json({ name: body.name.toUpperCase() })
})

In real applications, the third option—using a validator and accessing the validated data through c.req.valid()—is usually the best choice. The official guide recommends it as well.

Destructuring c.req.query() Starts Producing Errors Everywhere

I think this change will affect more codebases:

const { name } = c.req.query()
const upper: string = name.toUpperCase()

const all = c.req.queries()
const tags: string[] = all.tag

This passes on v4. On v5:

src/typecheck-query.ts(7,25): error TS18048: 'name' is possibly 'undefined'.
src/typecheck-query.ts(10,9): error TS2322: Type 'string[] | undefined' is not assignable to type 'string[]'.
  Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'string[]'.

Calling query() without a key now has a return type of Record<string, string | undefined>. Consequently, destructured values start producing errors.

The Interesting Part: Runtime Values Are Unchanged

I sent GET /q?a=1&a=2 and compared the actual results.

v4 v5
c.req.query() {"a":"1"} {"a":"1"}
c.req.queries() {"a":["1","2"]} {"a":["1","2"]}

They're identical.

In other words, v5 didn't change the runtime behavior. In v4, looking up a nonexistent key could already return undefined; the types merely insisted it was a string.

Only the types became more honest. Every newly flagged line was already a potential bug in v4.

4. Error Handling Has Been Redesigned

This is the most interesting v5 change to me.

What Changed?

In v4, onError() looked like this:

app.onError((err, c) => {
  console.error(err.message)
  return c.json({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }, 500)
})

There was one handler for the whole app, with the signature (err, c).

In v5:

// Path-scoped error middleware
app.onError('/api/*', async (c, next) => {
  console.error(c.error?.message)
  c.header('X-Error-Handler', 'api')
  await next()
})

// Omitting the path registers '*' under the current basePath
app.onError((c) => {
  return c.json({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }, 500)
})

The signature becomes (c, next), and you read the error from c.error. You can also specify a path and register multiple handlers.

The intention is stated explicitly in PR #5541:

The goal is to model error and not-found handling using Hono's routing system, including middleware composition, path scoping, sub-application handling, and Router-level decoration.

Error handling has been rebuilt on top of the routing system. Internally, the handlers are registered with reserved methods called @ERROR and @NOT_FOUND. That means error handlers are resolved using the same underlying mechanism as ordinary routes.

notFound() now follows the same pattern:

app.notFound(
  '/api/*',
  async (c, next) => {
    c.header('x-not-found', 'api')
    await next()
  },
  (c) => c.text('API resource not found', 404)
)

Measurement: Does Path Scoping Work?

I tested it directly:

Request X-Error-Handler Status Body
/api/error api 500 {"error":"Internal Server Error"}
/other/error (absent) 500 {"error":"Internal Server Error"}

It works: only /api/* receives the extra header, while the common handler produces the final response.

Trying the same thing in v4 yields:

this.errorHandler is not a function

v4's onError() accepts only one argument. It saves the path string as if it were the handler, then fails when a request arrives. Registration itself doesn't complain. notFound() similarly threw TypeError: onNotFound is not a function.

Gotcha #1: Composition Instead of Overwriting

I expect this to be one of the biggest migration pitfalls.

I registered onError() twice and recorded which handlers ran:

Handlers executed Response
v4 ["second"] second
v5 ["first", "second"] second

v4 uses last-registration-wins replacement; v5 composes handlers.

Code that depended on a later registration replacing an earlier handler will now execute both.

When the first handler returns a response, the chain stops:

Handlers executed Response
v5 ["first"] first

Call next() to continue; return a response to stop. These are ordinary middleware rules.

And this won't produce a type error. Once you update the signature to (c, next), tsc passes. You may not notice the behavioral change until you actually run the app.

Gotcha #2: Old v4 Handlers Cause Confusing Runtime Errors

I also wondered what happens if you run a v4-style handler under v5.

First, the type checker correctly stops it:

src/typecheck-onerror-v4style.ts(7,21): error TS2339: Property 'message' does not exist on type 'Context<BlankEnv, string, any>'.
src/typecheck-onerror-v4style.ts(8,12): error TS2339: Property 'json' does not exist on type 'Next'.

It shows exactly what's changed: the first argument is now Context, and the second is Next.

But if you suppress those errors with @ts-expect-error and execute the code, you get:

Context is not finalized. Did you forget to return a Response object or `await next()`?

That message doesn't identify the root cause at all.

These were the arguments I observed:

{ "firstArgCtor": "Context", "firstArgIsContext": true, "secondArgType": "function" }

What your v4-style handler thinks is c is now the next function. It has no c.text(), so an exception occurs and the context never gets finalized. That's why the runtime reports this message.

Suppressing a type error can turn a straightforward migration fix into a long debugging session.

Throwing Values That Aren't Error Instances

In v4, throwing a string or object from a handler could escape past app.fetch().

In v5, the value is wrapped in an Error and sent to onError():

v4 v5
throw 'oops' Escapes outward message: 'oops' / cause: 'oops'
throw { code: 42 } Escapes outward message: '' / cause: { code: 42 }

One detail matters: when you throw an object, message is empty. The original value appears only in cause.

app.onError((c) => {
  console.log(c.error?.message) // '' if an object was thrown
  console.log(c.error?.cause)   // { code: 42 }
  return c.json({ error: 'wrapped' }, 500)
})

If your logs only include c.error.message, you'll be left with an unhelpful empty entry. Check cause too.

Being able to catch strange thrown values from third-party libraries is a welcome improvement.

5. The Most Dangerous Change the Type Checker Won't Catch

The behavior of c.json(undefined) has changed.

v4 v5
c.json(undefined) 200 / body length 0 500
c.json(() => 1) 200 / empty body 500

This is the actual exception thrown in v5:

TypeError: Value is not JSON serializable

The official explanation is that it now matches Response.json(). That makes sense.

The problem is that this does not produce a type error.

If a conditional expression can yield undefined and you pass it to c.json(), you can run tsc as many times as you like and it won't complain. Without a custom onError handler, the built-in handler returns 500, and you might discover the problem only in production.

Of all the migration checks in this article, I would prioritize this one the highest. You need tests to catch it.

One likely example is returning a database lookup directly:

const user = await db.query.users.findFirst({ where: eq(users.id, id) })
return c.json(user) // undefined if no user is found

In v4, an overlooked missing-user case could return 200 with an empty body rather than the intended 404. In v5, it becomes a 500. That means many of the new 500s were bugs already present in v4—v5 merely exposes them.

Another possible case is passing the return value of a void function directly. TypeScript might catch that when the type is void, but it can slip through if any is involved.

6. Wildcard Matching Is Now Consistent

In v4, Different Routers Gave Different Results

I registered the same routes in four routers under v4 and exhaustively checked the matches.

Route Path SmartRouter RegExpRouter TrieRouter PatternRouter
/x*/y /x/y ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/x*/y /xz/y ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
/x*/y /x/z/y ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/x*y /xay ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild//card ❌ ❌ ✅ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild/a/card ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

The results disagreed in three of six cases.

For /wild/*/card, only TrieRouter matched /wild//card. In other words, switching routers could silently change which paths matched.

In v5, All Four Routers Agree

I repeated the same checks under v5:

Route Path SmartRouter RegExpRouter TrieRouter PatternRouter
/x*/y /x/y ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
/x*/y /xz/y ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
/x*/y /x/z/y ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/x*y /xay ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild//card ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild/a/card ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

All four agree, matching the table in the official documentation.

The rules are now:

  • A * at the end of a segment is a wildcard; it can match an empty remainder.
  • A * in the middle of a segment, as in /x*y, is not a wildcard.
  • A segment consisting of just * matches one nonempty segment.

The changed results are /x*/y versus /x/y (❌ → ✅ in every router), and /x*y versus /xay (✅ → ❌ for the regex-based routers). These changes also escape static type checking.

Gotcha #3: Adding One Route Changes the Router

This was the most interesting discovery of the whole experiment.

If you register both /x*/y and /x/*, v5's RegExpRouter cannot handle the combination:

UnsupportedPathError: /x/*

SmartRouter catches that exception and falls back to TrieRouter.

I checked which router the app eventually selected:

Registered routes Router selected in v5
/x/* only SmartRouter + RegExpRouter
/x*/y + /x/* SmartRouter + TrieRouter

Adding a single route changed the router used at runtime.

And when I tested those conflicting routes under v4 and v5, even the selected handler differed:

v4 v5
Request to /x/y Handler for /x/* Handler for /x*/y

Routing can change silently, making this difficult to spot without targeted tests.

Measurement: How Much Does Fallback Cost?

A different router should affect performance, so I measured 50,000 requests to GET /users/:id across 12 rounds.

Router Median Mean Minimum
No conflict SmartRouter + RegExpRouter 138.68 ms 152.28 ms 132.35 ms
Conflict SmartRouter + TrieRouter 148.57 ms 163.99 ms 146.25 ms
Difference +7.1% +7.7% +10.5%

The fallback was slower on all three measures.

A disclosure: I reran this benchmark. With just three rounds, I initially measured a 3.3% difference. On rerunning it, I got 8.1%. Three rounds weren't enough for a stable conclusion.

Even after increasing the count to 12 rounds, the raw data contained outliers such as 287 ms and 271 ms (possibly from garbage collection or OS scheduling). I therefore consider the +10.5% difference in minimum times, which is less affected by those outliers, closer to the underlying cost.

Why Would It Be Slower?

According to the official documentation, RegExpRouter compiles registered routes into one large regular expression and obtains a match in a single operation. TrieRouter uses a trie and supports the complete range of patterns, but isn't as fast as RegExpRouter.

SmartRouter defaults to [new RegExpRouter(), new TrieRouter()]. It tries the faster router first, then selects the more general implementation if necessary, continuing to use its choice thereafter. The design is essentially: try the fast one; fall back to the fully featured one if needed.

This test exercised that fallback path, so a performance difference was expected.

With RegExpRouter's consolidated expression, I would expect matching costs to remain fairly stable as routes are added. TrieRouter traverses a tree, so I would expect costs to depend on path segments and the route structure. If that's correct, the 7–10% gap I measured in this small app might be larger in an app with hundreds of routes.

Conversely, in a small application the fallback probably won't be noticeable.

But the exact 7–10% isn't the most important part. The bigger issue is that adding one route can silently switch the router. You won't see that in the logs or the types.

And this might be about more than speed. As shown above, a change in router selection can affect which handler matches. My measurements established that across v4 and v5; I suspect combinations and registration order within v5 could expose related issues, but I didn't test that hypothesis fully.

7. Is It Faster?

I also benchmarked the core routing performance.

Caution: this is an in-process microbenchmark using app.fetch().
It does not represent real HTTP-server or production Cloudflare Workers performance.
It includes no network, TLS, or process-boundary costs.

I ran 100,000 requests to GET /users/:id, with 20,000 warmup requests, alternating v4 and v5 for 10 rounds.

Statistic v4 v5 Difference
Median 270.53 ms 266.50 ms v5 1.5% faster
Mean 278.24 ms 271.85 ms v5 2.3% faster
Minimum 258.31 ms 255.59 ms v5 1.1% faster

My conclusion: the difference is within benchmark noise.

v5 was slightly faster by each metric, but the distributions overlap substantially: v4's minimum (258.31 ms) is lower than v5's median (266.50 ms). This test doesn't justify claiming that v5 is faster.

Benchmarks Without Round Counts Are Hard to Interpret

Another disclosure: at five rounds I measured a 2.9% difference. After increasing the test to ten rounds, it fell to 1.5%.

Same code, same machine, same day. Changing only the number of rounds nearly halved the apparent advantage.

The router fallback benchmark behaved similarly (3.3% at three rounds; 7.1% at twelve).

When discussing single-digit percentage differences in microbenchmarks, publishing the round count and the distribution matters. I learned that firsthand. Every measurement in this article includes its round count.

And unchanged core routing performance isn't bad news. Performance isn't the primary goal of v5's redesign.

8. What Actually Got “Smaller”?

In v5, runtime adapters were moved out of the core hono package into separate @hono/* packages. I expect people to describe that as “making Hono lighter,” so I measured what actually became smaller.

Installed Package Size Really Did Shrink

I queried the npm registry's unpackedSize field:

Unpacked size File count
hono@4.13.13 1.23 MB 574
hono@5.0.0-rc.1 0.66 MB 310
Difference -46% -46%

Running du -sh on my local node_modules showed 2.8 MB → 1.5 MB, also -46%.

Yusuke Wada's Hono Conference 2026 presentation reported 1.29 MB → 0.70 MB, again -46%, with file counts of 574 → 310. The file counts matched exactly. The slightly different absolute sizes probably reflect differences in the referenced versions.

Three independent ways of looking at it produced the same reduction. I think that number is trustworthy.

But the Bundle Got Bigger

Here's the catch: I built actual bundles with esbuild.

Entry point v4 v5 Difference
Core only 18,528 B 18,830 B +302 B (+1.6%)
With adapter 22,760 B 22,923 B +163 B (+0.7%)

It increased rather than decreased.

Thinking about it, that makes sense. The package shrank because the CJS build was removed and adapters were split into separate packages. A CJS build that your bundler never used wasn't contributing to the bundle anyway. And once you install @hono/bun, the adapter code still comes along.

Code previously excluded by tree shaking has simply been separated at the package level. The amount of code ultimately bundled hasn't meaningfully changed.

When saying “Hono v5 is lighter,” specify whether you mean installation size or final bundle size. The first is true; the second was not supported by my measurements.

9. ESM-Only Packaging and Adapter Separation

It's ESM-Only, but require() Still Works

v5 removes the CJS build and becomes ESM-only. The official guide requires Node.js 22.12 or later.

Interestingly, under that requirement, require('hono') still works.

Test Result
require('hono') in v4 OK
require('hono') in v5 OK
import('hono/bun') in v4 Resolves
import('hono/bun') in v5 ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED

Node.js 22.12 and later support loading eligible ESM modules with require(), so using require() doesn't necessarily fail just because a package is ESM-only. The official guide mentions this, and my test confirmed it.

However, subpaths such as hono/bun have disappeared from exports, so those definitely break. The issue is not necessarily CommonJS-style loading; it's the old subpath imports.

All Eight Adapters Were Published on September 28, 2026

I checked their initial publication dates in the npm registry.

Package First published
@hono/bun / @hono/deno / @hono/cloudflare-workers 2026-09-28
@hono/vercel / @hono/netlify 2026-09-28
@hono/aws-lambda / @hono/lambda-edge 2026-09-28
@hono/service-worker 2026-09-28

All eight released version 1.0.0 on the same day. They're the packages split out for v5.

@hono/node-server is not one of these eight. Its first release was on January 7, 2023, and it was already a separate package during v4. Don't confuse it with the newly extracted adapters.

Adapter Separation and Supply-Chain Security

I had heard the argument that separating adapters could reduce the attack surface for supply-chain compromises. I decided to investigate.

On June 23, 2026, Yusuke Wada presented “Hono Supply Chain Compromise Countermeasures: Lessons from Three Libraries” at GMO Flatt Security's meetup on what OSS developers should do about software supply-chain attacks.

The three case studies were axios, TanStack, and Mastra, each with a different attack path:

Library Attack path
axios Social engineering: malware on a maintainer's machine stealing credentials
TanStack Cache poisoning through pull_request_target (“Pwn Request”); possible even without merging the PR
Mastra npm account takeover

Among the Hono-side mitigations was removing adapter functionality from the core. Other measures included:

  • Moving npm publishing from local machines to GitHub Actions with OIDC trusted publishing.
  • Avoiding pull_request_target.
  • Pinning GitHub Actions to lock down the environment.
  • Removing Dev Containers and Gitpod configuration.

This suggests adapter separation is not only about package size; it's also about reducing the attack surface. Size and file count were emphasized at Hono Conference 2026, but the same change had been discussed in a security context back in June.

But It Doesn't Reduce the Dependency Count

Here's something I verified myself.

I queried npm registry metadata for dependencies:

Runtime dependencies
hono@4.13.13 0
hono@5.0.0-rc.1 0
@hono/bun@1.0.1 0 (only hono as a peer)

For comparison, express had 28 and axios had 4 in the registry data I checked.

Hono already had zero external runtime dependencies in v4. Splitting adapters didn't reduce that count. It's zero in both versions.

What decreased was the amount of code shipped in the core package. As shown in section 8, the file count dropped from 574 to 310.

For a zero-dependency library, the package's own distributed code is itself part of the supply-chain attack surface. In that sense, removing adapters is better understood not as shrinking the dependency graph, but as roughly halving the code shipped together in a single package.

10. defineHandler(): The “Fewer Choices” Philosophy in Action

The experimental defineHandler() API is the clearest example of the “abstracted, with fewer choices” goal from section 1. I tried it because it shows where the design is heading.

The simplest example is:

import { defineHandler } from 'hono/factory'

app.get('/ping', defineHandler(() => ({ pong: true })))

ping -> 200 {"pong":true}

There's no c.json(). The returned value is converted into a Response. An object becomes JSON, a string or JSX becomes HTML, and null or undefined produces a 204.

Request and response validation can also be defined in one place:

app.post(
  '/users',
  defineHandler({ json: NameSchema })((c, input) => ({
    name: input.json.name.toUpperCase(),
  }))
)

NameSchema can be anything implementing Standard Schema, including Zod schemas.

With invalid input, I received:

schema ng -> 400 {"error":"Validation failed","issues":[{"slot":"json","issues":[{"message":"name must be a string","path":"name"}]}]}

I ran into one surprise: if you pass an ordinary validation function rather than a Standard Schema and throw inside it, you get a 500 instead of a 400.

invalid -> 500 Internal Server Error

Because the API also accepts validation functions, I assumed failures would be handled identically. But in my testing, only the Standard Schema path wrapped failures into an HTTPException that returned 400. If you need that 400 response, use the Standard Schema format.

And the type definition contains a comment that captures the philosophy perfectly:

A JSON Response by c.json() is not accepted, because it bypasses the response validation. Return the value instead.

Returning c.json() is explicitly forbidden by the types, because doing so would bypass response validation.

This is a shift from “several approaches usually work” to “there's one preferred approach and the types prevent alternatives.” It's a concrete expression of the design goal described earlier.

Note that defineHandler() is experimental and may change before the stable release.

11. Migration Checklist

Here are my priorities based on what I actually measured.

First, Run tsc --strict (Type-Detectable Changes)

  • Direct property access on the result of c.req.json().
  • Destructuring such as const { x } = c.req.query().
  • Treating c.req.queries() values as guaranteed string[].
  • Changing app.onError((err, c) => ...) to (c) => ... and reading c.error.

The compiler will point these out. You can fix them systematically.

Next, Fix the Three Changes Types Can't Detect

  • Any place that might pass undefined to c.json(): it now returns 500. Without tests, this is easy to miss.
  • Multiple registrations of onError() or notFound(): handlers compose rather than overwrite one another.
  • Routes containing wildcards: /x*/y now matches /x/y.

This is the real migration work. Passing the type checker is not enough.

Also look for conflicting routes such as /x*/y and /x/*, which can trigger router fallback.

Update Imports and Removed APIs

  • hono/<runtime> → @hono/<runtime> (eight packages).
  • hono/cloudflare-pages: no direct replacement; migrate to Workers.
  • app.mount() → mount() from hono/mount.
  • app.fire() → fire(app) from @hono/service-worker.
  • c.req.routePath / c.req.matchedRoutes → hono/route.
  • getColorEnabledAsync() → getColorEnabled(c.env).
  • toSSG() hook options → plugins (explicitly include defaultPlugin() when needed).

One small detail: UnOfficalStatusCode was corrected to UnofficialStatusCode. A long-standing typo from v4 has finally been fixed.

12. What I Didn't Verify

I couldn't investigate everything. Here are the remaining questions:

  • Priority of sub-app notFound() handlers when they're integrated via route(). The PR describes deeper-nested sub-apps taking priority, and registration order breaking ties at the same depth, but I didn't test it.
  • How basePath() interacts with onError() path resolution.
  • Benchmarks through a real HTTP server; all my measurements used app.fetch().
  • Performance in an actual Cloudflare Workers environment.
  • Integration of @hono/zod-validator with c.req.valid().
  • Hono CLI 1.0 RC.

And again, v5 was still an RC during testing. These behaviors could change before the stable release.

13. Conclusion

What struck me most was this: the places that break in v5 are the places v4 was too permissive.

The any from c.req.json() and the overly confident string types from c.req.query() gave developers misleading information. v5 stops doing that. The actual query behavior hasn't changed at all. Making onError() composable similarly replaces a special-case singleton with ordinary middleware.

The direction is consistent with “abstracted, with fewer choices.” Even defineHandler() rejecting c.json() through the type system follows the same philosophy.

The migration cost isn't negligible. Fortunately, tsc --strict highlights much of it. The three things to watch most closely are the changes static types don't detect: c.json(undefined), composition of onError() handlers, and wildcard matching. You'll need tests or manual inspection for those.

Performance was effectively unchanged. Installation size dropped by nearly half, but bundle size did not. The reason to upgrade to v5 isn't speed or bundle size; it's a cleaner, more consistent API design.

Would I deploy the RC to production today? No, I'd wait for stable. But running a build of an existing project against hono@next is absolutely worthwhile. The resulting type errors will immediately give you an idea of the migration effort.

Finally, two predictions for the stable release:

If one of these changes gets revised, I think it'll be defineHandler(). It's explicitly marked experimental, and behavior such as “throwing in a validation function returns 500 rather than 400” still has rough edges. Conversely, the onError() redesign and wildcard unification seem well specified in their PRs and implemented thoroughly, so I expect them to remain.

My guess is that the removal of hono/cloudflare-pages will cause the most migration pain. Most changes can be fixed by rewriting code, but this one has no direct replacement and requires a separate move to Workers. c.req.query() may produce far more type errors, but those are mechanical fixes. A single change without a drop-in replacement can cost more time than hundreds of compiler errors.

I'll revisit these predictions when the stable version arrives.

As for my project? It broke, just as expected.

References

  • Migrating to v5 — Hono — Official breaking-change guide; the source for my test cases.
  • feat!: add routable error and not-found middleware (honojs/hono#5541) — onError() / notFound() redesign, reserved route methods, and sub-app priority rules.
  • Hono Conference 2026 — Yusuke Wada — The “Hono for AI” framing and package size figures.
  • honojs/hono releases — Release dates of 5.0.0-rc.0 (2026-10-08) and 5.0.0-rc.1 (2026-10-10).
  • Hono Supply Chain Compromise Countermeasures — Yusuke Wada — Case studies of axios, TanStack, and Mastra; adapter extraction as a mitigation. (Japanese)
  • “What Should OSS Developers Do Now?” meetup report — kouki_engineer — Attendee report on the June 23, 2026 GMO Flatt Security meetup. (Japanese)
  • npm registry: hono — Source for dependencies, unpackedSize, and fileCount.
  • Standard Schema — Common schema interface accepted by defineHandler().
  • Routers — Hono — RegExpRouter, TrieRouter, SmartRouter, and default selection.
  • Mount Middleware — Hono — Migration destination for the removed app.mount().

articles.title: TypeScript Is Unsound on Purpose: 7 Programs That Type-Check, Then Crash
articles.description: TypeScript's design goals rule out a sound type system. Here are 7 programs that pass tsc --strict, throw at runtime, and the fix for each.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Non-goal number three on the TypeScript Design Goals page reads: "Apply a sound or 'provably correct' type system. Instead, strike a balance between correctness and productivity." The team wrote that down on purpose.

The handbook says the same thing in its own words. The type compatibility chapter has a section called "A Note on Soundness" that says TypeScript "allows certain operations that can't be known at compile-time to be safe," and that the places where it does so "were carefully considered."

So a green tsc --strict run tells you your code stayed inside the trade-offs the team picked, and those trade-offs include programs that throw a TypeError. Below are seven programs that compile under --strict and fail at runtime, the rule that lets each one through, and what closes it, where something does. Every rule is linked to the doc that states it, so you can paste any snippet into the TypeScript playground and check it yourself.

What --strict covers, and what it skips

The strict flag turns on the strict family: strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, noImplicitAny, useUnknownInCatchVariables and five more. Two checks that matter below are not in that family: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes. The TypeScript 4.1 release notes say the index check "is not automatically enabled by the strict flag" because "it might be noisy for a lot of code."

Every snippet here assumes --strict and nothing else. One of them dies the moment you add a single line to tsconfig.json. The rest need a pattern, a lint rule, or a runtime check, because no flag exists for them.

Variance: the array and the method

1. A cat in the dog array 

class Animal {
  name = "animal";
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  bark() { return "woof"; }
}
class Cat extends Animal {
  meow() { return "meow"; }
}

function adoptCat(shelter: Animal[]) {
  shelter.push(new Cat());
}

const kennel: Dog[] = [new Dog()];
adoptCat(kennel);
for (const dog of kennel) dog.bark(); // TypeError on the Cat

Dog[] is assignable to Animal[] because arrays relate covariantly: if Dog fits Animal, then Dog[] fits Animal[]. That is safe for reading and wrong for writing. push takes an Animal, the Cat goes in, and the loop calls bark on a cat.

The fix: when a function only reads, type the parameter as readonly Animal[]. push doesn't exist on that type, so the write becomes a compile error. Callers can still pass a Dog[], because the handbook notes that a mutable array assigns to a ReadonlyArray but not the other way around.

2. The method that only takes strings 

interface Handler {
  handle(input: string | number): void;
}

const h: Handler = {
  handle(input: string) {
    console.log(input.toUpperCase());
  },
};

h.handle(42); // TypeError at runtime: no toUpperCase on 42

strictFunctionTypes arrived in TypeScript 2.6 and checks function parameters contravariantly. It skips methods on purpose. The release notes say the stricter check covers all function types "except those originating in method or constructor declarations," and that "methods are excluded specifically to ensure generic classes and interfaces (such as Array<T>) continue to mostly relate covariantly." The TSConfig reference adds that the team found "a large number of inherently unsafe class hierarchies, including some in the DOM" while building the flag.

So a member written in method syntax stays bivariant, and an implementation that only accepts string gets through. That same carve-out is why program 1 compiles: push is a method on Array<T>.

The fix: declare the member as a property, handle: (input: string | number) => void. Now the same object literal is a compile error. The typescript-eslint rule method-signature-style enforces property style by default, and its docs state that "methods are always bivariant in their arguments, while function properties are contravariant."

Promises the checker doesn't track

3. A narrowed field that changes under you 

interface Profile {
  readonly nickname: string | null;
}

function greet(p: Profile, onGreet: () => void) {
  if (p.nickname !== null) {
    onGreet();
    console.log(p.nickname.toUpperCase());
  }
}

const live = { nickname: "kit" as string | null };
greet(live, () => {
  live.nickname = null;
}); // TypeError at runtime: nickname is null

The object types handbook page says TypeScript "doesn't factor in whether properties on two types are readonly when checking whether those types are compatible, so readonly properties can also change via aliasing." live is mutable, greet sees it through a readonly lens, and the callback writes through the original reference. Delete readonly from Profile and the program still compiles. The modifier was never the guard.

What actually lets it through is narrowing. After p.nickname !== null, the compiler keeps that narrowing across the onGreet() call. Issue #9998, "Trade-offs in Control Flow Analysis", explains why: resetting every narrowing after every call is the pessimistic option, and Anders Hejlsberg called the optimistic assumption "the best compromise."

No flag covers this one. Copy the value into a local before you call out, const nick = p.nickname;, then check and use nick. A callback can't reassign your const, so that narrowing holds. And keep the asymmetry in mind: readonly arrays are checked, readonly properties are not.

4. The key that isn't there 

const ports: Record<string, number> = { web: 8080 };

const db = ports["db"]; // typed as number
console.log(db.toFixed(0)); // TypeError at runtime: db is undefined

An index signature like Record<string, number> promises a number for any string key. ports["db"] is typed number and holds undefined. Arrays behave the same way: reading past the end gives you the element type, not undefined.

The fix: noUncheckedIndexedAccess. It adds undefined to every read through an index signature and every array index, so db.toFixed stops compiling until you check it. The cost is noise in index-based for loops, and the 4.1 notes point you at for...of or forEach instead.

Information lost on the way up

5. The optional property that was there all along 

interface Base {
  id: string;
}
interface Job {
  id: string;
  retries?: number;
}

const raw = { id: "job-1", retries: "three" };
const base: Base = raw; // extra property: fine
const job: Job = base; // missing optional: fine

console.log(job.retries?.toFixed(0)); // TypeError at runtime

Two legal steps. raw to Base: excess property checks run only on a fresh object literal, and the handbook's excess property checks section says assigning the object to another variable gets around them. Base to Job: Base has no retries, and a missing property satisfies an optional one. In the middle, the compiler forgets retries existed. At the end it assumes number | undefined. The string "three" isn't nullish, so ?. doesn't save you.

Nothing in tsconfig closes this. exactOptionalPropertyTypes only controls whether you may write undefined into an optional property. Exact object types, which would close it, have been an open proposal in issue #12936 since December 2016. When a reader raised this case on his Effective TypeScript repo, Dan Vanderkam called it "definitely another source of unsoundness" and pointed to Item 48 of his book, which covers it. The pattern that works: don't round-trip objects through a narrower interface, and validate data at the boundary where it enters your program.

Where you told the compiler to trust you

6. The assertion that skipped the check 

interface Account {
  id: string;
  roles: string[];
}

const body = '{"id":"u1"}';
const data: unknown = JSON.parse(body);
const account = data as Account;

console.log(account.roles.includes("admin")); // TypeError

The everyday types handbook page says type assertions "are removed by the compiler," and that "there won't be an exception or null generated if the type assertion is wrong." The cast from unknown is allowed because assertions may move to a "more specific or less specific version of a type." account.roles is undefined at runtime.

The fix: replace the cast with a runtime check, either a schema validator such as Zod or a hand-written guard (see program 7 before you trust one). To ban casts outright, typescript-eslint's consistent-type-assertions accepts assertionStyle: "never", which still allows as const.

7. The type guard that lies 

type Cat = { kind: "cat"; meow(): string };
type Dog = { kind: "dog"; bark(): string };

function isCat(pet: Cat | Dog): pet is Cat {
  return "bark" in pet; // inverted check, still compiles
}

function adopt(): Cat | Dog {
  return { kind: "dog", bark: () => "woof" };
}

const pet = adopt();
if (isCat(pet)) {
  pet.meow(); // TypeError at runtime: a Dog has no meow
}

A type predicate is a promise you make. The compiler doesn't prove it. The narrowing handbook page says that whenever a guard is called, TypeScript "will narrow that variable to that specific type if the original type is compatible." It reads the signature. Nothing compares the body with the claim. Dan Vanderkam's post on unsoundness makes the same point: with a guard, "you're still asserting that your type guard really guards the type."

The fix: since TypeScript 5.5, the compiler can infer a predicate from the body when four conditions hold: no explicit return type or predicate annotation, a single return, no mutation of the parameter, and a boolean expression tied to a refinement of the parameter. An inferred predicate comes from the check itself, so the two can't disagree. Keep explicit predicates for checks the compiler can't follow, and give each one a unit test with a matching and a non-matching value.

Does TypeScript 7 change any of this?

TypeScript 7.0 shipped on July 8, 2026, with the compiler ported to Go in the typescript-go repo. The announcement says the port kept "the structure and logic of the original codebase" to keep results consistent, and that 7.0 "is made to be compatible with TypeScript 6.0's type-checking and command-line behavior."

The differences it lists are elsewhere: flags deprecated in 6.0 become hard errors, strict now defaults to true, template literal types preserve Unicode code points, JSDoc support was reworked, and changing the --checkers count can surface order-dependent results. None of those touch the seven rules above, so by the team's own compatibility statement all seven still compile on 7.0. The new strict default doesn't help either, since every program here already passes --strict.

The seven, side by side:

# Hole What closes it
1 Array covariance readonly T[] parameters
2 Method bivariance Property-style members, method-signature-style
3 Narrowing kept across a callback Copy to a const before callbacks
4 Unchecked index reads noUncheckedIndexedAccess
5 Optional-property widening Validate at the boundary (no flag)
6 Assertions Runtime validation, assertionStyle: "never"
7 Lying type guards Inferred predicates, tested guards

And the one config line that costs nothing to add:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true
  }
}

TypeScript gives you a checker that catches most mistakes and tells you in writing which ones it lets through. Add noUncheckedIndexedAccess today, and put the other six on your review checklist.

If this was useful

Every program in this post comes down to one question: what does assignability actually check? The TypeScript Type System is the book on that question. It covers variance and bivariance, including the function-versus-method split behind programs 1 and 2, plus the generic, conditional and branded types you reach for when the built-in rules are too loose.

The TypeScript Library has five books. Start with the first two if TypeScript is your main language, swap in a bridge book if you are coming from the JVM or PHP, and add the fifth if you ship TypeScript at work:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Day 1 of Building HYNA-Stage: Slaying OAuth Loops & Adding GitHub Auth on a $150 Phone
articles.description: Welcome to Day 1 of the public build log for HYNA-Stage.   For those catching up: We are HYNAWEB. I’m...
articles.body_html:
Welcome to Day 1 of the public build log for HYNA-Stage.

For those catching up: We are HYNAWEB. I’m Harun (12-year-old Founder & CEO) and my co-founder is Akhouri (CTO). We are building enterprise-grade developer infrastructure entirely on a $150 Android phone using Termux.

Our mission with HYNA-Stage? Spin up isolated Firecracker microVMs in <5 seconds so AI agents have a safe, instant place to test code.

Today’s mission wasn’t about adding flashy features. It was about fixing the foundation: Authentication.

If users can’t log in smoothly, the product is dead. Here are the 3 "Boss Fights" we faced and conquered today to make HYNAWEB's auth flow bulletproof.

🐛 Boss Fight 1: The OAuth Hash Loop

  • The Symptom: Users clicked "Login with GitHub," authenticated successfully, but got dumped at the root URL (/#access_token=...) instead of the dashboard.
  • The Root Cause: Supabase rejected our redirectTo URL due to a hyphen mismatch (hynastage vs hyna-stage) in the configuration, falling back to the default Site URL and leaving the token stranded in the hash.
  • The Fix: I wrote a vanilla JS hash interceptor in index.html to instantly catch the token, forward it to dashboard.html, and parse it before the session timed out.

🐛 Boss Fight 2: The 401 JWT Gateway Block

  • The Symptom: Our custom CLI API keys were getting hit with 401 Unauthorized before even reaching the function logic.
  • The Root Cause: Supabase Edge Functions enforce JWT verification by default. It saw our custom CLI request, didn't recognize the JWT, and slammed the door.
  • The Fix: Disabled "Verify JWT with legacy secret" in the Supabase Edge Function settings, allowing our custom API key validation logic to run unimpeded.

🐛 Boss Fight 3: The RLS Permission Denied

  • The Symptom: Database queries returned 0 rows, even though the API key was valid.
  • The Root Cause: New Supabase projects require explicit Postgres GRANT permissions for the service_role, even when using the sb_secret_ bypass key. Row-Level Security was blocking the backend from reading its own table.
  • The Fix: Executed GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON TABLE public.api_keys TO service_role; in the SQL editor.

🏆 The Result

GitHub Auth is now live and buttery smooth. The redirect works perfectly. The CLI can talk to the database without getting blocked by the gatekeeper.

Today's HYNAWEB Stats:

  • Bugs squashed: 3
  • Auth flows perfected: 1
  • Laptops used: 0

Building cloud infrastructure on a mobile terminal means you don't have the luxury of bloat or easy debugging tools. Every fix has to be precise.

Tomorrow, we tackle the deployment pipeline and the Termux text-truncation nightmare.

Follow the series to see how we build the infrastructure for the AI era, one bash script at a time.

We are HYNAWEB. We don't just build apps; we build the future. 🐯☁️🚀
