articles.title: Why Google Analytics breaks inside a Figma plugin, and what I built instead
articles.description: I make Figma plugins. The numbers Figma gives me about them are installs and likes on the Community...
articles.body_html:
I make Figma plugins. The numbers Figma gives me about them are installs and likes on the Community page. Neither one says whether anybody opened the plugin this week, or which of its buttons they pressed.

The usual answer on the web is Google Analytics. Paste the gtag snippet into a plugin's ui.html, open the console, and you get this:

SecurityError: Failed to read the 'cookie' property from 'Document':
Cookies are disabled inside 'data:' URLs.

The snippet is fine. The place it runs in is the problem, and that place turned out to be interesting enough that I ended up writing my own SDK for it. This post is about what I ran into.

A plugin is two programs

The first program is the main code, usually code.ts. It runs in a sandbox next to the document. It has the figma API and fetch. It has no DOM, no window and no document.

The second program is the UI. You pass an HTML string to figma.showUI(), and Figma loads that string into an iframe. The page gets a data: URL, so its origin is null.

Cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB all belong to an origin. A null origin owns none of them, and reading any of them throws. That is the error above.

The two programs cannot call each other. They talk through postMessage, and that is the only channel.

So the half that knows who the user is (the sandbox, through figma.currentUser) cannot see a click. The half that sees every click (the iframe) cannot remember anything and does not know who is clicking.

Web analytics assumes one page with a cookie jar. I had two halves and no jar.

Problem 1: the key is on one side, the buttons on the other

I wanted the developer to write the API key once. The sandbox is the right place for it, because the Figma data is there too:

// code.ts
import { tode } from '@tode-sdk/core';

figma.showUI(__html__);
await tode.init({ apiKey: 'your-api-key' });

init() reads the user id, the plugin id, the editor type (Figma, FigJam, Dev Mode, Slides) and posts all of it to the iframe in one message:

figma.ui.postMessage({ type: 'TODE_DATA', message: config });

The UI adapter listens for that message and configures itself. After that, both halves can send events with the same identity.

That is the happy path. It has a hole in it.

Problem 2: the first message gets lost

figma.showUI() returns before the iframe has loaded anything. If init() is fast and the UI bundle is slow, the config is posted to a page with no listener yet. Nobody hears it, the UI never becomes ready, and no error appears anywhere.

The same thing happens when a plugin closes its UI and calls showUI() again later. The new iframe starts empty.

The fix is a handshake that starts from the UI. When an adapter attaches its listener, it asks:

window.parent.postMessage(
  { pluginMessage: { type: 'TODE_UI_READY' }, pluginId: '*' },
  '*',
);

The sandbox answers by posting the config again. One detail matters here. Most plugins already set figma.ui.onmessage for their own messages, and assigning it a second time would overwrite their handler. figma.ui.on('message', ...) adds a listener next to it and leaves theirs alone, so the SDK uses that.

The plugin's own handler still receives the TODE_UI_READY message. It has to ignore message types it does not know, which a well-written handler does anyway.

Problem 3: events that fire before the SDK is ready

A common first event is "plugin opened". It fires on mount, before the config has crossed over from the sandbox.

My first version told developers to wrap every call in if (isReady). That is a rule people forget, and the event they lose is the most important one.

Now the SDK keeps early events in a queue with the time they happened, and sends them when the config arrives:

if (this._isReady && this._apiKey) {
  await this.send(event);
  return;
}
if (this._queue.length >= MAX_QUEUED_EVENTS) return; // 50
this._queue.push(event); // event.timestamp was set at call time

The cap is 50. If something calls trackAction in a loop while the SDK is not ready, I would rather drop events than grow an array forever inside someone else's plugin.

Problem 4: how long is a session

On a website, session length comes from page views with timestamps and a timeout. A plugin has no pages. It has a panel that is open for a while and then is gone.

I did not want to depend on an unload event firing in an iframe that Figma can remove at any moment. So I turned the question around. The UI opens a WebSocket when it becomes ready and holds it. The server writes down when the socket opened. When the socket closes, for any reason, the server writes one session row with the duration.

A closed panel, a closed tab and a crashed browser all look the same to the server: the socket is gone. No goodbye message is needed.

The client sends ping every 5 seconds. If the server hears nothing for 60 seconds, it ends the session itself, so a dead connection cannot inflate the numbers.

That covers a panel someone opens and closes. Three other cases needed more work.

The first is laptop sleep. People leave a plugin open, close the lid and come back hours later. The socket is dead and the panel is still on screen. The SDK reconnects with backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, capped at 30s) and never gives up while the UI is open. It also listens for the browser's online event and retries at once when the network is back.

The second follows from the first. Each reconnect is a new session row on the server. Every connection carries the same session_id, generated once per UI load, so the rows can be grouped later.

The third is React. Five components calling useTode() used to mean five sockets and five sessions for one person. The socket is now shared and reference-counted. The first caller opens it, and it closes when the last holder is gone.

Problem 5: analytics must never break the plugin

If my server is down, a designer's export button still has to work. So nothing in the SDK throws. init() and trackAction() catch everything and log to the console.

The sandbox made this harder than I expected. It has fetch, and it has no AbortController. Its fetch ignores signal. A request that hangs cannot be cancelled there, which means await tode.init() could block a plugin's startup.

The workaround is a race against a timer:

if (typeof AbortController === 'undefined') {
  const timeout = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timed out')), 10_000);
  });
  return Promise.race([fetch(url, rest), timeout])
    .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

The request itself may still be hanging somewhere. The plugin has stopped waiting for it, and that is the part I care about.

Counting people without a cookie

A cookie exists on the web because the page does not know who you are. A plugin does. figma.currentUser.id is stable for a Figma account, and you get it by adding one line to the manifest:

{
  "permissions": ["currentuser"],
  "networkAccess": {
    "allowedDomains": [
      "https://processing.usetode.dev",
      "wss://processing.usetode.dev"
    ]
  }
}

That id is enough to tell a new user from a returning one, which is where retention comes from. The SDK sends the id and nothing else about the person: no name, no email, no file contents.

Country is looked up on the server from the request IP. The IP is not stored.

Without the currentuser permission, figma.currentUser is null. The SDK sends an empty value in that case and events still arrive. You lose unique users and keep everything else.

What it looks like from the plugin side

After all of that, the part a plugin developer writes is small:

import { useTode } from '@tode-sdk/figma-react';

function ExportButton() {
  const { trackAction, trackActionWithMetric } = useTode();

  const onExport = async () => {
    const layers = await exportSelection();
    trackAction('export_clicked');
    trackActionWithMetric('layers_exported', layers.length);
  };

  return <button onClick={onExport}>Export</button>;
}

There are adapters for React, Vue, Angular, Svelte and plain TypeScript. They are thin. The queue, the handshake and the socket all live in the core package, so I only fix each bug once.

What I have not solved

There is no way to learn from plugin code that an event failed to deliver. Failures go to console.error and that is all. I chose silence over callbacks because I did not want analytics error handling in people's plugins, and I am still not sure it was the right call.

Sessions need a UI. A plugin that runs a command with no panel has no iframe to hold a socket, so it gets events and no session length.

And a reconnect still shows up as a separate row on the server. The shared session_id makes it fixable, and I have not built the merge yet.

If you want to look at the code

The SDK is MIT licensed and lives at github.com/kolebayev/tode-sdk. The service behind it is tode. It has a free plan for one plugin, and the paid plans are how I cover the servers.

If you came here for the Google Analytics error and want the long answer, I wrote up what the Measurement Protocol can and cannot do inside a plugin.

I would like to hear from people who build extensions for other hosts, like VS Code, Chrome or Sketch. How do you find out whether anyone uses what you shipped?

articles.title: A liquid glass tab bar: the magnifying lens is a scaled copy of the bar
articles.description: How the lens in a liquid glass tab bar magnifies the icon under it without SVG filters, and how a spring's velocity stretches it like a drop. Plain HTML/CSS/JS demo, plus the Framer Motion version.
articles.body_html:
Apple's liquid glass tab bars have a lens that sits on the selected tab and magnifies the icon under it. When you switch tabs it moves like a drop of water: it stretches on the way, then settles.

Most web versions of this effect use an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter. That only renders in Chromium browsers; Safari and Firefox skip it. I built one for a music-app demo and wanted it to look the same in every browser, so the lens uses no filter at all. It's a small window onto a second copy of the bar, scaled up 1.42 times.

This post covers three pieces:

  1. The glass bar (plain backdrop-filter).
  2. The lens: a clipped, scaled copy, and the one line of math that keeps it lined up.
  3. The drop: a spring whose speed sets the lens width.

There's a single-file demo at the end you can paste into CodePen. If you build with Cursor or Claude Code, it also works as a reference file to hand to your agent: it's short, and every number in it is explained here.

1. The glass bar

The bar itself is ordinary frosted glass. Blur plus saturation does most of the work. The inset shadows draw a light top edge and a faint 1px rim so the bar reads as a solid object on any background.

This is the CSS from the shipped component (tabbar-liquid.css):

.glassbar {
  position: absolute;
  border-radius: 32px;
  background: var(--glass);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.22),
    inset 0 0 0 1px var(--glass-line),
    0 18px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.45);
}

saturate(1.9) matters more than it looks. Blur alone washes colours out to grey. Saturation brings back the colour of whatever scrolls underneath, which is what makes it read as glass and not as a grey panel.

Keep the -webkit- prefix. Safari still wants it.

2. The lens is a copy, not a filter

Real magnification would need a displacement filter on whatever sits behind the lens. You can fake the part people actually notice, the icon under the lens getting bigger, with plain transforms:

  • Render the tabs a second time inside the lens element.
  • Give the lens overflow: hidden so you only see the part under it.
  • Scale the copy by M (1.42 here) around the lens centre.

The markup is a lens with an inner layer that holds the copy:

<div class="lens" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="lensIn"><!-- the same tabs again, not focusable --></div>
</div>

The copy must stay out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order, or a screen reader reads every tab twice. In the React component the copy is rendered with live={false}, which does exactly that:

const inert = live ? {} : { tabIndex: -1, 'aria-hidden': true as const };

The one line of math

.lensIn has transform-origin: 0 0 and fills the same box as the real bar. The lens has width w, height h, and centre (x, y) in bar coordinates, so its top-left corner is (lx, ly) = (x - w/2, y - h/2).

You want the point under the lens centre to stay where it is, with everything around it pushed outwards by M. Here's the render code from the shipped engine.ts:

const Ls = S.lens, lx = Ls.x - Ls.w / 2, ly = Ls.y - Ls.h / 2, M = 1.42;
lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx.toFixed(1)}px,${ly.toFixed(1)}px) scale(${Ls.sx.toFixed(4)},${Ls.sy.toFixed(4)})`;
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${(-lx + Ls.x - M * Ls.x).toFixed(2)}px,${(-ly + Ls.y - M * Ls.y).toFixed(2)}px) scale(${M})`;

Why it works: a point p of the copy lands at M·p + t inside the lens, and the lens sits at lx. On screen that is lx + M·p + (-lx + x - M·x), which simplifies to x + M·(p - x). At p = x you get x, so the centre stays put and everything else spreads out from it by M. It's the textbook "scale around a point" transform, with the lens offset cancelled out.

Since the copy is real DOM, you can style it apart from the bar. Trimmed from the shipped CSS (the comments are mine):

.lens {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; overflow: hidden; pointer-events: none;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,.07);
  backdrop-filter: blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 2px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.75),     /* bright top rim */
    inset 0 -2px 0 rgba(198,244,50,.55),     /* lime bottom rim */
    inset 0 -12px 20px rgba(139,108,255,.4),
    inset 5px 0 9px rgba(255,90,170,.35),    /* pink left edge */
    inset -5px 0 9px rgba(90,220,255,.35),   /* cyan right edge */
    0 0 0 1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.4),
    0 12px 28px rgba(0,0,0,.5),
    0 0 34px rgba(198,244,50,.42);
}
.lensIn { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; transform-origin: 0 0; }
.lensIn .tab { color: var(--volt); }        /* the magnified icon turns lime */
.lensIn .tab i { opacity: 0 !important; }   /* hide the label inside the lens */
.lensIn .tab svg { translate: 0 8px; }      /* and drop the icon into the middle */
.lensIn .dockc {
  filter: drop-shadow(1.6px 0 0 rgba(255,70,150,.6))
          drop-shadow(-1.6px 0 0 rgba(70,210,255,.6));
}

Two details from that block:

  • The pink and cyan inset shadows on the left and right edges, plus two 1.6px drop-shadows on the copy, fake the colour fringing you see where real glass bends light. They're cheap and they sell the effect more than anything else in the file.
  • The label is hidden inside the lens and the icon moves down 8px. A magnified label gets cut off by the lens edge and looks like a bug. A centred icon looks deliberate.

The cost of this approach is that the content renders twice. For five icons that's nothing. The same component reuses the trick for a bigger orb that lifts out of the bar: the orb's copy holds the whole screen, scaled with the same formula.

3. The drop: speed sets the width

A lens that slides at a fixed width looks like a highlight pill. It reads as liquid once it stretches while it moves and goes back to round when it stops.

In the React version the lens x-position is a Framer Motion spring, and useVelocity reads how fast that spring is moving:

// live mode: the lens rides a spring, and its speed stretches the drop
const x = useSpring(tabX(0), { stiffness: 380, damping: 26 });
const stretch = useVelocity(x);

Every frame, the speed (px/s) maps to the lens size:

const v = Math.abs(stretch.get());
S.lens = {
  x: lx, y: g.cy,
  w: mix(66 + Math.min(92, v / 9), 56, c),
  h: mix(52 - Math.min(10, v / 90), 56, c),
  /* ... */
};

Leave out mix(..., c) for now. That's the compact state, when the bar shrinks on scroll. What's left:

  • At rest the lens is 66 × 52.
  • It gets 1px wider for every 9 px/s of speed, up to 92px more.
  • It gets thinner by up to 10px, so a fast move reads as a long, thin drop.
  • The clamps stop a very fast flick from stretching it across the whole bar.

The spring's overshoot does the rest. With stiffness 380 and damping 26 the spring is underdamped (damping ratio about 0.67), so it passes the target a little and comes back. The width follows the speed, so you get a wobble on landing without writing one keyframe.

Switching tabs is one line: x.set(tabX(i)).

Keyboard and screen readers

The real tabs are a tablist. Each tab gets role="tab" and aria-selected, and left/right arrows move between them:

if (e.key !== 'ArrowRight' && e.key !== 'ArrowLeft') return;
e.preventDefault(); i = (i + (e.key === 'ArrowRight' ? 1 : 4)) % 5;
screen.current?.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-dock] [data-tab]')[i]?.focus();

(+ 4 is - 1 modulo 5, so left arrow from the first tab wraps to the last.)

The lens, the copy and the rings are all aria-hidden. Only the real tabs are announced.

The single-file version

No Framer Motion here. The spring is about ten lines of Hooke's law with damping, using the same stiffness and damping as the React version. Paste it into CodePen's HTML panel or save it as a .html file and open it:

const centerOf = (i) => tabs[i].offsetLeft + tabs[i].offsetWidth / 2;
let active = 0;

function select(i, focus) {
  active = (i + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
  tabs.forEach((t, j) => { t.setAttribute('aria-selected', j === active); t.tabIndex = j === active ? 0 : -1; });
  if (focus) tabs[active].focus();
  spring.target = centerOf(active);
  if (reduce.matches) { spring.x = spring.target; spring.v = 0; }
}

function paint() {
  const W = dock.clientWidth, H = dock.clientHeight;
  lensIn.style.width = W + 'px'; lensIn.style.height = H + 'px';
  const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);                        // px per second
  const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);                  // faster = longer drop
  const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);                 // ...and a little thinner
  const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));      // keep the drop inside the bar
  const y = H / 2, lx = x - w / 2, ly = y - h / 2;
  lens.style.width = w + 'px'; lens.style.height = h + 'px';
  lens.style.borderRadius = Math.min(w, h) / 2 + 'px';
  lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx}px, ${ly}px)`;

  lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;

let last = performance.now();
function frame(now) {
  const dt = Math.min(0.032, (now - last) / 1000); last = now;
  const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;   // Hooke + damping, mass 1
  spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;
  paint();
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

// tap, drag across the bar, or use the arrow keys
const nearest = (clientX) => {
  const r = dock.getBoundingClientRect(), px = clientX - r.left;
  return tabs.reduce((best, t, i) => Math.abs(centerOf(i) - px) < Math.abs(centerOf(best) - px) ? i : best, 0);
};
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => { tabsEl.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => { if (e.buttons) select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') { e.preventDefault(); select(active + 1, true); }
  if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft')  { e.preventDefault(); select(active - 1, true); }
});
addEventListener('resize', () => { spring.target = spring.x = centerOf(active); });

spring.x = spring.target = centerOf(0);
requestAnimationFrame(frame);
</script>

The parts worth reading in the demo:

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })
const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;
spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;

const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);              // px per second
const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);        // faster = longer drop
const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);       // ...and a little thinner
const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));   // keep the drop inside the bar
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;

The demo adds three things the shipped component doesn't have:

  • Drag along the bar and the lens follows your finger to the nearest tab, stretching over every tab it passes.
  • It clamps the drop inside the bar, because a 158px drop on the last tab hangs off the edge.
  • With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce it jumps straight to the new tab, with no stretch and no wobble. Do that in anything you ship. A drop that stretches across the screen is exactly the kind of motion that setting is for.

Easy ways to get it wrong

  • Scaling the copy around its own centre. The magnified icon drifts sideways as the lens moves. Use transform-origin: 0 0 and put the whole offset in the translate.
  • A CSS transition on the lens width. The width then lags behind the position. Set width, height and transform in the same frame, all read from the spring.
  • A focusable copy. Keyboard users tab through ten tabs instead of five. Mark the copy aria-hidden and give every button in it tabindex="-1".
  • Labels inside the lens. They get cut by the lens edge. Hide them in the copy.

About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign. The tab bar in this post is one of them, so this is partly a post about my own product. The demo above is MIT: copy it, change it, ship it. The full component adds the orb that turns into a full-screen player, the compact bar on scroll, the badge pop, a React + TypeScript + Tailwind + Framer Motion version, and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools. It's $3 on qodesign.dev. This week I'm also putting a few components on GitHub for free (MIT): two dashboards, a toast stack, a pricing switch and an upload dropzone. I'll add the link here when the repo is public.

If you build a lens with a real displacement map that works in Safari, I'd like to see it.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code excerpts are copied from the shipped component, and the demo was run and checked in a browser before publishing.

articles.body_html:
I'm a student in India and I kept doing two things by hand.

One: clone a repo, open the README, find out it needs a .env with eleven keys, a Postgres, and a pnpm version I don't have, spend twenty minutes, give up or not.

Two: see a landing page I like, open devtools, and poke around to see how they did the grid, what font that is, where the pricing data comes from.

So I wrote one command that does both.

npx breakinggood https://github.com/someone/some-repo
npx breakinggood https://tailwindcss.com

First one clones, scans the dependencies, sets up .env, installs, runs, opens the browser. Second one captures the page with your own Chrome and writes a Vite + React + Tailwind project that matches it, with a mock API server that replays the real API responses. It's MIT, on npm, repo is eklavya2201/breakinggood.

This post is about the second half, the website capture, because that's where all the interesting decisions were. The repo half is at the end.

Why not just screenshot-to-code

There are a lot of "paste a screenshot, get React" tools. I tried a few before writing this and the output always looked roughly right and was wrong in every detail. A picture loses:

  • the actual font (the model guesses Inter, every time)
  • exact colours (it eyeballs #1a1a1a as #000)
  • spacing and radii
  • all the text below the fold
  • and, the one that annoyed me most, the data. The pricing cards are hard-coded. The testimonials are lorem ipsum with a hat on.

A browser has all of that. So the capture doesn't start from a picture. It starts from the page.

The capture, step by step

Everything lives in one file, src/site/capture.ts, about 330 lines of Playwright.

1. Use the Chrome that's already installed. playwright-core can drive an installed Chrome or Edge through the channel option. So the first launch attempt is chromium.launch({ channel: "chrome" }), then msedge, then a Playwright Chromium if one happens to exist. Nobody downloads 150 MB of browser for a CLI they're trying once. There's a BREAKINGGOOD_BROWSER env var if you want to point it at a specific binary.

2. Record the network before navigating. A page.on("response") listener runs from the start. It keeps only xhr and fetch resource types, and for JSON responses under status 400 it reads the body and keeps the first 6000 characters. Everything else (images, scripts, CSS) is ignored. Then it deduplicates by method + URL-without-query and caps at 40 requests. This is the list that becomes the mock server later.

3. Load, settle, scroll. goto with domcontentloaded, then wait for networkidle with a 15 s cap (it's best-effort, SPAs never go idle). Then it clicks through a short list of cookie-banner button labels ("Accept all", "I agree", "Got it"...) because otherwise half of every screenshot is a GDPR modal. Then it scrolls the page in 700 px steps down to 12000 px so lazy-loaded sections actually render, and scrolls back to the top.

4. Read the computed styles, not the CSS. This is the part I'd argue is the whole trick. One page.evaluate walks the first 4000 elements in the body and calls getComputedStyle on each. For every leaf element with text it counts the font family, text colour, and font size. For every element with a non-transparent background it adds the background colour weighted by the element's area. Border radii get counted too. Then it takes the top N of each map.

Weighting backgrounds by area matters. Without it, the most common background is whatever colour the 300 tiny icon wrappers have. With it, the page background and the hero colour come out first. Text colour is weighted by count instead, because body text is a lot of small elements and that's correct.

The result is a small token block that goes into the prompt:

fonts: Inter | JetBrains Mono
text colours: rgb(15, 23, 42) | rgb(100, 116, 139) | ...
backgrounds (by area): rgb(255, 255, 255) | rgb(248, 250, 252) | ...
border radii: 8px | 12px | 9999px
content max-width: 1280px
dark mode: false

Dark mode is decided from the luminance of the page background, which is the body background, else the html background, else the largest painted background. Transparent counts as white.

5. A simplified DOM. The full HTML of a modern page is hundreds of KB of class soup. The capture walks the body recursively and keeps only the tag name, a handful of attributes (href, src, alt, placeholder, type, role, aria-label, title), and the text. Scripts, styles, SVG internals, iframes go. Anything display: none goes. Classes go, all of them, because Tailwind classes from the original are noise once you have the computed tokens. Text nodes are capped at 300 characters, depth at 14, and the whole thing at 45 KB.

The model gets this plus a semantic outline (every header, nav, section, h1-h3 with its first 80 characters), the first 80 links, and the first 40 real images with their natural sizes. Images use the original public URLs, so the rebuild shows the real pictures.

6. Tiled screenshots. Full-page screenshots of long pages are 8000+ px tall and the vision APIs reject or downscale them. So the page is sliced from the top into JPEG tiles, 1800 px tall at 1440 wide, max four tiles. Then the viewport switches to 390 x 844 and takes three more tiles for mobile. JPEG at quality 82 keeps each tile under a few hundred KB. The mobile tiles are what tell the model how the grid collapses.

7. Fingerprints. Cheap checks: __NEXT_DATA__, #__nuxt, __remixContext, data-wf-site, wp-content, a generator meta tag. They go in the prompt as "likely original stack" and don't do much, but they're nice to see in the output.

The prompt

The system prompt is about 30 lines. It asks for a fixed set of files (package.json, vite config, src/App.jsx, one component per major section, mock/db.json, mock/server.js), Tailwind v4 with an @theme block built from the captured palette and fonts, real text from the DOM, original image URLs, and a dependency-free Node HTTP server on port 8787 that serves every captured API path from db.json. The Vite config proxies /api to it. The React code has to fetch from /api/... wherever the original site fetched data, so the clone actually makes network calls instead of hard-coding the pricing table.

Two lines in that prompt took the most iterations:

Stay compact: aim for under 1500 lines in total. Put repeated content (nav items, feature cards, logos, testimonials, footer columns) in plain arrays and render with .map().

Without that, tailwindcss.com produced a 3000-line App.jsx and the model ran out of output tokens halfway through the footer. With it, it's around 900 lines across eight files.

File format. The model writes:

=== FILE: src/App.jsx ===
...
=== END FILE ===

Not JSON. JSON means every file is one giant escaped string, and a single unescaped quote in a 1000-line response kills the whole thing. The delimiter format is parsed with one regex, tolerates a stray code fence inside a block, and refuses any path with ... If package.json or src/App.jsx is missing from the output, it fails loudly instead of running half a project.

Providers. The capture is the same regardless of model. There's a thin provider layer for Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini and Ollama, picked from whichever API key you have in your environment. Screenshots only go to models that take images. Text-only models still get the DOM, the tokens and the API bodies, and the output is noticeably worse but usable.

What went wrong

  • 8000 px screenshots. First version sent one full-page PNG. The API silently downscaled it to a blur. Tiles fixed it.
  • The model running out of output. See the "stay compact" line above. maxTokens is 128k but the fix was asking for less, not allowing more.
  • Workspace packages flagged as foreign. On the repo side, the scanner looked at resolved in the lockfile and flagged packages/foo workspace links as non-registry packages. Now it only flags entries whose resolved has a URL scheme that isn't the npm or yarn registry.
  • Cookie banners in every screenshot. The label list above. It's not clever and it works on most sites.
  • The hero is a video or a canvas. Nothing to do. The screenshot shows a frame, the DOM shows a <video>, the model puts a placeholder. Fine.

The repo side, briefly

npx breakinggood <github url> shallow-clones, detects the stack (Node package manager from lockfiles, Python, Go, Rust, Docker Compose), and before installing anything runs a scan in src/repo/scan.ts:

  • lockfile packages with hasInstallScript: true that aren't on a list of about 70 well-known native packages (esbuild, sharp, prisma, playwright...)
  • packages whose resolved URL is outside the public registry
  • direct dependencies published less than 90 days ago (one registry fetch per dep, 6 s total budget, skipped silently if offline)
  • preinstall / postinstall / prepare hooks that match curl ... | sh, powershell -enc, base64 -d, eval(atob(
  • setup.py / pyproject.toml calling os.system, subprocess, urllib, exec
  • source files with 200+ character base64 blobs or long \x escape runs
  • a committed real .env

High findings ask before continuing. It is not a sandbox and I say so in the README. It catches the obvious stuff, which is the stuff that actually shows up in the npm incidents I've read about.

Then it copies .env.example to .env, fills anything named like a secret (SECRET, JWT, SESSION, SALT, and so on) with a random value so the app at least boots, installs, runs the dev script, watches its output for the localhost URL or port it prints, and opens the browser there.

Limits

  • Pages behind a login, Cloudflare challenges, and bot walls don't capture. There's an open issue to at least detect the challenge page and say so instead of rebuilding it.
  • Heavy canvas or WebGL pages come out as a static frame.
  • It rebuilds structure and style of public pages. The content and the brand belong to whoever owns the site. There's a --sanitize flag that swaps the brand name and logo for neutral placeholders, and every clone writes a provenance file saying where it came from.
  • The quality ceiling is the model. Same capture, different model, visibly different output.

Try it 

npx breakinggood https://tailwindcss.com

The README has untouched before/after screenshots of Hacker News and tailwindcss.com. If you run it on something and it does badly, open an issue with the URL, that's the most useful thing right now. There are a few good first issues too: Svelte output, a --framework next option, Deno and Bun detection.

articles.title: Turn a list of company names into hiring signals (8 ATS platforms, no scraping of HTML)
articles.description: If you sell B2B software, recruit, or invest, who is hiring what is one of the best public signals...
articles.body_html:
If you sell B2B software, recruit, or invest, who is hiring what is one of the best public signals there is. A company opening five data-engineering roles in a month is buying data tooling. A company posting its first "Head of Sales" is about to build a go-to-market team.

The good news: most companies publish their jobs through an applicant tracking system (ATS) that exposes a public, unauthenticated JSON feed for their careers page. No HTML parsing, no headless browser, no proxies.

This post shows:

  1. the public endpoints for 8 ATS platforms,
  2. how to figure out which ATS a company uses from just its name or domain,
  3. how to turn raw postings into company-level signals (velocity, function mix, tech stack).

1. The public job-board endpoints

ATS Endpoint
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}?includeCompensation=true
Workable https://apply.workable.com/api/v1/widget/accounts/{slug}?details=true
SmartRecruiters https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/{CompanyId}/postings
Recruitee https://{slug}.recruitee.com/api/offers/
Personio https://{slug}.jobs.personio.de/xml (or .com)
Teamtailor https://{slug}.teamtailor.com/jobs.rss

A few things I learned the hard way:

  • Unknown slugs: seven of them return 404. SmartRecruiters returns 200 with totalFound: 0, so check the count, not the status.
  • SmartRecruiters' list endpoint has no description; you need one extra call per posting (/postings/{id}) if you want the text.
  • Recruitee and Teamtailor career sites often live on the company's own domain (careers.company.com). The same feeds work there: https://careers.company.com/api/offers/ and https://careers.company.com/jobs.rss.
  • Greenhouse double-escapes HTML in content (<p>), so decode entities before stripping tags.
  • Lever's EU instance is api.eu.lever.co.

2. Which ATS does this company use?

Given only a name ("Hugging Face") or a domain ("linear.app"):

  1. Derive slug candidates: huggingface, hugging-face; for a domain, the first label (linear). Strip suffixes like Inc, GmbH, Ltd.
  2. Probe every ATS with every candidate, in parallel with a small concurrency limit.
  3. If several boards match (old boards are surprisingly common), prefer the one whose job URLs point at the company's own domain, then the one with the most jobs. 
const PROBES = {
  greenhouse: (s) => `https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/${s}/jobs`,
  lever: (s) => `https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/${s}?mode=json`,
  ashby: (s) => `https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/${s}`,
  workable: (s) => `https://apply.workable.com/api/v1/widget/accounts/${s}`,
  recruitee: (s) => `https://${s}.recruitee.com/api/offers/`,
};

function slugCandidates(name) {
  const base = name.replace(/^www\./, '').split('.')[0];
  const words = base.replace(/\b(inc|ltd|gmbh|llc)\b\.?/gi, ' ').toLowerCase().split(/[^a-z0-9]+/).filter(Boolean);
  return [...new Set([words.join(''), words.join('-')])];
}

async function detect(name) {
  const hits = [];
  for (const slug of slugCandidates(name)) {
    await Promise.all(Object.entries(PROBES).map(async ([ats, url]) => {
      const res = await fetch(url(slug));
      if (!res.ok) return;
      const data = await res.json();
      const jobs = data.jobs ?? data.offers ?? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : []);
      hits.push({ ats, slug, count: jobs.length });
    }));
  }
  return hits.sort((a, b) => b.count - a.count)[0] ?? null;
}

console.log(await detect('Hugging Face')); // { ats: 'workable', slug: 'huggingface', count: 6 }

For a careers-page URL, fetch the HTML first and look for embeds such as boards.greenhouse.io/embed/job_board?for=…, jobs.lever.co/… or jobs.ashbyhq.com/…. It is usually right there.

3. From postings to signals

Raw postings get interesting once you aggregate them per company:

  • Velocity: jobs posted in the last 7 / 30 / 90 days. Compare the last 30 days with the average of the previous 60 to label the trend accelerating, steady or slowing.
  • Function mix: classify each title (engineering, data, sales, marketing, customer…) with keyword rules. A spike in sales and marketing roles means go-to-market expansion.
  • Leadership hiring: Head of, Director, VP titles often come before budget decisions.
  • Tech stack: match a dictionary of technologies against descriptions. Watch for common-word traps: "go", "rust", "spark", "slack" and "excel" need case-sensitive or contextual patterns, or you will "detect" Go in every job that says go above and beyond.
  • Salaries: Ashby and Recruitee expose structured compensation; elsewhere, parse ranges from the text, but require an explicit currency, or "5-7 years" becomes a salary.
  • Change tracking: store the job IDs per company and diff on the next run to get new and closed roles.

Here is what a company row looks like once you put it together (real output, Notion, October 2026):

{
  "companyName": "Notion",
  "ats": "ashby",
  "openJobs": 129,
  "jobsPostedLast7Days": 7,
  "jobsPostedLast30Days": 31,
  "engineeringShare": 38,
  "salesAndMarketingJobs": 48,
  "leadershipJobs": 8,
  "topFunctions": "engineering (46), sales (41), people (11), finance (7), marketing (7), customer (4)",
  "techStack": "Python, Salesforce, TypeScript, SQL, Node.js, LLMs, React, ...",
  "salaryMin": 85000,
  "salaryMax": 400000,
  "signals": "7 new roles posted in the last 7 days • Hiring 46 engineering roles • Hiring 41 sales roles • Leadership hiring: General Manager, DACH; Head of Early Career Recruiting; Head of Demand Engine • Go-to-market expansion: 48 sales/marketing roles (37% of openings) • Hiring across 9 countries"
}

Don't want to maintain it?

I packaged all of the above (8 platforms, name/domain/careers-page auto-detection, enrichment, change tracking) as an Apify actor: Hiring Signals. Paste company names and get job rows plus one signal row per company, as CSV, JSON, or straight into Sheets or Clay. There are also single-platform versions for Workable (with keyword search across all Workable employers), SmartRecruiters, Recruitee and Personio.

All of these read only publicly published job postings, with no logins and no personal contact data.

Written with AI assistance; the endpoints and outputs were verified against live data before publishing.
